children.title: Matroid Cryptomorphism-Structure Theory
children.top_down_role: Equivalent finite-matroid descriptions and the local exchange structures needed by later duality, polyhedral, and algorithmic branches.

children.title: Independent-Set View
children.top_down_role: Independence-system presentation of finite matroids.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid precisely when \(\mathcal I\) satisfies the three independence axioms.

notation.meaning: family of independent subsets of the ground set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-matroid independence-axiom view.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \(\mathcal I\subseteq 2^E\) is the independent-set family of a matroid on \(E\) if: \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\); whenever \(I\in\mathcal I\) and \(J\subseteq I\), one has \(J\in\mathcal I\); and whenever \(I,J\in\mathcal I\) with \(|I|<|J|\), there exists \(e\in J\setminus I\) such that \(I\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). Members of \(\mathcal I\) are called independent sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite matroid is specified by a nonempty hereditary family satisfying augmentation: a smaller independent set can acquire an element from any larger independent set.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Set View

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Dependent-Set View
children.top_down_role: Dependence-system presentation complementary to the independent-set perspective.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal D=2^E\setminus\mathcal I\), and \(X\in\mathcal D\) exactly when \(X\) is not independent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence as the complement of independence in \(2^E\).

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dependent-set family is \(\mathcal D:=2^E\setminus\mathcal I\). Thus \(D\subseteq E\) is dependent exactly when \(D\notin\mathcal I\). Equivalently, \(\mathcal D\) is upward closed: if \(D\in\mathcal D\) and \(D\subseteq X\subseteq E\), then \(X\in\mathcal D\). Moreover, every \(D\in\mathcal D\) contains an inclusion-minimal member of \(\mathcal D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dependent sets are exactly the nonindependent subsets. They are closed under taking supersets, and every dependent set contains an inclusion-minimal dependent set.
knowledge_statements.title: Dependent-Set View

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Set-View Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural translation between independent-set data and dependent-set data.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-View Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complement correspondence between independent and dependent subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\mathcal D:=2^E\setminus\mathcal I\). Then, for every \(X\subseteq E\), \[X\in\mathcal I\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X\notin\mathcal D.\] Conversely, starting from this dependent-set family and defining \(\mathcal I':=2^E\setminus\mathcal D\) recovers \(\mathcal I'=\mathcal I\). Hence the independent-set and dependent-set views contain exactly the same set-system data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent and dependent subsets partition the power set, so taking complements converts either representation into the other without losing information.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal I\subseteq 2^E\) satisfies the matroid independence axioms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal D=2^E\setminus\mathcal I\) and \(\mathcal I=2^E\setminus\mathcal D\), so either family uniquely determines the other.

children.title: Basis Families
children.top_down_role: Presentation of matroids through their collections of bases.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B\) is a matroid basis family exactly when it satisfies basis exchange.

notation.meaning: replace an element in a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matroids represented axiomatically by their bases.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty family \(\mathcal B\subseteq 2^E\) is a matroid basis family if, for all \(B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B\) and every \(x\in B_1\setminus B_2\), there exists \(y\in B_2\setminus B_1\) such that \((B_1\setminus\{x\})\cup\{y\}\in\mathcal B\). The members of \(\mathcal B\) are called bases; the exchange axiom implies that all of them have the same cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty collection is a matroid basis family when any element exclusive to one basis can be exchanged for a suitable element exclusive to another basis.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Families

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Maximal Independent Sets
children.top_down_role: Maximal members of the independent-set system.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is maximal independent exactly when \(B\in\mathcal I\) and \(B\cup\{e\}\notin\mathcal I\) for every \(e\in E\setminus B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion maximality within the independent-set family.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(B\subseteq E\) is a maximal independent set if \(B\in\mathcal I\) and no strict superset of \(B\) belongs to \(\mathcal I\). By heredity, this is equivalent to the one-element condition \[B\in\mathcal I\quad\text{and}\quad B\cup\{e\}\notin\mathcal I\ \text{ for every }e\in E\setminus B.\] Maximality here is by inclusion, not merely maximal cardinality among a separately specified subfamily.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal independent set is independent but ceases to be independent after adding any ground-set element outside it.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Independent Sets

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Basis–Maximality Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural identification of bases with maximal independent sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B=\max_{\subseteq}(\mathcal I)\), and \(\mathcal I=\{I\subseteq E: I\subseteq B\text{ for some }B\in\mathcal B\}\).

notation.meaning: inclusion-maximal members of a set family

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cryptomorphic recovery of bases from independence and conversely.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bases are exactly the inclusion-maximal independent sets: \[\mathcal B=\max_{\subseteq}(\mathcal I).\] Every independent set extends to a basis, and therefore the inverse recovery formula is \[\mathcal I=\{I\subseteq E: I\subseteq B\text{ for some }B\in\mathcal B\}.\] Consequently, the independence family and basis family uniquely determine one another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bases are precisely the maximal independent sets, while all independent sets are recovered as subsets of bases.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis–Maximality Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Bases as Maximal Independent Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bases through inclusion-maximal independence, states their equicardinality, and formulates the minimum-weight basis problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(E,\mathcal I)$ be a matroid. An independent set $I\in\mathcal I$ is maximal if $I\cup\{e\}\notin\mathcal I$ for every $e\in E\setminus I$. Every maximal independent set has the same cardinality, and the maximal independent sets are called bases. Given element weights $w:E\to\mathbb R$, the matroid optimization problem is $\min\{\sum_{e\in B}w(e):B\text{ is a basis}\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal independent set cannot be enlarged by another ground-set element while preserving independence. In a matroid, all maximal independent sets have equal size and are called bases; minimum-weight matroid optimization seeks a basis of least total weight.
assumptions_latex: w:E\to\mathbb R\text{ for the optimization formulation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I\text{ is a basis}\iff I\in\mathcal I\ \land\ \forall e\in E\setminus I,\ I\cup\{e\}\notin\mathcal I;\qquad \min_{B\text{ basis}}\sum_{e\in B}w(e)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basis of a Matroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a matroid basis as a maximal member of its independent-set family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M=(E,\mathcal I) be a matroid. A set B\subseteq E is a basis of M if and only if B\in\mathcal I and there is no B'\in\mathcal I with B\subsetneq B'.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis of a matroid is a maximal independent set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\text{ is a basis of }M\iff B\in\mathcal I\text{ and }\nexists B'\in\mathcal I\text{ such that }B\subsetneq B'

children.title: Ordinary Basis Exchange
children.top_down_role: The standard single-element exchange regime for bases.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each \(x\in B_1\setminus B_2\), some \(y\in B_2\setminus B_1\) makes \(B_1-x+y\) a basis.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard one-sided basis-exchange property.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B(M)\) and every \(x\in B_1\setminus B_2\), there exists \(y\in B_2\setminus B_1\) such that \[B_1-x+y\in\mathcal B(M).\] Only the exchanged version of \(B_1\) is required to be a basis in this ordinary form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given two bases, any element belonging only to the first can be replaced by a suitable element belonging only to the second.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Basis Exchange

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Symmetric Basis Exchange
children.top_down_role: Exchange regimes preserving bases on both sides of a swap.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each \(x\in B_1\setminus B_2\), some \(y\in B_2\setminus B_1\) simultaneously preserves both exchanged bases.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric single-element basis-exchange theorem.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B(M)\) and every \(x\in B_1\setminus B_2\), there exists \(y\in B_2\setminus B_1\) such that both \[B_1-x+y\in\mathcal B(M)\quad\text{and}\quad B_2-y+x\in\mathcal B(M).\] Thus one choice of \(y\) makes the reciprocal exchanges valid simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two bases and an element exclusive to the first, one can choose an element exclusive to the second so that exchanging them preserves both bases.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Basis Exchange

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Multiple Basis Exchange
children.top_down_role: Simultaneous exchange of subsets between bases.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Some \(Y\subseteq B_2\setminus B_1\) makes both \((B_1\setminus X)\cup Y\) and \((B_2\setminus Y)\cup X\) bases.

notation.meaning: a selected subset exchanged from the first basis
the matching subset exchanged from the second basis

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong multiple symmetric basis-exchange theorem.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists \(Y\subseteq B_2\setminus B_1\) such that \(|Y|=|X|\) and both \[(B_1\setminus X)\cup Y\in\mathcal B(M)\quad\text{and}\quad (B_2\setminus Y)\cup X\in\mathcal B(M).\] Hence an arbitrarily prescribed subset of one basis can be exchanged for an equally large subset of another while preserving both bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any selected subset exclusive to one basis can be swapped with an equally large subset exclusive to another so that both resulting sets remain bases.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Basis Exchange

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Exchange-Regime Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Comparative strength and applicability of the principal basis-exchange regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Exchange-Regime Hierarchy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specialization hierarchy among basis-exchange formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite matroids, the exchange regimes satisfy \[\mathrm{MBE}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{SBE}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{BE}.\] Here \(\mathrm{SBE}\) is the singleton specialization of \(\mathrm{MBE}\), while \(\mathrm{BE}\) retains only the one-sided exchanged-basis conclusion of \(\mathrm{SBE}\). Every finite matroid satisfies all three regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple symmetric exchange specializes to symmetric single-element exchange, whose one-sided conclusion is ordinary basis exchange; every finite matroid satisfies all three regimes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{MBE}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{SBE}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{BE}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Circuit Created by Extending an Independent Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuit recovery after a one-element extension makes an independent set dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matroid, let \(I\subseteq E(M)\) be independent, and let \(e\in E(M)\) satisfy that \(I\cup\{e\}\) is dependent. Then exactly one circuit of \(M\) is contained in \(I\cup\{e\}\), and that circuit contains \(e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If adding one element to an independent set creates dependence, the enlarged set contains exactly one circuit, and that circuit contains the added element.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left|\{C\in\mathcal C(M):C\subseteq I\cup\{e\}\}\right|=1\), and the unique such \(C\) satisfies \(e\in C\).

children.title: Minimal Dependent Sets
children.top_down_role: Circuits viewed through inclusion-minimal dependence.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is a circuit exactly when \(C\in\mathcal D\) and every proper subset of \(C\) lies in \(\mathcal I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuits as inclusion-minimal dependent sets.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A subset \(C\subseteq E\) is a circuit of \(M\) if it is inclusion-minimal in \(\mathcal D\). Equivalently, \[C\in\mathcal C(M)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C\notin\mathcal I\ \text{ and }\ C\setminus\{e\}\in\mathcal I\ \text{ for every }e\in C.\] Thus every proper subset of a circuit is independent, while the circuit itself is dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A circuit is a dependent set all of whose proper subsets are independent; equivalently, it is an inclusion-minimal dependent set.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Dependent Sets

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuits as minimal dependent sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes recovery of independent sets from circuits and uniqueness of the circuit representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matroid \(M\), a circuit is an inclusion-minimal dependent subset of \(E(M)\), and the circuit family is denoted \(\mathcal C(M)\). A circuit of cardinality \(n\) is an \(n\)-circuit. For every \(I\subseteq E(M)\), \(I\) is independent if and only if it contains no circuit of \(M\). Hence \(M\) is uniquely determined by \(\mathcal C(M)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A circuit is a minimal dependent set. A subset is independent exactly when it contains no circuit, so the circuit family uniquely determines the matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I\in\mathcal I(M)\iff \nexists C\in\mathcal C(M)\text{ such that }C\subseteq I;\quad \mathcal C(M)\text{ uniquely determines }M.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuit of an Independence System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuits as inclusion-minimal dependent sets, with the graphic-matroid specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an independence system $(S,\mathcal I)$, a circuit is an inclusion-minimal dependent set $C\subseteq S$. Equivalently, $C\notin\mathcal I$ and every proper subset of $C$ belongs to $\mathcal I$. In the forest matroid of a graph $G$, these circuits are exactly the graph-theoretic circuits of $G$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A circuit of an independence system is an inclusion-minimal dependent set. In a forest matroid, the matroid circuits are exactly the graph's circuits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is a circuit}\iff C\notin\mathcal I\text{ and }(\forall D\subsetneq C)\ D\in\mathcal I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The fundamental-circuit property for an element whose addition makes an independent set dependent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuits of an Independence System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines circuits as inclusion-minimal dependent sets and records conditional loop and graphic-matroid specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an independence system $M=(E(M),\mathcal I(M))$, the dependent sets are $2^{E(M)}\setminus\mathcal I(M)$, and the circuit family is
\[
\mathcal C(M):=\{X\subseteq E(M):X\notin\mathcal I(M)\text{ and }X\setminus\{e\}\in\mathcal I(M)\ \forall e\in X\}.
\]
Thus circuits are the inclusion-minimal dependent sets. A one-element circuit of a matroid is called a loop. If $M$ is the graphic matroid of a graph $G$, then its circuits are the cycles of $G$, and its loops are precisely the graph loops.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an independence system, circuits are the inclusion-minimal dependent sets. A one-element matroid circuit is a loop. In a graphic matroid, circuits are graph cycles and matroid loops are graph loops.
assumptions_latex: M=(E(M),\mathcal I(M))\text{ is an independence system}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal C(M)=\{X\subseteq E(M):X\notin\mathcal I(M),\ X\setminus\{e\}\in\mathcal I(M)\ \forall e\in X\}

children.title: Circuit Elimination
children.top_down_role: The elimination structure governing circuit families.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(C_3\in\mathcal C(M)\) with \(C_3\subseteq(C_1\cup C_2)\setminus\{e\}\).

notation.meaning: two distinct circuits sharing an element

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak circuit-elimination axiom for finite matroids.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are distinct circuits and \(e\in C_1\cap C_2\), then there exists a circuit \(C_3\) such that \[C_3\subseteq (C_1\cup C_2)\setminus\{e\}.\] The conclusion requires containment in the union with the selected common element removed; it does not require equality with that entire set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct circuits sharing an element contain another circuit in their union after that chosen common element is removed.
knowledge_statements.title: Circuit Elimination

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong circuit elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuit elimination retaining a specified element of the first circuit outside the second.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M be a matroid with circuit family \mathcal C(M). If C_1,C_2\in\mathcal C(M), e\in C_1\cap C_2, and f\in C_1\setminus C_2, then there exists C_3\in\mathcal C(M) such that f\in C_3\subseteq(C_1\cup C_2)\setminus\{e\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If two matroid circuits share e and f lies only in the first, eliminating e yields a circuit inside their union that still contains f.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists C_3\in\mathcal C(M)\text{ such that }f\in C_3\subseteq(C_1\cup C_2)\setminus\{e\}

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists C_3\in\mathcal C:\ C_3\subseteq (C_1\cup C_2)\setminus\{e\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Series-set-preserving circuit elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A circuit-elimination specialization for two circuits sharing a positive-support element in a series arc set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a series arc set and let \(\pi_1,\pi_2\) be circuits. If \(\operatorname{supp}^{+}(\pi_1)\cap\operatorname{supp}^{+}(\pi_2)\cap S\neq\varnothing\), then there exists a circuit \(\pi\) such that \(\operatorname{supp}^{+}(\pi)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}^{+}(\pi_1)\cup\operatorname{supp}^{+}(\pi_2)\), \(\operatorname{supp}^{-}(\pi)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}^{-}(\pi_1)\cup\operatorname{supp}^{-}(\pi_2)\), and \(\operatorname{supp}^{+}(\pi)\cap S=(\operatorname{supp}^{+}(\pi_1)\cup\operatorname{supp}^{+}(\pi_2))\cap S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If two circuits share a positive-support arc in a series set, there is a circuit introducing no support outside their signed support unions and retaining every positive-support series-set arc in their union.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is a series arc set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\pi\text{ a circuit}:\ \operatorname{supp}^{+}(\pi)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}^{+}(\pi_1)\cup\operatorname{supp}^{+}(\pi_2),\ \operatorname{supp}^{-}(\pi)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}^{-}(\pi_1)\cup\operatorname{supp}^{-}(\pi_2),\ \operatorname{supp}^{+}(\pi)\cap S=(\operatorname{supp}^{+}(\pi_1)\cup\operatorname{supp}^{+}(\pi_2))\cap S

knowledge_statements.title: Dependence-to-Circuit Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-matroid recovery of a circuit from any dependent set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid. If \(X\subseteq E\) is dependent, then \(X\) contains an inclusion-minimal dependent subset \(C\). Consequently, \(C\) is a circuit of \(M\) and \(C\subseteq X\). Conversely, every subset containing a circuit is dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite set is dependent exactly when it contains a circuit; a circuit is recovered by taking an inclusion-minimal dependent subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists C\subseteq X\) such that \(C\) is a circuit of \(M\).

notation.meaning: family of independent sets of the matroid
an inclusion-minimal dependent set, hence a circuit

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fundamental circuits and cuts form cycle and cocycle bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphic specialization of the fundamental circuit–cocircuit pair relative to a maximal undirected-acyclic subgraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be a digraph and let $T$ be a maximal subgraph containing no undirected circuit. The $|E(G)\setminus E(T)|$ fundamental circuits with respect to $T$ form a cycle basis of $G$, and the $|E(T)|$ fundamental cuts with respect to $T$ form a cocycle basis of $G$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a digraph and a maximal subgraph with no undirected circuit, the fundamental circuits indexed by edges outside the subgraph form a basis of the cycle space, and the fundamental cuts indexed by its edges form a basis of the cocycle space.
assumptions_latex: T\subseteq G\text{ is maximal subject to containing no undirected circuit}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{\zeta(C_e):e\in E(G)\setminus E(T)\}\text{ is a cycle-space basis, and }\{\zeta(D_e):e\in E(T)\}\text{ is a cocycle-space basis.}

knowledge_statements.title: Fundamental Circuits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental circuit relative to a basis in a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid, let \(B\) be a basis, and let \(e\in E\setminus B\). The set \(B\cup\{e\}\) contains a unique circuit, denoted \(C_M(e,B)\), called the fundamental circuit of \(e\) with respect to \(B\). Moreover, \(e\in C_M(e,B)\subseteq B\cup\{e\}\), and for every \(b\in B\), \(b\in C_M(e,B)\) if and only if \((B\setminus\{b\})\cup\{e\}\) is a basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a nonbasis element to a basis creates one unique circuit; its basis elements are exactly those exchangeable with the added element.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_M(e,B)\) is the unique circuit in \(B\cup\{e\}\), with \(b\in C_M(e,B)\iff B-b+e\) a basis.

notation.meaning: fundamental circuit of e relative to B

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fundamental circuits and realization of arbitrary circuits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a basis-relative fundamental circuit, together with the stated realization property for all matroid circuits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $B$ be a basis of a matroid $M$ and let $e\in E(M)\setminus B$. The unique circuit $C(e,B)\subseteq B\cup\{e\}$ is called the fundamental circuit of $e$ with respect to $B$. Moreover, every circuit $C$ of $M$ equals $C(e,B)$ for some basis $B$ of $M$ and some $e\in E(M)\setminus B$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unique circuit formed by adding an external element e to a basis B is called the fundamental circuit of e with respect to B. Every circuit of a matroid is fundamental with respect to some basis.
assumptions_latex: For the definition, $B$ is a basis of $M$ and $e\in E(M)\setminus B$.
For the realization property, $C$ is a circuit of $M$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: $C(e,B)$ is the fundamental circuit of $e$ with respect to $B$, and $(\forall C\in\mathcal C(M))(\exists B\text{ a basis of }M)(\exists e\in E(M)\setminus B)\;C=C(e,B)$.

knowledge_statements.title: Fundamental Cocircuits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental cocircuit relative to a basis in a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid, let \(B\) be a basis, and let \(b\in B\). The set \((E\setminus B)\cup\{b\}\) contains a unique cocircuit, denoted \(D_M(b,B)\), called the fundamental cocircuit of \(b\) with respect to \(B\). Moreover, \(b\in D_M(b,B)\), and for every \(e\in E\setminus B\), \(e\in D_M(b,B)\) if and only if \((B\setminus\{b\})\cup\{e\}\) is a basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis element determines one unique cocircuit among itself and the nonbasis elements; membership records valid one-element basis exchanges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_M(b,B)\) is the unique cocircuit in \((E\setminus B)\cup\{b\}\), with \(e\in D_M(b,B)\iff B-b+e\) a basis.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\) with basis \(B\). For every \(e\in E\setminus B\) and \(b\in B\), \[b\in C_M(e,B)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad e\in D_M(b,B)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (B\setminus\{b\})\cup\{e\}\text{ is a basis of }M.\] Define \(A\in\{0,1\}^{(E\setminus B)\times B}\) by \(A_{e,b}=1\) exactly when \(b\in C_M(e,B)\), and define \(Q\in\{0,1\}^{B\times(E\setminus B)}\) by \(Q_{b,e}=1\) exactly when \(e\in D_M(b,B)\). Then \(A=Q^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis element belongs to a nonbasis element's fundamental circuit exactly when the nonbasis element belongs to that basis element's fundamental cocircuit, equivalently when exchanging the two elements produces a basis. Consequently, the explicitly indexed circuit- and cocircuit-incidence matrices are transposes.

knowledge_statements.title: Circuit–Cocircuit Orthogonality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic orthogonality in an arbitrary finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\). For every circuit \(C\) of \(M\) and every cocircuit \(D\) of \(M\), their intersection cannot have cardinality one: \[|C\cap D|\ne 1.\] Equivalently, if \(e\in C\cap D\), then there exists \(f\in (C\cap D)\setminus\{e\}\). This is set-theoretic matroid orthogonality and does not assert that \(|C\cap D|\) is always even.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A circuit and a cocircuit never meet in exactly one element; their intersection may otherwise be empty or have at least two elements.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a circuit and \(D\) is a cocircuit of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|C\cap D|\ne 1.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Signability and Orientability via Signed Circuit–Cocircuit Incidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed overlap conditions for signability and orientability, together with their class relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For signed circuit and cocircuit incidence vectors, define \(S_+(C,C^*)=\{e\in E(M):v'_C(e)=v'_{C^*}(e)
e0\}\) and \(S_-(C,C^*)=\{e\in E(M):v'_C(e)=-v'_{C^*}(e)
e0\}\). A matroid \(M\) is signable if signings can be chosen such that \(|S_+(C,C^*)|=|S_-(C,C^*)|\) for every circuit \(C\) and cocircuit \(C^*\). It is orientable if signings can be chosen such that \(C\cap C^*
e\varnothing\) implies both \(S_+(C,C^*)\) and \(S_-(C,C^*)\) are nonempty. Every signable matroid is orientable, and the class of signable matroids equals the class of binary orientable matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Signability requires every signed circuit–cocircuit overlap to contain equally many agreeing and opposing signs. Orientability only requires both kinds to occur whenever the overlap is nonempty. Every signable matroid is orientable, and a matroid is signable exactly when it is both binary and orientable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ signable}\Rightarrow M\text{ orientable},\qquad M\text{ signable}\iff\bigl(M\text{ is binary and orientable}\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cocircuits characterized by circuit orthogonality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes cocircuits as the inclusion-minimal nonempty sets having no singleton intersection with any circuit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matroid on \(S\). The cocircuits of \(M\) are exactly the inclusion-minimal nonempty subsets \(D\subseteq S\) such that \(|D\cap C|\ne 1\) for every circuit \(C\) of \(M\). Equivalently, every circuit and cocircuit have intersection size different from one, and every nonempty \(D\subseteq S\) satisfying \(|D\cap C|\ne1\) for every circuit \(C\) contains a cocircuit and hence is dependent in \(M^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cocircuit is precisely an inclusion-minimal nonempty set that never intersects a circuit in exactly one element. Every nonempty set with this property contains a cocircuit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ is a cocircuit}\iff D\text{ is inclusion-minimal among nonempty sets satisfying }\forall C\in\mathcal C(M),\ |D\cap C|\ne1

knowledge_statements.title: Rank View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matroids represented by integer-valued rank functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(r:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) is the rank function of a matroid on finite \(E\) exactly when, for all \(X,Y\subseteq E\), \(0\le r(X)\le |X|\), \(X\subseteq Y\) implies \(r(X)\le r(Y)\), and \[r(X)+r(Y)\ge r(X\cup Y)+r(X\cap Y).\] The represented independent sets are precisely \(\mathcal I_r=\{I\subseteq E:r(I)=|I|\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized, cardinality-bounded, monotone, submodular integer functions are exactly finite-matroid rank functions; equality with cardinality identifies independent sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\) is a matroid rank function if and only if it satisfies the displayed rank axioms.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank characterizations of independent sets, bases, and circuits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses three fundamental matroid set classes entirely through rank data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matroid with rank function \(r\), and let \(X\subseteq E(M)\). Then: (i) \(X\) is independent if and only if \(|X|=r(X)\); (ii) \(X\) is a basis if and only if \(|X|=r(X)=r(M)\); and (iii) \(X\) is a circuit if and only if \(X\ne\varnothing\) and, for every \(x\in X\), \(r(X\setminus\{x\})=|X|-1=r(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is independent exactly when its rank equals its size. It is a basis exactly when this value also equals the matroid rank. It is a circuit exactly when it is nonempty and its rank, as well as the rank of every one-element deletion, equals one less than its size.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is a matroid with rank function }r
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\in\mathcal I(M)\iff |X|=r(X);\quad X\in\mathcal B(M)\iff |X|=r(X)=r(M);\quad X\in\mathcal C(M)\iff X\ne\varnothing\ \land\ \forall x\in X,\ r(X\setminus\{x\})=|X|-1=r(X).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid restriction and subset rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines subset rank through restriction and records the restriction's circuits, elementary rank bounds, and monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a matroid and \(X\subseteq E\). Define \(\mathcal I|X=\{I\subseteq X:I\in\mathcal I\}\). The restriction is \(M|X=(X,\mathcal I|X)=M\setminus(E-X)\), with \(\mathcal C(M|X)=\{C\in\mathcal C(M):C\subseteq X\}\). The rank \(r_M(X)\) is the cardinality of any basis of \(M|X\), and \(r(M)=r_M(E)\). Moreover, \(0\le r_M(X)\le |X|\), and for all \(X\subseteq Y\subseteq E\), \(r_M(X)\le r_M(Y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting a matroid to X retains its independent sets contained in X and exactly its circuits contained in X. The rank of X is the common size of the bases of this restriction. Rank is bounded by set size and is monotone under inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M|X=(X,\mathcal I|X),\quad \mathcal C(M|X)=\{C\in\mathcal C(M):C\subseteq X\},\quad r_M(X)=|B|\text{ for every basis }B\text{ of }M|X,\quad 0\le r_M(X)\le |X|,\quad X\subseteq Y\subseteq E\Rightarrow r_M(X)\le r_M(Y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank-function axioms for finite matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent global and local characterizations of matroid rank functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and \(r:2^E\to\mathbb Z_+\). The following are equivalent: (i) \(r\) is the rank function of a matroid on \(E\), whose independent sets are \(\mathcal F=\{F\subseteq E:r(F)=|F|\}\); (ii) for all \(X,Y\subseteq E\), \(r(X)\le |X|\), \(X\subseteq Y\Rightarrow r(X)\le r(Y)\), and \(r(X\cup Y)+r(X\cap Y)\le r(X)+r(Y)\); (iii) \(r(\varnothing)=0\), for all \(X\subseteq E\) and \(y\in E\), \(r(X)\le r(X\cup\{y\})\le r(X)+1\), and for all \(x,y\in E\), if \(r(X\cup\{x\})=r(X\cup\{y\})=r(X)\), then \(r(X\cup\{x,y\})=r(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative integer-valued set function on a finite ground set is a matroid rank function exactly when it satisfies either the global boundedness, monotonicity, and submodularity axioms or the stated equivalent local axioms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r\text{ is a matroid rank function}\iff\text{the global rank axioms hold}\iff\text{the stated local rank axioms hold}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Rank Characterization and Rank under Deletion and Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-function cryptomorphism for finite matroids together with the definitions and rank effects of single-element deletion and contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) and \(F\subseteq E\), all maximal independent subsets of \(F\) have the same cardinality, called \(r(F)\). The rank function satisfies \(r(\varnothing)=0\), monotonicity, \(r(S)\leq |S|\), and submodularity. Moreover, \(S\in\mathcal I\iff r(S)=|S|\), so \(r\) uniquely determines \(M\); conversely, every integer-valued \(r:2^E\to\mathbb Z\) satisfying these four properties is the rank function of a unique matroid. Deletion of \(e\) restricts \(\mathcal I\) to \(E\setminus\{e\}\). If \(\{e\}\in\mathcal I\), contraction has independent sets \(\{S\setminus\{e\}:e\in S\in\mathcal I\}\); if \(\{e\}\notin\mathcal I\), it equals deletion. For \(F\subseteq E\setminus\{e\}\), \(r_{M\setminus e}(F)=r_M(F)\) and \(r_{M/e}(F)=r_M(F\cup\{e\})-r_M(\{e\})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid rank is the common size of maximal independent subsets of a set. Normalization, monotonicity, subcardinality, submodularity, and integer values characterize matroid rank functions. Deletion preserves rank on remaining subsets, while contraction obeys the stated rank formula, including the loop case.
assumptions_latex: M=(E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a finite matroid}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\in\mathcal I\iff r(S)=|S|,\qquad r_{M\setminus e}(F)=r_M(F),\qquad r_{M/e}(F)=r_M(F\cup\{e\})-r_M(\{e\}).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank-function characterization of finite matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Whitney's local rank-increment characterization and the induced independent-set representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(r\) is the rank function of a matroid on \(E\), then \(r(\varnothing)=0\); for every \(A\subseteq E\) and \(e\notin A\), \(r(A\cup\{e\})\in\{r(A),r(A)+1\}\); and for \(e_1,e_2\notin A\), if \(r(A\cup\{e_1\})=r(A\cup\{e_2\})=r(A)\), then \(r(A\cup\{e_1,e_2\})=r(A)\). Conversely, if a function \(r\) on the subsets of a finite set \(E\) satisfies these conditions, then \(\mathcal I=\{I\subseteq E:r(I)=|I|\}\) is the independent-set family of a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid rank is zero on the empty set, increases by zero or one when a single new element is added, and remains unchanged when two elements are added together if each separately leaves it unchanged. Conversely, on a finite ground set these conditions define a matroid through the subsets whose rank equals their cardinality.
assumptions_latex: For the forward implication, \(r\) is the rank function of a matroid on \(E\).
For the converse, \(E\) is finite and \(r\) is a function on \(2^E\) satisfying the three stated conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal I=\{I\subseteq E:r(I)=|I|\}\text{ is the independent-set family of a matroid, and every matroid rank function satisfies the stated conditions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Rank-Function Axioms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-function definition of a matroid on a ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function $r:2^S\to\mathbb Z_+$ is a matroid rank function if, for all $X,Y\subseteq S$, (i) $r(X)\leq |X|$; (ii) $X\subseteq Y$ implies $r(X)\leq r(Y)$; and (iii) $r(X\cup Y)+r(X\cap Y)\leq r(X)+r(Y)$. The pair $(S,r)$ is then called a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative integer-valued set function is a matroid rank function when it is bounded by cardinality, monotone, and submodular. The ground set together with such a rank function is a matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (S,r)\text{ is a matroid when }r\text{ satisfies the stated rank-function axioms.}

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a matroid on a finite ground set \(E\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M\) on \(E\) with rank function \(r_M\), define its nullity function by \[n_M(X)=|X|-r_M(X)\qquad(X\subseteq E).\] For every \(X\subseteq E\), \(n_M(X)\) equals the number of elements of \(X\) outside any inclusion-maximal independent subset of \(X\). For every \(I\subseteq E\), \(I\) is independent exactly when \(n_M(I)=0\), and \(I\) is dependent exactly when \(n_M(I)>0\). Hence \(n_M\) determines \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nullity of a subset is its cardinality minus its rank, equivalently the number of its elements outside any inclusion-maximal independent subset. Zero-nullity sets are exactly the independent sets, so the nullity function determines the finite matroid.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank–Nullity Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mutually inverse conversion between rank and nullity on a finite ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite. Rank and nullity functions of a matroid on \(E\) determine one another pointwise by \[n(X)=|X|-r(X),\qquad r(X)=|X|-n(X)\qquad(X\subseteq E).\] Under this correspondence, rank monotonicity becomes \(n(Y)-n(X)\le |Y\setminus X|\) for \(X\subseteq Y\), rank submodularity becomes nullity supermodularity, and the independent subsets are exactly the zero sets of \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank and nullity are complementary to subset cardinality and therefore encode the same finite matroid, with submodularity converted to supermodularity.
assumptions_latex: \(r\) and \(n\) are respectively the rank and nullity functions of one matroid on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n(X)=|X|-r(X)\) and \(r(X)=|X|-n(X)\) for every \(X\subseteq E\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed sets, matroid closure, and redundant nonclosed rank inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines closedness for an independence system, states existence and uniqueness of matroid closure, and records the associated rank-inequality redundancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an independence system $M$, a set $T\subseteq E(M)$ is closed if $r_M(T\cup\{e\})>r_M(T)$ for every $e\in E(M)\setminus T$. If $M$ is a matroid, every $T$ has a unique maximal superset $\operatorname{cl}_M(T)$ satisfying $r_M(\operatorname{cl}_M(T))=r_M(T)$. Consequently, if $T$ is not closed, then under nonnegativity the inequality $x(T)\le r_M(T)$ follows from $x(\operatorname{cl}_M(T))\le r_M(T)$ and $-x_j\le0$ for $j\in\operatorname{cl}_M(T)\setminus T$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is closed when every outside element increases its rank. In a matroid, every set has a unique maximal same-rank superset, called its closure or span. The rank inequality of a nonclosed set is therefore implied by the closure inequality and nonnegativity.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is an independence system for the definition of closedness}
M\text{ is a matroid for existence and uniqueness of }\operatorname{cl}_M(T)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_M(\operatorname{cl}_M(T))=r_M(T),\qquad x(\operatorname{cl}_M(T))\le r_M(T),\ x\ge0\Longrightarrow x(T)\le r_M(T)

children.title: Closure Operators
children.top_down_role: Matroid structure expressed through closure behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a matroid on \(E\) with rank function \(r_M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operator \(\operatorname{cl}_M\) satisfies extensivity, monotonicity, idempotence, and Mac Lane–Steinitz exchange; conversely, these axioms characterize closure operators of unique matroids on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matroids represented by closure operators satisfying exchange.

source_refs.locator: Section 5.1, Independence and rank, p. 173

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matroid on a finite set \(E\), with rank function \(r_M\), and define \[\operatorname{cl}_M(X)=\{e\in E:r_M(X\cup\{e\})=r_M(X)\}\qquad(X\subseteq E).\] For all \(X,Y\subseteq E\), this operator is extensive, monotone, and idempotent: \(X\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\), \(X\subseteq Y\Rightarrow\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_M(Y)\), and \(\operatorname{cl}_M(\operatorname{cl}_M(X))=\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\). For all \(X\subseteq E\) and \(x,y\in E\), it also satisfies Mac Lane–Steinitz exchange: \[y\in\operatorname{cl}_M(X\cup\{x\})\setminus\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\in\operatorname{cl}_M(X\cup\{y\}).\] Conversely, every map \(\operatorname{cl}:2^E\to2^E\) satisfying these four properties is the closure operator of a unique matroid on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid closure consists of the elements whose addition does not increase rank. It is extensive, monotone, idempotent, and satisfies exchange; conversely, an operator on a finite ground set with these properties determines a unique matroid.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Operators

children.title: Matroid Span
children.top_down_role: Spanning relationships induced by closure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(X\subseteq E\) and \(e\in E\), \(X\text{ spans }e\iff e\in\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\iff r_M(X\cup\{e\})=r_M(X)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank and circuit characterizations of spanning elements and sets.

source_refs.locator: Sections 5.1–5.2, Independence and rank; Circuits and connectivity, pp. 173–176

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\). For every \(X\subseteq E\) and \(e\in E\), the set \(X\) spans \(e\) when \(e\in\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\), equivalently when \(r_M(X\cup\{e\})=r_M(X)\). If \(e\notin X\), these conditions are equivalent to the existence of a circuit \(C\) of \(M\) such that \(e\in C\subseteq X\cup\{e\}\). For \(Y\subseteq E\), the set \(X\) spans \(Y\) when \(Y\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\), and \(X\) spans \(M\) when \(\operatorname{cl}_M(X)=E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set spans an element exactly when adding that element does not increase rank; for an element outside the set, this is also equivalent to completing a circuit supported by the set. A set spans another set when it spans every one of its elements, and it spans the matroid when its closure is the whole ground set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Axiomatization of matroid span functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the set-valued operators on a finite ground set that are exactly matroid span functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be finite. A map \(\operatorname{span}:\mathcal P(S)\to\mathcal P(S)\) is the span function of a matroid if and only if: (i) \(T\subseteq\operatorname{span}(T)\) for every \(T\subseteq S\); (ii) for \(T,U\subseteq S\), if \(U\subseteq\operatorname{span}(T)\), then \(\operatorname{span}(U)\subseteq\operatorname{span}(T)\); and (iii) if \(T\subseteq S\), \(t\in S\setminus T\), and \(s\in\operatorname{span}(T\cup\{t\})\setminus\operatorname{span}(T)\), then \(t\in\operatorname{span}(T\cup\{s\})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite ground set, an operator is a matroid span function exactly when it is extensive, maps every subset of an existing span back into that span, and satisfies the stated exchange law for newly spanned elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{span}\text{ is the span function of a matroid}\iff\text{conditions (i)--(iii) hold}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid span, spanning sets, and flats
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines matroid span from rank and records its basic rank, spanning, flat, and independence characterizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matroid \(M=(S,\mathcal I)\) and \(T\subseteq S\), define \(\operatorname{span}_M(T)=\{s\in S:r_M(T\cup\{s\})=r_M(T)\}\). Then \(T\subseteq\operatorname{span}_M(T)\), \(r_M(\operatorname{span}_M(T))=r_M(T)\), and \(T\) is spanning if and only if \(\operatorname{span}_M(T)=S\). A subset \(F\subseteq S\) is a flat if and only if \(\operatorname{span}_M(F)=F\). Moreover, \(I\subseteq S\) is independent if and only if, for every \(y\in I\), there exists a flat \(F\) such that \(I\setminus\{y\}\subseteq F\) and \(y\notin F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The span of a set consists of the elements whose addition does not increase its rank. Span contains the original set and has the same rank; a set is spanning exactly when its span is the ground set. Flats are the fixed points of span, and independence is characterized by a flat separating each element from the rest of the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{span}_M(T)=\{s\in S:r_M(T\cup\{s\})=r_M(T)\},\quad T\subseteq\operatorname{span}_M(T),\quad r_M(\operatorname{span}_M(T))=r_M(T),\quad [T\text{ spanning}\iff\operatorname{span}_M(T)=S],\quad [F\text{ flat}\iff\operatorname{span}_M(F)=F],\quad [I\in\mathcal I\iff \forall y\in I\;\exists F\text{ flat}:I\setminus\{y\}\subseteq F,\ y\notin F].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Span-Preserving Ordered Exchange Lemma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient ordered-exchange conditions ensuring simultaneous exchanges preserve independence and matroid span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(S,\mathcal I)\), let \(J\in\mathcal I\), and let \(p_1,q_1,\ldots,p_k,q_k\) be distinct elements satisfying, for \(1\le i\le k\),
\[
p_i\notin J,\quad q_i\in J,\quad J\cup\{p_i\}\notin\mathcal I,\quad (J\cup\{p_i\})\setminus\{q_i\}\in\mathcal I,
\]
and, for \(1\le i<j\le k\),
\[
(J\cup\{p_i\})\setminus\{q_j\}\notin\mathcal I.
\]
If
\[
J'=J\mathbin{\triangle}\{p_1,q_1,\ldots,p_k,q_k\},
\]
then
\[
J'\in\mathcal I\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{span}(J')=\operatorname{span}(J).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If each outside element p_i can replace its paired element q_i in an independent set J, while no earlier p_i can replace a later q_j, then simultaneously exchanging all pairs produces an independent set with the same span as J.
assumptions_latex: M=(S,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid and }J\in\mathcal I.
p_i\notin J\text{ and }q_i\in J\text{ for }1\le i\le k.
J\cup\{p_i\}\notin\mathcal I\text{ and }(J\cup\{p_i\})\setminus\{q_i\}\in\mathcal I\text{ for }1\le i\le k.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J'=J\triangle\{p_1,q_1,\ldots,p_k,q_k\}\in\mathcal I\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{span}(J')=\operatorname{span}(J).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\). A subset \(F\subseteq E\) is a flat of \(M\) when \(\operatorname{cl}_M(F)=F\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\), with \(r(M)=r_M(E)\). A subset \(H\subseteq E\) is a hyperplane when it is a maximal proper flat: \(H\) is a flat, \(H\subsetneq E\), and no flat \(F\) satisfies \(H\subsetneq F\subsetneq E\). Equivalently, \(H\) is a flat with \(r_M(H)=r(M)-1\). Equivalently, \(E\setminus H\) is a cocircuit of \(M\). These equivalences remain valid for matroids with loops or coloops.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hyperplane is a maximal proper flat, equivalently a flat whose rank is one less than the matroid rank. Its complement is a cocircuit, including in matroids with loops or coloops.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a flat of positive corank by exactly that many hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a flat of a matroid \(M\). If \(r_M(X)=r(M)-k\) for an integer \(k\ge1\), then there exist hyperplanes \(H_1,\ldots,H_k\) of \(M\) such that \[X=\bigcap_{i=1}^{k}H_i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every flat of positive corank k in a matroid is the intersection of k hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,H_1,\ldots,H_k\text{ hyperplanes of }M\text{ such that }X=\bigcap_{i=1}^{k}H_i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hyperplane Axioms for Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the set families that occur as the hyperplanes of a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal H be a family of subsets of E. Then \mathcal H is the family of hyperplanes of a matroid on E if and only if: (H1) E\notin\mathcal H; (H2) \mathcal H is a clutter; and (H3) whenever H_1,H_2\in\mathcal H are distinct and e\in E\setminus(H_1\cup H_2), there exists H_3\in\mathcal H such that H_3\supseteq(H_1\cap H_2)\cup\{e\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family of subsets of E is the hyperplane family of a matroid exactly when it excludes E itself, is a clutter, and satisfies the stated intersection-extension condition for every two distinct members and every element outside their union.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal H\text{ is the hyperplane family of a matroid on }E\iff \text{(H1), (H2), and (H3) hold.}

children.title: Closure–Flat Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural passage between closure data and the family of flats.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq E\) is a flat exactly when \(\operatorname{cl}_M(F)=F\), and every closure is the least flat containing its argument.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-matroid correspondence between closed sets and flats.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(X\subseteq E\), the set \(\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\) is a flat and is the unique least flat containing \(X\). A subset \(F\subseteq E\) is a flat if and only if \(\operatorname{cl}_M(F)=F\). Consequently, the flats are precisely the fixed points, equivalently the image, of \(\operatorname{cl}_M\), and
\[
\operatorname{cl}_M(X)=\bigcap\{F\subseteq E:F\text{ is a flat and }X\subseteq F\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The flats are exactly the closure operator's fixed points, and the closure of a set is the intersection of all flats containing it.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure–Flat Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal L(M)\) denotes the family of flats ordered by inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L(M)\) is a finite atomic semimodular lattice with meet \(F\cap G\) and join \(\operatorname{cl}_M(F\cup G)\).

notation.meaning: Lattice of flats of the matroid.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite geometric lattice associated with a matroid's flats.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The poset \(\mathcal L(M)\) is a finite geometric lattice. For flats \(F,G\in\mathcal L(M)\), its operations are
\[
F\wedge G=F\cap G,
\qquad
F\vee G=\operatorname{cl}_M(F\cup G).
\]
Its bottom and top are \(\operatorname{cl}_M(\varnothing)\) and \(E\), respectively; its atoms are the rank-one flats; and its lattice height function is the matroid rank restricted to flats. Semimodularity is expressed by
\[
r(F)+r(G)\ge r(F\cap G)+r(\operatorname{cl}_M(F\cup G)).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The flats of a finite matroid form a geometric lattice whose meet is intersection, join is closure of union, and height is matroid rank.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric-Lattice View

children.title: Matroid Loops
children.top_down_role: Local structure of elements excluded from every basis.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e\) is a loop if and only if \(r(\{e\})=0\), equivalently \(e\in\operatorname{cl}_M(\varnothing)\).

notation.meaning: Collection of bases of the matroid.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent rank, closure, circuit, and basis characterizations.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The element \(e\) is a loop of \(M\) when the singleton \(\{e\}\) is dependent. Equivalently, each of the following holds:
\[
r(\{e\})=0,
\qquad
e\in\operatorname{cl}_M(\varnothing),
\qquad
\{e\}\text{ is a circuit},
\qquad
e\notin B\text{ for every }B\in\mathcal B(M).
\]
Thus adding a loop to any subset does not increase rank: \(r(X\cup\{e\})=r(X)\) for every \(X\subseteq E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A loop is an element of rank zero; it forms a singleton circuit and belongs to no basis.
knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Loops

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loop Characterization by Basis Exclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes a matroid loop by its exclusion from every basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M$ be a matroid and $e\in E(M)$. Then $e$ is a loop of $M$ if and only if no basis of $M$ contains $e$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An element of a matroid is a loop exactly when it belongs to no basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e\text{ is a loop of }M\iff (\forall B\in\mathcal B(M))\ e\notin B

children.title: Matroid Coloops
children.top_down_role: Local structure of elements present in every basis.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e\) is a coloop if and only if \(e\) belongs to every basis, equivalently \(r(E)=r(E\setminus\{e\})+1\).

notation.meaning: Collection of bases of the matroid.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent basis, rank, cocircuit, and dual-loop characterizations.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The element \(e\) is a coloop of \(M\) when it belongs to every basis of \(M\). Equivalently,
\[
r(E)=r(E\setminus\{e\})+1,
\]
\(\{e\}\) is a cocircuit of \(M\), or \(e\) is a loop of the dual matroid \(M^*\). In particular, for every \(X\subseteq E\setminus\{e\}\), one has \(r(X\cup\{e\})=r(X)+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coloop belongs to every basis; deleting it lowers rank by one, and it is a loop in the dual matroid.
knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Coloops

children.title: Parallel Classes
children.top_down_role: Equivalence classes arising from parallel nonloop elements.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Parallel classes are the equivalence classes of \(e\sim f\) defined on \(E\setminus L\) by \(\operatorname{cl}_M(\{e\})=\operatorname{cl}_M(\{f\})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel classes include singleton equivalence classes of nonloops.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(e,f\in E\setminus L\), define \(e\sim f\) when \(\operatorname{cl}_M(\{e\})=\operatorname{cl}_M(\{f\})\). This is an equivalence relation, and its equivalence classes are the parallel classes of \(M\). For distinct nonloops \(e\) and \(f\),
\[
e\sim f
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
r(\{e,f\})=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\{e,f\}\text{ is a circuit}.
\]
A nontrivial parallel class is one containing at least two elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel classes group nonloops having the same singleton closure; two distinct nonloops are parallel exactly when together they form a circuit.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Classes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parallel-Element Basis-Replacement Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes parallelism to a nonloop through replacement in every basis containing that element.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M$ be a matroid and let $e_1,e_2\in E(M)$, where $e_1$ is not a loop. Then $e_2$ is parallel to $e_1$ if and only if, for every basis $B$ of $M$ containing $e_1$, the set $(B\setminus\{e_1\})\cup\{e_2\}$ is also a basis of $M$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If e1 is not a loop, then e2 is parallel to e1 exactly when replacing e1 by e2 in every basis containing e1 produces another basis.
assumptions_latex: e_1\text{ is not a loop of }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e_2\parallel_M e_1\iff (\forall B\in\mathcal B(M)\text{ with }e_1\in B)\ (B\setminus\{e_1\})\cup\{e_2\}\in\mathcal B(M)

children.title: Series Classes
children.top_down_role: Dual equivalence classes arising from series noncoloop elements.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is the set of coloops of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The series classes of \(M\) are the parallel classes of \(M^*\) on \(E\setminus C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Series classes defined through parallelism in the dual matroid.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(e,f\in E\setminus C\), declare \(e\) and \(f\) to be in series in \(M\) when they are parallel in the dual matroid \(M^*\). The resulting equivalence classes are the series classes of \(M\). For distinct noncoloops \(e\) and \(f\), they lie in the same series class if and only if \(\{e,f\}\) is a cocircuit of \(M\). A series class is nontrivial when it contains at least two elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Series classes are parallel classes in the dual; two distinct noncoloops are in series exactly when they form a cocircuit.

children.title: Loop–Coloop Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual correspondence between the two exceptional element types.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid on ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An element is a loop of \(M\) if and only if it is a coloop of \(M^*\), and conversely.

notation.meaning: Set of loops of a matroid.
Set of coloops of a matroid.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementwise loop–coloop correspondence under matroid duality.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(e\in E\),
\[
e\in L(M)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
e\in C(M^*),
\qquad
e\in C(M)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
e\in L(M^*).
\]
Equivalently, singleton circuits of \(M\) are singleton cocircuits of \(M^*\), while singleton cocircuits of \(M\) are singleton circuits of \(M^*\). Since \((M^*)^*=M\), the two correspondences are mutually inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duality exchanges loops and coloops: each loop becomes a coloop in the dual, and each coloop becomes a loop.
knowledge_statements.title: Loop–Coloop Duality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coloops and series under matroid duality

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matroid M and e\in E(M), e is a coloop of M if and only if e is a loop of M^*; equivalently, e belongs to every basis of M. If elements are parallel in M^*, then they are in series in M.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An element is a coloop precisely when it is a loop of the dual, equivalently when it belongs to every basis. Elements parallel in the dual are series in the original matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e\text{ is a coloop of }M\iff e\text{ is a loop of }M^*\iff (\forall B\in\mathcal B(M))\ e\in B;\quad x,y\text{ parallel in }M^*\Rightarrow x,y\text{ in series in }M

children.title: Parallel–Series Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual correspondence between parallel classes and series classes.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid on ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A subset is a parallel class of \(M\) if and only if it is a series class of \(M^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classwise parallel–series correspondence under matroid duality.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For distinct elements \(e,f\in E\),
\[
\{e,f\}\text{ is a circuit of }M
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\{e,f\}\text{ is a cocircuit of }M^*.
\]
Consequently, every parallel class of \(M\) is a series class of \(M^*\), and every series class of \(M\) is a parallel class of \(M^*\). These class correspondences respect the exclusions of loops and coloops because duality exchanges those element types.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid duality exchanges parallel and series classes because two-element circuits become two-element cocircuits.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specializes parallel–series duality to extensions of abstractly dual planar graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be a planar graph and let $H$ be an abstract dual of $G$. For every series extension $G'$ of $G$, there is a parallel extension $H'$ of $H$ that is an abstract dual of $G'$. Moreover, every parallel extension of $H$ is an abstract dual of some series extension of $G$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a planar graph and an abstract dual, each series extension of the primal has a corresponding parallel extension of the dual, and every parallel extension of the dual arises from some series extension of the primal.

children.top_down_role: Reduction removing loop and parallel redundancy.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid with loop set \(L\).
\(P_1,\ldots,P_k\) are its parallel classes on \(E\setminus L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Choosing \(p_i\in P_i\) and \(S=\{p_1,\ldots,p_k\}\), the restriction \(M|S\) is a simplification of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplification by deletion and representative selection.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose one representative \(p_i\in P_i\) from each parallel class and set \(S=\{p_1,\ldots,p_k\}\). A simplification of \(M\) is
\[
\operatorname{si}(M)=M|S.
\]
Equivalently, it is obtained by deleting every loop and deleting all but one element from each nontrivial parallel class. The resulting matroid has no loops and no two-element circuits. Different choices of representatives yield isomorphic matroids, although no canonical labeled simplification is determined in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplification deletes all loops and retains one representative from each parallel class; its isomorphism type is independent of the choices.
knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Simplification

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Matroid Cosimplification
children.top_down_role: Dual reduction removing coloop and series redundancy.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid with coloop set \(C\).
\(Q_1,\ldots,Q_k\) are its series classes on \(E\setminus C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Choosing \(q_i\in Q_i\) and \(T=\{q_1,\ldots,q_k\}\), the contraction \(M/(E\setminus T)\) is a cosimplification of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cosimplification as the dual operation to simplification.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose one representative \(q_i\in Q_i\) from each series class and set \(T=\{q_1,\ldots,q_k\}\). A cosimplification of \(M\) is
\[
\operatorname{co}(M)=M/(E\setminus T).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{co}(M)=\bigl(\operatorname{si}(M^*)\bigr)^*.
\]
Operationally, one contracts every coloop and all but one element from each nontrivial series class. The result has no coloops and no two-element cocircuits, and its isomorphism type is independent of the representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cosimplification contracts all coloops and all but one member of each series class; equivalently, it dualizes simplification of the dual.
knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Cosimplification

source_witnesses.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cosimplicity and matroid cosimplification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines cosimplicity and gives both the dual and operational representations of cosimplification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matroid is cosimple if its dual is simple. For any matroid $N$, its cosimplification is $\operatorname{co}(N)=(\operatorname{si}(N^*))^*$. Equivalently, $\operatorname{co}(N)$ is obtained from $N$ by contracting every coloop and all but one element of each nontrivial series class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is cosimple when its dual is simple. Its cosimplification is the dual of the simplification of its dual, equivalently the result of contracting all coloops and all but one element from every nontrivial series class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N\text{ is cosimple}\iff N^*\text{ is simple},\qquad \operatorname{co}(N)=(\operatorname{si}(N^*))^*

children.title: Simple Matroid Core
children.top_down_role: Structural information retained by simplification.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N\) is simple, \(r_N(S)=r_M(E)\), and its flat lattice is isomorphic to that of \(M\).

notation.meaning: A simplification of the original matroid.
Representative ground set of the simplification.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank and flat-lattice invariants of the simple core.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The matroid \(N\) is simple: it has neither loops nor two-element circuits. It preserves total rank,
\[
r_N(S)=r_M(E).
\]
Moreover, its flats encode exactly the flat geometry of \(M\). The maps
\[
F\longmapsto\operatorname{cl}_M(F)
\quad\text{and}\quad
G\longmapsto G\cap S
\]
are mutually inverse, inclusion-preserving bijections between the flats \(F\) of \(N\) and the flats \(G\) of \(M\). Thus every simplification realizes the same simple matroid core up to isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplification is a simple, rank-preserving core whose lattice of flats is naturally isomorphic to the original matroid's flat lattice.
knowledge_statements.title: Simple Matroid Core

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Cosimple Matroid Core
children.top_down_role: Structural information retained by cosimplification.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N\) is cosimple, and \(N^*=\operatorname{si}(M^*)\) up to representative choice and isomorphism.

notation.meaning: A cosimplification of the original matroid.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual rank and flat-geometry invariants of the cosimple core.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The matroid \(N\) is cosimple: it has neither coloops nor two-element cocircuits. Its dual is a simplification of the dual of \(M\), namely
\[
N^*\cong\operatorname{si}(M^*).
\]
Hence the dual rank is preserved:
\[
r_{N^*}(E(N))=r_{M^*}(E).
\]
The flat lattice of \(N^*\) is isomorphic to the flat lattice of \(M^*\). Therefore every cosimplification realizes the same cosimple matroid core up to isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cosimplification is a cosimple core; its dual is the simple core of the dual matroid, preserving dual rank and dual flat geometry.
knowledge_statements.title: Cosimple Matroid Core

source_witnesses.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

children.title: Simplification–Cosimplification Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual relationship between the two redundancy reductions.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid on ground set \(E\).
Simplification retains one representative from each nonloop parallel class; cosimplification is defined dually.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{co}(M)=(\operatorname{si}(M^{*}))^{*}\) and \(\operatorname{si}(M)=(\operatorname{co}(M^{*}))^{*}\), up to the canonical choices of retained representatives.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-matroid duality, with representative choices understood up to isomorphism.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid. Deleting its loops and retaining one element from each nonloop parallel class produces \(\operatorname{si}(M)\). Define cosimplification by \(\operatorname{co}(M):=(\operatorname{si}(M^{*}))^{*}\). Consequently, simplification and cosimplification are exchanged by duality: \[\operatorname{co}(M)=(\operatorname{si}(M^{*}))^{*},\qquad \operatorname{si}(M)=(\operatorname{co}(M^{*}))^{*}.\] Equivalently, series classes of \(M\) are parallel classes of \(M^{*}\), while coloops of \(M\) are loops of \(M^{*}\). The identities are canonical up to the choices of class representatives and the resulting matroid isomorphisms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duality exchanges loops with coloops and parallel classes with series classes, so simplifying the dual and dualizing back gives cosimplification.
knowledge_statements.title: Simplification–Cosimplification Duality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Duality and the Dual Rank Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes preservation of the matroid property under independence-system duality and, under the matroid hypothesis, gives the dual rank function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(E,\mathcal F)$ be an independence system, let $(E,\mathcal F^*)$ be its dual, and let $r$ and $r^*$ be their rank functions. Then
\[
(E,\mathcal F)\text{ is a matroid}\iff(E,\mathcal F^*)\text{ is a matroid}.
\]
If $(E,\mathcal F)$ is a matroid, then for every $F\subseteq E$,
\[
r^*(F)=|F|+r(E\setminus F)-r(E).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independence system is a matroid exactly when its dual is a matroid. When it is a matroid, the dual rank of a set equals its cardinality plus the primal rank of its complement minus the rank of the ground set.
assumptions_latex: r\text{ and }r^*\text{ are the corresponding rank functions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl((E,\mathcal F)\text{ is a matroid}\iff(E,\mathcal F^*)\text{ is a matroid}\bigr)\ \land\ \bigl((E,\mathcal F)\text{ is a matroid}\Rightarrow \forall F\subseteq E,\ r^*(F)=|F|+r(E\setminus F)-r(E)\bigr)

children.title: Basis Duality
children.top_down_role: Duality expressed through complementary bases.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B(M^{*})=\{E\setminus B:B\in\mathcal B(M)\}\).

notation.meaning: family of bases of the matroid

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis definition of duality for finite matroids.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal B)\), the dual matroid \(M^{*}\) has the same ground set and basis family \[\mathcal B(M^{*})=\{E\setminus B:B\in\mathcal B\}.\] Thus \(B^{*}\subseteq E\) is a basis of \(M^{*}\) if and only if \(E\setminus B^{*}\) is a basis of \(M\). In particular, every dual basis has cardinality \(|E|-r_M(E)\), and applying the construction twice returns the original basis family, so \((M^{*})^{*}=M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bases of the dual matroid are exactly the complements, in the common ground set, of the original matroid's bases.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Duality

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal B^*(M)=\{E(M)\setminus B:B\in\mathcal B(M)\}\text{ is the basis family of a matroid on }E(M)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterization by the Dual Basis-Exchange Axiom
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An if-and-only-if basis-family characterization using nonemptiness and the reverse-oriented exchange condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal B\) be a set of subsets of \(E\). Then \(\mathcal B\) is the collection of bases of a matroid on \(E\) if and only if \(\mathcal B\neq\varnothing\) and, for all \(B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B\) and \(x\in B_2\setminus B_1\), there exists \(y\in B_1\setminus B_2\) such that \((B_1\setminus\{y\})\cup\{x\}\in\mathcal B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family of subsets is a matroid basis family exactly when it is nonempty and satisfies the dual-form basis-exchange condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal B\text{ is the basis family of a matroid on }E\iff \mathcal B\neq\varnothing\ \land\ \forall B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B\ \forall x\in B_2\setminus B_1\ \exists y\in B_1\setminus B_2:\ (B_1\setminus\{y\})\cup\{x\}\in\mathcal B

children.top_down_role: Duality expressed through primal and dual rank data.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid on \(E\) with rank function \(r_M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(X\subseteq E\), \(r_{M^{*}}(X)=|X|+r_M(E\setminus X)-r_M(E)\).

notation.meaning: rank function of the dual matroid

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-function form of finite-matroid duality.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\), and let \(M^{*}\) be defined by complementary bases. For every subset \(X\subseteq E\), its dual rank is \[r_{M^{*}}(X)=|X|+r_M(E\setminus X)-r_M(E).\] In particular, \(r_{M^{*}}(E)=|E|-r_M(E)\). This formula determines \(M^{*}\) uniquely from \(r_M\) and is involutive: substituting the displayed expression for the rank of \(M^{*}\) recovers \(r_M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual rank equals the subset size plus the primal rank of its complement, minus the primal rank of the whole ground set.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank Duality

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r^D(A)=|A|+r(E\setminus A)-r(E)

children.top_down_role: Duality expressed through closure structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}_{M^{*}}(X)=\{e\in E:|X\cup\{e\}|+r_M(E\setminus(X\cup\{e\}))=|X|+r_M(E\setminus X)\}\).

notation.meaning: rank function of the original matroid

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure obtained by applying the rank-duality formula.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\subseteq E\), dual closure is determined from primal rank by \[\operatorname{cl}_{M^{*}}(X)=\left\{e\in E:|X\cup\{e\}|+r_M\bigl(E\setminus(X\cup\{e\})\bigr)=|X|+r_M(E\setminus X)\right\}.\] Indeed, the displayed equality is precisely \(r_{M^{*}}(X\cup\{e\})=r_{M^{*}}(X)\) after applying rank duality. For \(e\notin X\), it equivalently says that deleting \(e\) from \(E\setminus X\) lowers its primal rank by one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual closure is computed from primal ranks of complements; an outside element is dual-spanned exactly when deleting it lowers the complementary primal rank.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Duality

children.title: Cryptomorphism Compatibility under Duality
children.top_down_role: Compatibility among basis, rank, and closure perspectives after dualization.

assumptions_latex: Each standard cryptomorphism is interpreted on the same labeled ground set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dualizing through bases, ranks, circuits, or closure yields the same matroid \(M^{*}\), and dualization is involutive.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of standard finite-matroid cryptomorphisms with dualization.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53
Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(M^{*}\) by complementary bases. Translating this definition through the standard matroid cryptomorphisms gives the dual rank formula, identifies dual circuits with primal cocircuits, and determines dual closure by rank equality. Conversely, each of these translated data determines exactly the same dual basis family. Hence the diagrams obtained by first converting between bases, ranks, circuits, and closure and then dualizing commute with those obtained in the opposite order. Under every such presentation, dualization remains involutive: \((M^{*})^{*}=M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Converting among bases, rank, circuits, and closure commutes with dualization; every presentation defines the same involutive dual matroid.
knowledge_statements.title: Cryptomorphism Compatibility under Duality

source_witnesses.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53
