knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cographic matroid of \(G\), also called its bond matroid, is \(M^*(G):=M(G)^*\). Thus \(B\subseteq E\) is a basis of \(M^*(G)\) exactly when \(E\setminus B\) is a maximal forest of \(G\). The circuits of \(M^*(G)\) are precisely the bonds: the inclusion-minimal nonempty edge cuts whose deletion increases \(c(G)\). Consequently, \(X\subseteq E\) is independent in \(M^*(G)\) exactly when \(X\) contains no bond of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cographic matroid is the dual of a graph's cycle matroid. Its circuits are the graph's inclusion-minimal nonempty edge cuts, called bonds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cographic Matroids and Graph-Cut Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines cographic matroids as dual cycle matroids and describes their bases, independent sets, circuits, rank, and planar duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), the cographic matroid is \(M^*(G)=M(G)^*\). Its bases are the complements of maximal forests; \(F\subseteq E\) is independent exactly when \((V,E\setminus F)\) has the same number of components as \(G\); and its circuits are the inclusionwise minimal nonempty cuts of \(G\). For every \(F\subseteq E\), \(r_{M^*(G)}(F)=|F|-\kappa(V,E\setminus F)+\kappa(V,E)\). If \(G\) is planar with planar dual \(G^*\), then \(M(G^*)\cong M^*(G)\). A matroid is both graphic and cographic if and only if it is isomorphic to the cycle matroid of a planar graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cographic matroid of a graph is the dual of its cycle matroid. Its bases complement maximal forests, its circuits are minimal nonempty cuts, and its rank is determined by the component count after deleting selected edges. For a planar graph it is the cycle matroid of the planar dual. A matroid is both graphic and cographic exactly when it is the cycle matroid of a planar graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M^*(G)=M(G)^*,\quad r_{M^*(G)}(F)=|F|-\kappa(V,E\setminus F)+\kappa(V,E);\quad G\text{ planar}\Rightarrow M(G^*)\cong M^*(G)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bond Matroids, Cographic Matroids, and Bonds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the bond matroid and cographic class together with the underlying edge-cut terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G\), the dual \(M^*(G)\) of its cycle matroid is called the bond matroid, or cocycle matroid, of \(G\). A matroid \(M\) is cographic if \(M\cong M^*(G)\) for some graph \(G\). For \(X\subseteq E(G)\), \(X\) is an edge cut if \(G\setminus X\) has more connected components than \(G\); an edge \(e\) is a cut-edge if \(\{e\}\) is an edge cut, and an inclusion-minimal edge cut is a bond or cocycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of a graph's cycle matroid is its bond or cocycle matroid, and a matroid is cographic when it is isomorphic to such a dual. An edge cut is a set whose deletion increases the number of connected components; singleton edge cuts are cut-edges, and minimal edge cuts are bonds or cocycles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is cographic}\iff \exists G\;\bigl(M\cong M^*(G)\bigr),\qquad X\text{ is a bond}\iff X\text{ is an inclusion-minimal edge cut of }G.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite bicircular matroid in its pseudoforest formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\mathcal I_B=\{F\subseteq E:\text{every connected component of }(V,F)\text{ contains at most one cycle}\}\). Equivalently, \(F\in\mathcal I_B\) if and only if every nonempty subgraph \(H\) of \((V,F)\) satisfies \(|E(H)|\le |V(H)|\). The family \(\mathcal I_B\) is the independent-set family of a matroid on \(E\), called the bicircular matroid \(B(G)\). Its circuits are the inclusion-minimal edge sets inducing a connected subgraph with two cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bicircular matroid has graph edges as elements and pseudoforests, whose components each contain at most one cycle, as independent sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Bicircular Matroids

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pseudoforest formulation is standard, but no source supports the specialized definition or the circuit characterization. A source should also state the latter using minimal failure of the pseudoforest condition or cyclomatic number two, avoiding ambiguity in “two cycles.”

children.title: Frame Matroids
children.top_down_role: Matroids represented through biased-graph frame structure.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid on ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is a frame matroid exactly when it possesses a basis \(B\) satisfying the stated two-element spanning condition.

notation.meaning: A distinguished basis witnessing the frame property

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite-matroid definition using a framing basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The matroid \(M\) is a frame matroid if there exists a basis \(B\) of \(M\) such that, for every \(e\in E\), some subset \(X_e\subseteq B\) with \(|X_e|\le 2\) satisfies \(e\in\operatorname{cl}_M(X_e)\). Equivalently, after deleting loops, every element \(e\in E\setminus B\) has a fundamental circuit \(C(e,B)\) with \(|C(e,B)|\le 3\). Such a basis \(B\) is called a frame for \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A frame matroid has a basis such that every element is spanned by at most two basis elements; equivalently, each fundamental circuit has at most three elements.
knowledge_statements.title: Frame Matroids

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The framing-basis condition and fundamental-circuit equivalence are mathematically plausible and fit the leaf, but frame-matroid conventions vary and no exact source is supplied.

children.title: Graphic–Cographic Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual relationship between cycle and bond matroids.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite connected plane graph and \(G^*\) is its geometric dual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(G)^*=M(G^*)\) under the natural edge correspondence.

notation.meaning: Cycle matroid of the plane graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Plane-graph form of graphic-cographic duality.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53
0.2 Graph Theory p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Identify each edge \(e\in E(G)\) with the dual edge \(e^*\in E(G^*)\). For every \(B\subseteq E(G)\), \(B\) is a spanning-tree edge set of \(G\) if and only if \(\{e^*:e\in E(G)\setminus B\}\) is a spanning-tree edge set of \(G^*\). Hence the bases of \(M(G)^*\) and \(M(G^*)\) coincide under this correspondence, so \(M(G)^*=M(G^*)\). Thus every planar graphic matroid has a graphic dual, represented by a plane dual graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a connected plane graph, complements of spanning trees correspond to spanning trees of the geometric dual, so the dual cycle matroid is again graphic.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphic–Cographic Duality

children.top_down_role: Containment and separation among the principal graph-derived matroid classes.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is the multigraph with two vertices joined by four parallel edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B(G)\cong U_{2,4}\), while \(U_{2,4}\) is neither graphic nor cographic.

notation.meaning: Bicircular matroid represented by the graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separation of bicircular matroids from graphic and cographic classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every edge subset of \(G\) having at most two elements induces at most one cycle, whereas every three-edge subset induces two cycles. Therefore \(B(G)\cong U_{2,4}\). The matroid \(U_{2,4}\) is not representable over \(\mathbb F_2\), since a rank-two binary vector space has only three nonzero one-dimensional subspaces. Every graphic and every cographic matroid is binary. Consequently, \(B(G)\) is neither graphic nor cographic, so graph-derived matroid constructions do not define a single matroid class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four parallel edges yield the bicircular matroid U(2,4), which is nonbinary and therefore neither graphic nor cographic, separating these graph-derived classes.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Derived Class Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The four-parallel-edge construction does yield the nonbinary matroid U_{2,4}, separating bicircular matroids from graphic and cographic matroids, but none of the nontrivial class-boundary claims has a cited source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-Simplex Characterization of Transversal Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric characterization of loopless rank-$r$ transversal matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $r\geq1$, a loopless rank-$r$ matroid $M$ is transversal if and only if there are disjoint finite subsets $J,S\subseteq\mathbb R^{r-1}$ such that: (i) $|J|=r$ and the elements of $J$ form a simplex; (ii) $M$ is isomorphic to the affine matroid $N$ on $S$; and (iii) every $e\in S$ is freely added to a face $F_e$ of the simplex $J$ such that, for every flat $X$ of $N$ containing $e$, the closure of $X$ in the affine matroid on $S\cup J$ contains $F_e$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A loopless rank-r matroid is transversal exactly when it admits the stated finite affine realization together with an r-element simplex, with each represented element freely added to a suitable face satisfying the specified closure condition for every flat containing it.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is a loopless matroid of rank }r.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is transversal if and only if there exist disjoint finite }J,S\subseteq\mathbb R^{r-1}\text{ satisfying conditions (i)--(iii).}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transversal Matroids and Their Rank Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines transversal matroids from partial transversals and records their bases, rank formula, field representability, and principal subclasses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) be a family of subsets of a finite set \(S\). The partial transversals of \(\mathcal X\) form the independent sets of a matroid on \(S\), called the transversal matroid induced by \(\mathcal X\). It has an inducing subfamily possessing a transversal, so its bases can be represented as full transversals. For every \(U\subseteq S\), \[r(U)=\min_{T\subseteq U}\left(|U\setminus T|+|\{i:X_i\cap T\ne\varnothing\}|\right)=\min_{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}\left(n-|I|+\left|\bigcup_{i\in I}(X_i\cap U)\right|\right).\] Every transversal matroid is representable over all fields except possibly finitely many finite fields. Partition matroids and uniform matroids are special cases of transversal matroids; partition matroids are graphic and cographic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial transversals of a finite family of sets form a transversal matroid. Its bases can be represented as full transversals of a suitable inducing subfamily, and its rank has two equivalent matching-deficiency minimum formulas. Each transversal matroid is representable over all but possibly finitely many finite fields. Partition and uniform matroids are transversal, and partition matroids are graphic and cographic.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\text{ is a family of subsets of a finite set }S
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (S,\{I\subseteq S:I\text{ is a partial transversal of }\mathcal X\})\text{ is a matroid with the stated rank formula}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transversals and partial transversals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines transversals and partial transversals of a finite indexed set family and gives the equivalent bipartite-matching representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be finite and let \(\mathcal A=(A_j:j\in J)\) be a finite indexed family of subsets of \(S\), with repetitions allowed. A transversal is a set \(T\subseteq S\) for which there exists a bijection \(\psi:J\to T\) satisfying \(\psi(j)\in A_j\) for every \(j\in J\). A subset \(X\subseteq S\) is a partial transversal if, for some \(K\subseteq J\), it is a transversal of \((A_j:j\in K)\). Define the bipartite graph \(\Delta[\mathcal A]\) with vertex classes \(S\) and \(J\), where \(xj\) is an edge exactly when \(x\in A_j\). Then \(X\) is a partial transversal if and only if \(\Delta[\mathcal A]\) has a matching that saturates \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transversal chooses a distinct representative from every member of an indexed set family. A partial transversal does so for some subfamily. Equivalently, a subset is a partial transversal exactly when it can be matched injectively to family indices in the associated incidence bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\text{ is a partial transversal of }\mathcal A\iff\Delta[\mathcal A]\text{ has a matching saturating }X.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transversal matroids and their presentations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the matroid presented by a set family and records the stated uniform-matroid and large-field representability properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite family \(\mathcal A\) of subsets of a finite set \(S\), let \(M[\mathcal A]\) denote the matroid on \(S\) whose independent sets are the partial transversals of \(\mathcal A\). A matroid \(M\) is a transversal matroid if \(M\cong M[\mathcal A]\) for some such family \(\mathcal A\); in that case, \(\mathcal A\) is a presentation of \(M\). Every uniform matroid is transversal, and every transversal matroid is representable over every sufficiently large field.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The matroid defined by the partial transversals of a set family A is denoted M[A]. A matroid is transversal if it is isomorphic to M[A] for some A, which is then called a presentation. Uniform matroids are transversal, and transversal matroids are representable over all sufficiently large fields.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gammoids, strict gammoids, and the linkage rank formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines gammoids by vertex-disjoint directed linkage and records their strict representation, bases, and rank formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D=(V,A)$ be a directed graph and let $U,S\subseteq V$. Sets $X,Y\subseteq V$ are linked if $|X|=|Y|$ and there are $|X|$ pairwise vertex-disjoint directed paths with initial-vertex set $X$ and terminal-vertex set $Y$. Set $\mathcal I=\{I\subseteq S:\text{some }U'\subseteq U\text{ is linked to }I\}$. Then $M=(S,\mathcal I)$ is a matroid, called a gammoid. If $S=V$, it is a strict gammoid. Gammoids are exactly restrictions of strict gammoids. In the strict gammoid induced by $(D,U)$, the bases are precisely the sets $B\subseteq V$ such that $U$ is linked to $B$. For every $X\subseteq S$, $$r_M(X)=\min\{|Y|:Y\subseteq V\text{ intersects every directed }U\text{-}X\text{ path}\}.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex sets linkable from subsets of U by pairwise vertex-disjoint directed paths form the independent sets of a gammoid. Strict gammoids use the whole vertex set as ground set, and every gammoid is a restriction of one. Strict-gammoid bases are exactly the sets linked from U, while rank is the minimum size of a vertex set meeting every U-to-X path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M=(S,\mathcal I)\text{ is a gammoid; gammoids are exactly restrictions of strict gammoids, with the stated base and rank characterizations.}

Deletion of elements outside the selected ground set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction, equivalently deletion-minor, passage from strict gammoids to gammoids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The strict gammoid \(N:=L(D,T)\) has ground set \(V\). children.title: Gammoid Representation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of directed-linkage presentations for matroid classes.

assumptions_latex: \(D\) has four source vertices \(S=\{s_1,s_2,s_3,s_4\}\), two targets \(T=\{t_1,t_2\}\), and every arc \(s_i t_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(D,T)|S\cong U_{2,4}\), a gammoid not representable over \(\mathbb F_2\).

notation.meaning: Uniform rank-two matroid on four elements

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary showing that gammoid status does not imply binary representability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A subset \(I\subseteq S\) links to \(T\) exactly when \(|I|\le 2\), because each source reaches either target directly and the paths must have distinct endpoints. Thus \(L(D,T)|S\cong U_{2,4}\). If \(U_{2,4}\) had a rank-two representation over \(\mathbb F_2\), its four nonparallel elements would require four distinct one-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb F_2^2\), but only three exist. Hence this gammoid is not binary. Directed-linkage representability therefore does not imply representability over every field.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete four-source, two-target linkage presentation gives U(2,4), a gammoid that is not binary, so gammoid representation does not ensure every-field linear representability.
knowledge_statements.title: Gammoid Representation Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The linkage construction yields U_{2,4}, and its nonrepresentability over F_2 is correctly stated, but the boundary record lacks a source for the gammoid presentation and representability claim.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence and projective equivalence of matroid matrix representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines equivalence notions for labeled matrix representations over a fixed field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M have rank r\ge 1 on E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}. For i\in\{1,2\}, let A_i be a nonzero matrix over \mathbb F with n columns labeled by E, and suppose the identity on E is an isomorphism M\cong M[A_i]. The representations A_1 and A_2 are equivalent if A_2 is obtainable from A_1 using row interchange, nonzero row scaling, row addition, adjoining or removing a zero row, interchange of labeled columns, nonzero column scaling, and entrywise application of a field automorphism. They are projectively equivalent if such a sequence exists without a field-automorphism operation; otherwise they are projectively inequivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two labeled matrices representing the same positive-rank matroid are equivalent when connected by the seven listed operations. They are projectively equivalent when no field automorphism is used.
assumptions_latex: M\cong M[A_i]\text{ via the identity on }E\quad(i=1,2)
A_1,A_2\text{ are nonzero matrices over }\mathbb F\text{ with columns labeled by }E
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A_1\sim A_2\iff A_2\text{ is obtainable from }A_1\text{ by operations 6.3.1--6.3.7},\qquad A_1\sim_{\mathrm{proj}}A_2\iff\text{such a sequence uses no field automorphism}.

Under this correspondence, matroid circuits are the inclusion-minimal linearly dependent column sets, bases are column bases, and \(r_M(X)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}A[X]\) for every \(X\subseteq E\). A matroid admitting such a matrix is representable over \(\mathbb F\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fundamental-Circuit Incidence Matrix and Partial Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the support matrix associated with a standard matroid representation and chosen basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M be a rank-r matroid with r\ge 1, represented over a field by [I_r\mid D], with columns labelled e_1,\ldots,e_n, and let B=\{e_1,\ldots,e_r\}. Let D^{\#} be obtained by replacing every nonzero entry of D by 1. For k\in\{r+1,\ldots,n\}, the column of D^{\#} indexed by e_k is the incidence vector of C(e_k,B)\setminus\{e_k\}. The matrix D^{\#} is the B-fundamental-circuit incidence matrix of M, and [I_r\mid D^{\#}] is called a partial representation of M.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a standard representation, replacing every nonzero entry of the nonidentity block by 1 produces a matrix whose columns record the basis elements in the corresponding fundamental circuits. This is the basis-fundamental-circuit incidence matrix; adjoining it to the identity is called a partial representation.

B=\{e_1,\ldots,e_r\}\text{ is the basis indexed by the identity columns}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matrix representations of matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Column-independence representations, induced rank functions, and closure of fixed-field representability under duals and minors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}\), let \(S=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and define \(\mathcal I=\{I\subseteq S:\operatorname{rank}(A_I)=|I|\}\). Then \((S,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid represented by the columns of \(A\), and \(r_M(U)=\operatorname{rank}(A_U)\) for every \(U\subseteq S\). A matroid is representable over \(\mathbb F\) when it is isomorphic to one obtained this way. If \(M\) is representable over \(\mathbb F\), then \(M^*\) and every minor of \(M\) are also representable over \(\mathbb F\). Not every matroid is representable over a field.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The linearly independent column subsets of a matrix form a matroid, and the rank of each subset equals the rank of its corresponding submatrix. This defines representability over a field. Representability over a fixed field is preserved by duality and minors, but nonrepresentable matroids exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(S,\{I\subseteq S:\operatorname{rank}(A_I)=|I|\}\right)\text{ is a matroid},\qquad r_M(U)=\operatorname{rank}(A_U),\qquad M\text{ representable over }\mathbb F\Rightarrow M^*\text{ and every minor of }M\text{ are representable over }\mathbb F.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Standard representative matrices of a vector matroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-preserving matrix operations and standard forms relative to a chosen basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}\) have labelled columns and let \(M=M[A]\). The matroid is unchanged by elementary row operations, adjoining or deleting a zero row, permuting columns together with their labels, multiplying a column by a nonzero field element, or applying one automorphism of \(\mathbb F\) entrywise. If \(A\ne0\), operations of the first four kinds, including labelled column permutations, can put the representation in the form \([I_r\mid D]\), where \(r=r(M)\). The identity-column labels form a basis \(B\); \([I_r\mid D]\) is a standard representative matrix with respect to \(B\), and the correspondingly labelled \(D\) is a reduced standard representative matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The listed row, zero-row, labelled-column, scaling, and field-automorphism operations preserve a vector matroid. A nonzero representation can be put in standard form [I_r | D], where r is the matroid rank and the identity-column labels form a basis; D is the associated reduced standard representative.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be full-row-rank matrices over \(\mathbb F\), with columns indexed by the same labeled set \(E\). They are projectively equivalent if there exist an invertible matrix \(P\in\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbb F)\) and an invertible diagonal matrix \(D\in\mathbb F^{E\times E}\) such that \(B=PAD\). Thus projective equivalence permits elementary changes of coordinates in the ambient vector space and independent nonzero rescaling of columns, while preserving column labels. Projectively equivalent matrices represent the same matroid on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two labeled matrix representations are projectively equivalent when one is obtained from the other by invertible row operations and independent nonzero column scalings.
knowledge_statements.title: Projective Equivalence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimal Representations and Projective Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimality and projective comparison of matrix representations of linear matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A representation of a linear matroid is minimal if its rows are linearly independent. For full-row-rank matrices \(A,A'\in K^{r\times n}\), projective equivalence means that there exist \(B\in\operatorname{GL}_r(K)\) and a nonsingular diagonal matrix \(D\in K^{n\times n}\) such that \(A'=BAD\). This is an equivalence relation. Projectively equivalent matrices represent the same matroid, but matrices representing the same matroid need not be projectively equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A representation is minimal when its rows are linearly independent. Two full-row-rank matrices over the same field are projectively equivalent if one is obtained from the other by an invertible row transformation and nonzero column scalings. Projective equivalence preserves the represented matroid, but the converse fails in general.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\sim_{\mathrm{proj}}A'\implies M(A)=M(A'),\qquad M(A)=M(A')\centernot\implies A\sim_{\mathrm{proj}}A'\text{ in general.}

Projective equivalence restricts to an equivalence relation on this set. Its equivalence classes are \([A]_{\mathrm{proj}}=\{PAD:P\in\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbb F),\ D\text{ invertible diagonal}\}\), intersected with \(\operatorname{Rep}_{\mathbb F}(M)\). The representation-equivalence space is the quotient \(\operatorname{Rep}_{\mathbb F}(M)/{\sim_{\mathrm{proj}}}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matroid \(M\) on a fixed labeled ground set \(E\) is uniquely representable over \(\mathbb F\) if it is \(\mathbb F\)-representable and any two full-row-rank \(\mathbb F\)-matrices \(A\) and \(B\) representing \(M\) are projectively equivalent. Equivalently, for every such pair there are \(P\in\operatorname{GL}_{r(M)}(\mathbb F)\) and an invertible diagonal matrix \(D\in\mathbb F^{E\times E}\) satisfying \(B=PAD\). Hence unique representability is exactly the condition that \(\operatorname{Rep}_{\mathbb F}(M)/{\sim_{\mathrm{proj}}}\) has one element.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines regularity through universal field representability; equivalent matrix characterizations are omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite matroid \(M\) is regular if, for every field \(\mathbb F\), there exists a matrix over \(\mathbb F\) whose column-dependence matroid is \(M\). knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is regular}\iff (\forall\text{ fields }\mathbb F)\;M\text{ is representable over }\mathbb F\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular Matroids and Totally Unimodular Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines regular matroids and records their equivalent field-independent representability characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matroid \(M\) is regular if it is representable over \(\mathbb{R}\) by a totally unimodular matrix, that is, a matrix for which the determinant of every square submatrix belongs to \(\{0,1,-1\}\). Equivalently, \(M\) is regular if and only if it is representable over every field. A totally unimodular matrix represents the same matroid over every field.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is regular when it has a real representation by a matrix whose square subdeterminants are all 0, 1, or -1. Equivalently, regular matroids are exactly the matroids representable over every field; a totally unimodular matrix represents the same matroid over every field.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is regular}\iff M\text{ is representable over every field}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-compatible characterization of a positive-rank regular matroid by a real totally unimodular standard representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is representable over a fixed field \(\mathbb F\) if there exists a matrix \(A\in\mathbb F^{r(M)\times E}\), with columns labeled by \(E\), such that for every subset \(I\subseteq E\), one has \(I\in\mathcal I\) exactly when the columns of \(A[I]\) are linearly independent over \(\mathbb F\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is representable over a fixed field when its independent sets are exactly the linearly independent column sets of a matrix over that field.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R_{\mathbb F}\) be the class of finite matroids representable over \(\mathbb F\). A finite matroid \(N\) is an excluded minor for \(\mathbb F\)-representability if \(N\notin\mathcal R_{\mathbb F}\) but every proper minor of \(N\), obtained by at least one deletion or contraction, belongs to \(\mathcal R_{\mathbb F}\). Writing the set of these minimal obstructions as \(\mathcal X_{\mathbb F}\), a finite matroid \(M\) is \(\mathbb F\)-representable exactly when no minor of \(M\) is isomorphic to a member of \(\mathcal X_{\mathbb F}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An excluded minor is minimally nonrepresentable over the fixed field: it fails representability while every proper minor satisfies it.

assumptions_latex: Representability is by finite matrices over fields, with the column-dependence matroid convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Char}(M)\) can depend essentially on field characteristic; specifically, \(\operatorname{Char}(F_7)=\{2\}\) and \(\operatorname{Char}(F_7^-)=\{0\}\cup\{p:p\text{ is prime and }p\ne2\}\).

notation.meaning: Set of field characteristics over which M is representable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-matroid representability over arbitrary fields, including characteristic zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M\), define \(\operatorname{Char}(M)=\{\operatorname{char}(K):K\text{ is a field over which }M\text{ is representable}\}\), where characteristic zero is recorded as \(0\). Representability is not determined solely by rank or ground-set size and may depend sharply on characteristic. The Fano matroid satisfies \(\operatorname{Char}(F_7)=\{2\}\), whereas its relaxation, the non-Fano matroid, satisfies \(\operatorname{Char}(F_7^-)=\{0\}\cup\{p:p\text{ is prime and }p\ne2\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid may be representable only in selected characteristics: the Fano matroid requires characteristic two, while the non-Fano matroid requires characteristic different from two.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduction of Representation Fields by Characteristic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction from an arbitrary representation field to a finite field in positive characteristic or an algebraic number field in characteristic zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that a matroid $M$ is representable over a field $\mathbb F$. If $\operatorname{char}(\mathbb F)=0$, then $M$ is representable over $\mathbb Q(\alpha)$ for some $\alpha$ algebraic over $\mathbb Q$, and hence $M$ is representable over $\mathbb C$.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\mathbb F_q^r\). The ground set of \(\operatorname{PG}(r-1,q)\) is the set of one-dimensional linear subspaces of \(V\). Choose one nonzero vector from each such subspace. A set of projective points is independent exactly when the corresponding chosen vectors are linearly independent over \(\mathbb F_q\); this condition is independent of the choices because replacing a representative by a nonzero scalar multiple preserves linear dependence. Thus \(\operatorname{PG}(r-1,q)\) is a simple rank-\(r\) matroid with \((q^r-1)/(q-1)\) elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projective geometry is the simple linear matroid whose elements are one-dimensional subspaces of a finite vector space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Enumeration in Finite Projective Geometries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts flats, independent sets, and circuits in a finite projective geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\) be a nonnegative integer. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine geometries and affine matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines affine geometry over a field, gives its normalized representation, characterizes finite affine matroids, and records basic finite-geometry invariants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\in\mathbb Z\) with \(n\ge -1\) and a field \(\mathbb F\), the affine geometry \(AG(n,\mathbb F)\) is obtained from \(PG(n,\mathbb F)\) by deleting the points of a hyperplane. Equivalently, after a coordinate choice its points are represented by \(\{(1,x_2,\ldots,x_{n+1}):x_i\in\mathbb F\}\); its isomorphism type is independent of the chosen hyperplane. A finite matroid \(M\) is affine over \(\mathbb F\) if and only if \(M\) has no loops and \(\operatorname{si}(M)\cong AG(n,\mathbb F)|S\) for some \(n\ge-1\) and finite \(S\subseteq AG(n,\mathbb F)\). For a prime power \(q\), \(AG(r-1,q)\) has rank \(r\), has \(q^{r-1}\) elements when \(r\ge1\), and every rank-\(k\) flat is isomorphic to \(AG(k-1,q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine geometry is obtained from projective geometry by deleting a hyperplane and admits a normalized vector representation with first coordinate one. A finite matroid is affine over a field exactly when it is loopless and its simplification is a finite restriction of an affine geometry. Finite affine geometry AG(r−1,q) has rank r, q^(r−1) points for r at least one, and rank-k flats isomorphic to AG(k−1,q).
assumptions_latex: M\text{ and }S\text{ are finite in the affine-matroid characterization}
q\text{ is a prime power for the finite-geometry assertions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: AG(n,\mathbb F)\cong PG(n,\mathbb F)\setminus H,\qquad M\text{ affine over }\mathbb F\iff M\text{ is loopless and }\operatorname{si}(M)\cong AG(n,\mathbb F)|S.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The frame matroid of the complete \(G\)-gain graph with joints is the rank-\(n\) Dowling geometry \(Q_n(G)\).

notation.meaning: Dowling geometry of rank n associated with G

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial definition through complete gain graphs and frame matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take vertices \(1,ldots,n\), one distinguished unbalanced loop at each vertex, and, for every \(i<j\) and \(g\in G\), an edge \(e_{ij}^g\) directed from \(i\) to \(j\). Reversing an edge inverts its gain, and a cycle is balanced when its directed gain product equals \(1_G\). The Dowling geometry \(Q_n(G)\) is the frame matroid of this biased graph: an edge set is independent exactly when it contains no balanced cycle and every connected component contains at most one cycle. The distinguished loops are the joints of the geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Dowling geometry is the frame matroid of a complete group-labeled graph augmented by one unbalanced joint at each vertex.
knowledge_statements.title: Dowling Geometries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The specialized gain-graph convention requires authoritative support. The statement also contains the malformed vertex text "1,ldots,n" and includes explanatory justification unsuitable for a proof-free knowledge statement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dowling Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ground set, balance rule, and circuit description of the Dowling geometry associated with a finite group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A be a finite multiplicative group with identity 1. Set Q_0(A)=U_{0,0}. For r\ge 1, construct K_r^A on vertices \{1,\ldots,r\} with an edge \alpha_{ij} for every 1\le i<j\le r and \alpha\in A, and a distinguished loop b_i at each vertex i. Its ground set is \{b_1,\ldots,b_r\}\cup\{\alpha_{ij}:1\le i<j\le r,\ \alpha\in A\}. A cycle with at least two edges is balanced when the traversal-adjusted product of its group labels is 1; a single-edge cycle and every other cycle are unbalanced. The circuits of Q_r(A) are the balanced cycles and the \Theta-graphs, loose handcuffs, and tight handcuffs having no balanced cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite group A, the Dowling geometry is built from the complete A-labeled graph on r vertices with one distinguished loop at each vertex. Its circuits are the balanced cycles and the theta or handcuff configurations containing no balanced cycle; Q0(A) is the empty rank-zero matroid.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is a finite multiplicative group with identity }1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q_r(A)\text{ is the rank-}r\text{ Dowling geometry with the stated ground set and circuit family.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following conditions are equivalent: \(M\) is representable over \(\mathbb F_q\); and there exists a subset \(X\) of the points of \(\operatorname{PG}(r-1,q)\) such that \(M\cong\operatorname{PG}(r-1,q)|X\). Indeed, in any full-rank \(\mathbb F_q\)-matrix representing a simple matroid, no column is zero and no two columns are scalar multiples, so its columns determine distinct projective points. Conversely, choosing representatives of any set of projective points yields an \(\mathbb F_q\)-matrix for the corresponding restriction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Base-Field Change Rules for Algebraic Independence

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathbb K/\mathbb F be a field extension, and let T,U\subseteq\mathbb K be finite with U algebraically independent over \mathbb F. children.title: Representation Rigidity
children.top_down_role: Constraints on variation among inequivalent representations.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite rank-\(r\) matroid on a labeled ground set \(E\).
\(K\) is a field over which \(M\) is representable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is projectively rigid over \(K\) exactly when all its labeled \(K\)-representations lie in one projective-equivalence class.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projective rigidity for labeled representations over one fixed field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two full-rank \(K\)-matrices \(A\) and \(A'\), with columns labeled by \(E\), are projectively equivalent when \(A'=UAD\) for some \(U\in\operatorname{GL}_r(K)\) and some invertible diagonal \(E\times E\) matrix \(D\). The matroid \(M\) is projectively rigid over \(K\) when every pair of labeled \(K\)-representations of \(M\) is projectively equivalent. This convention permits elementary row changes and independent nonzero column scalings, but does not identify representations using a nontrivial automorphism of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is projectively rigid over a field when every labeled representation differs only by invertible row operations and nonzero column scalings.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation Rigidity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally precise for labeled representations, but rigidity conventions can differ regarding field automorphisms and relabeling; the selected convention requires a source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representability and Representation Multiplicity of Jointed Free Swirls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connectivity, finite-field representability, and multiplicity of inequivalent representations for jointed rank-r free swirls.

children.title: Partial-Field Universality
children.top_down_role: Coordination of field-specific representations through universal partial-field data.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid admitting a partial-field representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Universality means that every partial-field representation of \(M\), up to the stated equivalence, is induced from \(A_M\) by a homomorphism out of \(\mathbb U_M\).

notation.meaning: A universal partial field for M

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal mapping property for partial-field representations of a fixed matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A partial field \(\mathbb U_M\), equipped with a \(\mathbb U_M\)-representation \(A_M\) of \(M\), is universal for \(M\) when the following property holds: for every partial field \(\mathbb P\) and every \(\mathbb P\)-representation \(A\) of \(M\), there exists a partial-field homomorphism \(\varphi:\mathbb U_M\to\mathbb P\) such that the entrywise image \(\varphi(A_M)\) is equivalent to \(A\) under basis changes, row operations, and nonzero column scalings allowed for partial-field representations. The pair \((\mathbb U_M,A_M)\) is unique only up to the corresponding universal isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A universal partial field parametrizes every partial-field representation of a fixed matroid through homomorphisms and standard representation equivalences.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Field Universality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asserted universal property, existence scope, representation equivalence, and uniqueness formulation are specialized and cannot be validated without an authoritative citation.

children.title: Characteristic-Set Realizability

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is characteristic-set realizable if and only if \(S=\operatorname{Char}(M)\) for some finite matroid \(M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential realizability by finite matroids; no classification of realizable sets is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(S\) is characteristic-set realizable when there exists a finite matroid \(M\) such that \[S=\operatorname{Char}(M)=\{\operatorname{char}(K):K\text{ is a field over which }M\text{ is representable}\}.\] Thus realizability requires both directions: every \(c\in S\) occurs as the characteristic of at least one representing field, and no field whose characteristic lies outside \(S\) represents \(M\). The quantifier ranges over all fields, not merely finite fields or prime fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set of characteristics is realizable when it is exactly the set of characteristics of fields representing some finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.title: Characteristic-Set Realizability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement gives a coherent existential definition, but no source establishes the terminology. Its mathematical role is a definition rather than a condition, so the selected content kind also requires correction after sourcing.

knowledge_statements.title: Graphic-Matroid Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision problem for a finite labeled matroid supplied by an independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid presented by an independence oracle. The graphic-matroid recognition problem asks whether there exists a finite undirected multigraph \(G\), with a bijection \(\phi:E\to E(G)\), such that \(X\in\mathcal I\) exactly when \(\phi(X)\) is a forest of \(G\). A positive output may additionally return such a graph \(G\) and bijection \(\phi\); loops of \(M\) correspond to graph loops, and parallel matroid elements correspond to parallel graph edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decide whether the input matroid is the cycle matroid of a graph and, in the constructive version, return such a graph.
assumptions_latex: Access to \(M\) is through an independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is graphic}\iff \exists G,\phi\;\forall X\subseteq E:\ X\in\mathcal I\iff \phi(X)\text{ is a forest of }G.\)

notation.meaning: cycle matroid of the graph G
bijection from matroid elements to graph edges

review_flags: Exact recognition theorem and oracle-complexity source are not supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The decision-problem definition is mathematically coherent and fits the recognition leaf, but no inspectable source supports the oracle model or constructive-output formulation.

children.title: Cographic-Matroid Recognition

knowledge_statements.title: Cographic-Matroid Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition through duality with the cycle matroid of a graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid presented by an independence oracle. The cographic-matroid recognition problem asks whether there exist a finite undirected multigraph \(G\) and a bijection \(\phi:E\to E(G)\) such that \(M\cong M(G)^*\). Equivalently, it asks whether the dual matroid \(M^*\) is graphic. In the constructive version, a positive output returns \(G\) and \(\phi\), thereby representing the cocircuits of \(M\) as the cycles of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decide whether the input matroid is the dual of a graph's cycle matroid; construct the graph when requested.
assumptions_latex: Access to \(M\) is through an independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is cographic}\iff M^*\text{ is graphic}\iff \exists G:\ M\cong M(G)^*.\)
review_flags: Exact constructive recognition source and oracle model require confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual characterization is correct and the definition fits the recognition leaf, but the oracle and constructive formulations have no cited source.

children.title: Regular-Matroid Recognition

knowledge_statements.title: Regular-Matroid Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision problem using representability over every field as the regularity criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid given by an independence oracle. Regular-matroid recognition asks whether \(M\) is representable over every field. Equivalently, it asks whether \(M\) has a real matrix representation that is projectively equivalent to a totally unimodular matrix. A constructive positive output consists of a totally unimodular matrix \(A\), whose columns are labeled by \(E\), such that \(X\subseteq E\) is independent in \(M\) exactly when the columns \(A_X\) are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decide whether a matroid is representable over every field and, constructively, return a totally unimodular matrix representation.
assumptions_latex: Access to \(M\) is through an independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is regular}\iff M\text{ is representable over every field}.\)

notation.meaning: submatrix formed by columns labeled by X

review_flags: A source for the equivalence and the precise recognition algorithm is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The regularity criterion and constructive matrix formulation require an authoritative source, particularly for the oracle-input reconstruction claim and the projective-equivalence wording.

children.title: Recognition-Class Relationships
children.top_down_role: Containments, dual correspondences, plus boundaries separating the three recognition tasks.

knowledge_statements.title: Recognition-Class Relationships
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Containment and duality relations among graphic, cographic, and regular matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every finite matroid \(M\), graphicness and cographicness are exchanged by duality, while regularity is preserved by duality. Every graphic matroid and every cographic matroid is regular. Consequently,
\[
M\text{ graphic}\iff M^*\text{ cographic},\qquad M\text{ regular}\iff M^*\text{ regular},
\]
and
\[
\{\text{graphic matroids}\}\cup\{\text{cographic matroids}\}\subseteq\{\text{regular matroids}\}.
\]
Neither inclusion of the graphic or cographic class in the regular class is an equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphic and cographic classes are dual; both lie properly inside the dual-closed class of regular matroids.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ graphic}\iff M^*\text{ cographic}\), and graphic or cographic \(M\) implies regular \(M\).

knowledge_statements.title: Field-Representability Decision Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representability over a fixed field for an oracle-presented finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a field \(\mathbb F\). Given a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), the \(\mathbb F\)-representability decision problem asks whether there exist an integer \(r\) and a matrix \(A\in\mathbb F^{r\times E}\), with columns labeled by \(E\), such that for every \(X\subseteq E\),
\[
X\in\mathcal I\iff \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A_X)=|X|.
\]
The constructive version must return such a matrix when the answer is positive; its computational complexity depends essentially on how \(M\) and \(\mathbb F\) are encoded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed field, decide whether the matroid's independent sets are exactly the linearly independent column sets of some matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb F\) and its effective encoding are fixed or supplied explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is }\mathbb F\text{-representable}\iff \exists A\in\mathbb F^{r\times E}\;\forall X\subseteq E:\ X\in\mathcal I\iff \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A_X)=|X|.\)

notation.meaning: columns of A indexed by X

review_flags: Complexity varies with the field and input model; no precise source locator was supplied.

children.title: Representation Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Recovery of a representation from oracle data, structural data, or partial representation data.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-to-matrix reconstruction over a specified field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) through an independence oracle and a field \(\mathbb F\), under the promise that \(M\) is \(\mathbb F\)-representable. A representation-reconstruction algorithm queries the oracle and either outputs a matrix \(A\in\mathbb F^{r(M)\times E}\) satisfying
\[
X\in\mathcal I\iff \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A_X)=|X|\quad\text{for every }X\subseteq E,
\]
or reports that reconstruction is unsupported under its stated field or access model. Correctness requires every returned matrix to represent the labeled input matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given oracle access and a representability promise, construct a labeled matrix whose column dependencies reproduce the matroid.
assumptions_latex: An independence oracle for \(M\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ output}\implies M(A)=M.\)
review_flags: Existence and complexity of reconstruction depend on the field and oracle model.
A concrete reconstruction algorithm source is needed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives an output specification rather than a concrete reconstruction algorithm. Whether reconstruction is possible from an independence oracle depends materially on the field and access model, so a precise sourced algorithm is required.

children.title: Representation Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Comparison regimes for deciding whether representations encode the same matroid structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projective equivalence for labeled matrix representations over one fixed field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A,B\in\mathbb F^{r\times E}\) be full-row-rank matrices whose columns share the same labels. They are projectively equivalent over \(\mathbb F\) if there exist \(P\in\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbb F)\) and a nonsingular diagonal matrix \(D\in\mathbb F^{E\times E}\) such that
\[
B=PAD.
\]
Thus equivalence permits invertible row operations and independent nonzero scaling of columns, but no relabeling. Projectively equivalent matrices represent the same labeled matroid because these operations preserve all column-dependence relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two labeled representations are equivalent when invertible row operations and nonzero column scalings transform one into the other.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) have full row rank over the same field.
Their columns have the same fixed labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B=PAD\implies M(B)=M(A).\)

notation.meaning: invertible r by r matrices over the field

review_flags: A source should confirm whether the intended convention also identifies field automorphisms.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated labeled projective-equivalence convention is coherent, but no source establishes that this leaf intends equivalence without relabeling or field automorphisms.

children.title: Reconstruction Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing canonical recovery or uniqueness up to accepted transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Reconstruction Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness relative to labeled projective equivalence over a fixed field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite \(\mathbb F\)-representable matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is uniquely representable over \(\mathbb F\) if any two full-row-rank \(\mathbb F\)-matrices \(A\) and \(B\), with columns labeled by \(E\) and satisfying \(M(A)=M(B)=M\), are projectively equivalent. Explicitly, uniqueness means that there exist \(P\in\operatorname{GL}_{r(M)}(\mathbb F)\) and a nonsingular diagonal matrix \(D\) such that \(B=PAD\). Hence any correct reconstruction determines one equivalence class, not necessarily one literal matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is uniquely representable when all its labeled matrices over the field differ only by row operations and column scalings.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is finite and representable over \(\mathbb F\).
Representations use the same element labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall A,B:\ M(A)=M(B)=M\implies \exists P,D:\ B=PAD.\)
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports unique representability.

children.title: Representation Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Nonuniqueness, incompatible reconstructions, plus field-sensitive ambiguity.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of reconstruction uniqueness over a fixed labeled field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Representation ambiguity occurs when a finite matroid \(M\) has two \(\mathbb F\)-representations \(A\) and \(B\) with the same labeled ground set but no matrices \(P\in\operatorname{GL}_{r(M)}(\mathbb F)\) and nonsingular diagonal \(D\) satisfy \(B=PAD\). In that case an independence oracle determines the matroid but does not determine a unique projective representation. For fields with suitable distinct cross-ratios, rank-two uniform matroids provide families of such inequivalent representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same labeled matroid may have inequivalent matrix representations, so its independence data need not determine a unique reconstruction.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) has at least two representations over \(\mathbb F\).
Equivalence permits only row operations and nonzero column scalings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(A)=M(B)=M\ \land\ \nexists P,D:\ B=PAD\implies M\text{ is not uniquely }\mathbb F\text{-representable}.\)
review_flags: The cross-ratio example requires a precise field-dependent source and formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-of-uniqueness criterion fits the failure-boundary leaf, but the cross-ratio example and its field conditions are too source-dependent to approve without a precise locator.

children.title: Matroid Structural Decomposition Theory
children.top_down_role: Classical structural theory retained at the level needed for representation, recognition, and algorithmic decomposition; enumerative and algebraic invariants are outside this chapter.

children.title: Connected Matroids
children.top_down_role: Structural features of connected matroids, including component boundaries relevant to decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Connected Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connectivity defined by absence of a nontrivial direct-sum separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,r)\) be a finite matroid with \(|E|\ge 2\), and define
\[
\lambda_M(X)=r(X)+r(E\setminus X)-r(E).
\]
The matroid \(M\) is connected if \(\lambda_M(X)>0\) for every nonempty proper subset \(X\subset E\). Equivalently, \(M\) admits no partition \(E=X\mathbin{\dot\cup}Y\) into nonempty sets with \(r(X)+r(Y)=r(E)\); equivalently, every pair of distinct elements belongs to a common circuit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is connected when no nonempty partition separates its rank additively; equivalently, every two elements share a circuit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ connected}\iff \forall\varnothing\ne X\subsetneq E:\ \lambda_M(X)>0.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-cocircuit forced by deletion-critical elements of a circuit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates disconnection after deleting specified circuit elements to the existence of a two-element cocircuit among those elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a connected matroid with at least two elements, and let \(\{e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_m\}\) be a circuit of \(M\). If \(M\setminus e_i\) is disconnected for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m-1\}\), then \(\{e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_{m-1}\}\) contains a two-element cocircuit of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a connected matroid with at least two elements, if deleting each of the first m−1 elements of a circuit disconnects the matroid, then those m−1 elements contain a two-element cocircuit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists C^*\subseteq\{e_1,\ldots,e_{m-1}\}:\ C^*\text{ is a cocircuit of }M\text{ and }\lvert C^*\rvert=2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: The circuit-connectivity relation is an equivalence relation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes that circuit-connectivity partitions every matroid ground set into components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every matroid M, the relation \xi on E(M), defined by
\[
e\mathrel{\xi}f\iff e=f\lor\exists C\in\mathcal C(M)\text{ with }\{e,f\}\subseteq C,
\]
is an equivalence relation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique decomposition into connected components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness up to permutation of the direct-sum decomposition into nonempty connected matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(T_1,\ldots,T_k\) are the connected components of a matroid \(M\), then \[M=(M|T_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus(M|T_k).\] Moreover, if \[M_1\oplus\cdots\oplus M_n=N_1\oplus\cdots\oplus N_m,\] where every \(M_i\) and \(N_j\) is connected and nonempty, then \(m=n\) and there is a permutation \(\sigma\in S_n\) such that \(M_i=N_{\sigma(i)}\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every matroid is the direct sum of its restrictions to its connected components, and any decomposition into nonempty connected summands is unique up to reordering.
assumptions_latex: T_1,\ldots,T_k\text{ are the connected components of }M
M_i\text{ and }N_j\text{ are connected and nonempty in the uniqueness assertion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^k(M|T_i),\quad \left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^nM_i=\bigoplus_{j=1}^mN_j\right)\Rightarrow\left(m=n\land\exists\sigma\in S_n\ \forall i,\ M_i=N_{\sigma(i)}\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterizations and dual invariance of connected matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent rank and circuit criteria for matroid connectedness, together with invariance under duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(S,\mathcal I)\) be a matroid. Then \(M\) is connected if and only if \(r_M(U)+r_M(S\setminus U)>r_M(S)\) for every nonempty proper subset \(U\subset S\). Equivalently, for every \(s,t\in S\), there is a circuit \(C\) of \(M\) containing both \(s\) and \(t\). Moreover, \(M\) is connected if and only if \(M^*\) is connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is connected exactly when every nontrivial partition of its ground set has rank sum strictly greater than the total rank. Equivalently, every two elements lie in a common circuit. Connectedness is invariant under matroid duality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is connected}\iff \forall\,\varnothing\ne U\subsetneq S,\ r_M(U)+r_M(S\setminus U)>r_M(S)\iff \forall s,t\in S\ \exists C\in\mathcal C(M):\{s,t\}\subseteq C,\qquad M\text{ is connected}\iff M^*\text{ is connected}.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard exact two-separation defined by the matroid connectivity function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,r)\) be a finite matroid. A two-separation of \(M\) is a partition \((X,E\setminus X)\) such that
\[
|X|\ge 2,\qquad |E\setminus X|\ge 2,\qquad \lambda_M(X)=1,
\]
where \(\lambda_M(X)=r(X)+r(E\setminus X)-r(E)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-separation partitions the ground set into two sides of size at least two whose ranks exceed the total rank by exactly one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((X,E\setminus X)\text{ is a two-separation}\iff |X|,|E\setminus X|\ge 2\ \land\ \lambda_M(X)=1.\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-connectivity boundary distinguishing direct-sum separations from two-separations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,r)\) be finite and let \(E=X\mathbin{\dot\cup}Y\) with \(X,Y\ne\varnothing\). The partition is a one-sum boundary exactly when
\[
\lambda_M(X)=0,
\]
in which case \(M=M|X\oplus M|Y\). If instead \(|X|,|Y|\ge2\) and \(\lambda_M(X)=1\), the partition is a two-separation. Thus connectivity excludes one-sum boundaries but does not exclude two-separations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Connectivity value zero gives a direct-sum split, whereas value one with both sides of size at least two defines a two-separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_M(X)=0\iff M=M|X\oplus M|Y\), while \(|X|,|Y|\ge2\land\lambda_M(X)=1\) defines a two-separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Three-Connected Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matroids, using the standard separation definition of 3-connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on a ground set \(E\) with rank function \(r\), and define \(\lambda_M(X)=r(X)+r(E\setminus X)-r(E)\). The matroid \(M\) is three-connected if \(|E|\ge 4\) and there is no partition \((X,E\setminus X)\) for which either \(|X|,|E\setminus X|\ge 1\) and \(\lambda_M(X)=0\), or \(|X|,|E\setminus X|\ge 2\) and \(\lambda_M(X)\le 1\). Thus a three-connected matroid has neither a 1-separation nor a 2-separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is three-connected when it has at least four elements and admits neither a 1-separation nor a 2-separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is three-connected}\iff M\text{ has no 1-separation or 2-separation}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matroid \(k\)-connectivity defined by exclusion of all lower-order separations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\ge 2\), and let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\) with \(|E|\ge 2(k-1)\). For \(1\le j<k\), a \(j\)-separation is a partition \((X,E\setminus X)\) satisfying \(|X|,|E\setminus X|\ge j\) and \(\lambda_M(X)\le j-1\). The matroid \(M\) is \(k\)-connected if it has no \(j\)-separation for any \(j<k\). Equivalently, every \(X\subseteq E\) with \(|X|,|E\setminus X|\ge j\) satisfies \(\lambda_M(X)\ge j\) for each \(1\le j<k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite matroid is k-connected when every separation of order below k is excluded, subject to the usual side-size requirements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is }k\text{-connected}\iff M\text{ has no }j\text{-separation for }1\le j<k.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity-Level Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity of the finite matroid connectivity hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\ge 2\), and let \(M\) be a finite matroid. Under the convention that \(q\)-connectivity excludes every \(j\)-separation with \(1\le j<q\), \((k+1)\)-connectivity implies \(k\)-connectivity. Thus the connectivity classes form a nested hierarchy. The reverse implication fails in general: a \(k\)-connected matroid possessing a \(k\)-separation is not \((k+1)\)-connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every (k+1)-connected matroid is k-connected, while a k-connected matroid with a k-separation is not (k+1)-connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is }(k+1)\text{-connected}\Longrightarrow M\text{ is }k\text{-connected}.\)

notation.meaning: a partition of order at most j with both sides of size at least j

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tutte's Triangle Lemma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derives a triad from the failure of two specified triangle-element deletions to preserve 3-connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M$ be a $3$-connected matroid with $|E(M)|\ge 4$, and suppose that $\{e,f,g\}$ is a triangle of $M$. If neither $M\setminus e$ nor $M\setminus f$ is $3$-connected, then $M$ has a triad containing $e$ and exactly one of $f$ and $g$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a 3-connected matroid with at least four elements, if deleting either of two specified elements e and f of a triangle destroys 3-connectivity, then a triad contains e and exactly one of f and g.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists T^*\text{ a triad of }M:\ e\in T^*\text{ and }|T^*\cap\{f,g\}|=1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Criterion for placing one element on either side of an exact separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when adjoining one element to either side of a partition yields exactly k-separating bipartitions for one common integer k.

children.title: Vertical Connectivity

knowledge_statements.title: Vertical Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-based vertical connectivity for finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\). For an integer \(j\ge 1\), a vertical \(j\)-separation is a partition \((X,E\setminus X)\) such that \(\lambda_M(X)\le j-1\) and \(r(X),r(E\setminus X)\ge j\). For \(k\ge 2\), the matroid \(M\) is vertically \(k\)-connected if it has no vertical \(j\)-separation for any \(1\le j<k\). Unlike ordinary connectivity, the side constraints use rank rather than cardinality, so low-rank sides do not witness failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertical k-connectivity excludes lower-order separations whose two sides both have sufficiently large rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is vertically }k\text{-connected}\iff M\text{ has no vertical }j\text{-separation for }1\le j<k.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank-based definition is plausible, but vertical-connectivity indexing and side-rank conventions vary. An authoritative source with a definition-level locator is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertical Separations and Vertical Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines vertical separations, vertical connectivity, and vertical connectedness, with their stated cocircuit consequences and uniform-matroid values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matroid $M$ and a positive integer $k$, a partition $(X,Y)$ of $E(M)$ is a vertical $k$-separation if $\lambda_M(X)<k$ and $\min\{r(X),r(Y)\}\ge k$. Any such separation satisfies $2k-r(M)\le r(X)+r(Y)-r(M)\le k-1$; consequently $k\le r(M)-1$, $\max\{r(X),r(Y)\}\le r(M)-1$, and each of $X$ and $Y$ contains a cocircuit. Conversely, two disjoint cocircuits imply a vertical $k$-separation for some positive integer $k\le r(M)-1$. If $M$ has two disjoint cocircuits, $\kappa(M)$ is the least positive integer $j$ for which $M$ has a vertical $j$-separation; otherwise $\kappa(M)=r(M)$. Hence $\kappa(M)=r(M)$ if and only if $M$ has no two disjoint cocircuits. Moreover, $\kappa(U_{r,n})=n-r+1$ when $n\le 2r-2$, and $\kappa(U_{r,n})=r$ otherwise. A matroid $M$ is vertically $q$-connected when $2\le q\le\kappa(M)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertical k-separation has connectivity value below k while both sides have rank at least k. Vertical connectivity is the least order of such a separation when two disjoint cocircuits exist, and otherwise equals the matroid rank. The extract also gives cocircuit consequences, uniform-matroid values, and the definition of vertical connectedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \kappa(M)=\begin{cases}\min\{j\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:M\text{ has a vertical }j\text{-separation}\},&M\text{ has two disjoint cocircuits},\\r(M),&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

children.title: Cyclic Connectivity
children.top_down_role: Cyclic separation structure plus its dual interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Cyclic Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-rank version of vertical connectivity for finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\), with dual rank function \(r^*\). For \(j\ge 1\), a cyclic \(j\)-separation is a partition \((X,E\setminus X)\) satisfying \(\lambda_M(X)\le j-1\) and \(r^*(X),r^*(E\setminus X)\ge j\). For \(k\ge 2\), the matroid \(M\) is cyclically \(k\)-connected if no cyclic \(j\)-separation exists for \(1\le j<k\). Equivalently, \(M\) is cyclically \(k\)-connected exactly when its dual \(M^*\) is vertically \(k\)-connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cyclic k-connectivity is vertical k-connectivity in the dual matroid and uses dual ranks on both sides of a separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is cyclically }k\text{-connected}\iff M^*\text{ is vertically }k\text{-connected}.\)

notation.meaning: rank function of the dual matroid

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed dual-rank definition is plausible, but the precise cyclic-connectivity convention and its equivalence with vertical connectivity of the dual require an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cyclic Separations and Cyclic Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines cyclic separation, the exceptional circuit-disjointness case, the dual identity, and cyclic n-connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matroid, let \(k\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), and let \((X,Y)\) partition \(E(M)\). The partition is a cyclic \(k\)-separation if \(\lambda_M(X)<k\) and both \(X\) and \(Y\) contain circuits of \(M\). If \(M\) has a pair of disjoint circuits, \(\kappa^*(M)\) is the least positive integer \(j\) for which \(M\) has a cyclic \(j\)-separation; otherwise, \(\kappa^*(M)=r^*(M)\). For every matroid, \(\kappa^*(M)=\kappa(M^*)\). The matroid \(M\) is cyclically \(n\)-connected when \(n\in\mathbb Z\) and \(2\le n\le\kappa^*(M)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cyclic k-separation is a partition with connectivity value below k whose two sides both contain circuits. Cyclic connectivity is the least order of such a separation when a pair of disjoint circuits exists, and otherwise equals the dual rank. It equals the vertical connectivity of the dual. A matroid is cyclically n-connected when 2 ≤ n ≤ its cyclic connectivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (X,Y)\text{ is a cyclic }k\text{-separation}\iff\lambda_M(X)<k\text{ and both }X,Y\text{ contain circuits of }M;\quad \kappa^*(M)=\begin{cases}\min\{j\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:M\text{ has a cyclic }j\text{-separation}\},&M\text{ has a pair of disjoint circuits},\\r^*(M),&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\quad \kappa^*(M)=\kappa(M^*)

knowledge_statements.title: Local Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-theoretic local connectivity between two subsets of a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\) be a finite matroid with rank function \(r\), and let \(X,Y\subseteq E(M)\). The local connectivity of \(X\) and \(Y\) is
\[\sqcap_M(X,Y)=r(X)+r(Y)-r(X\cup Y).\]
It is symmetric and satisfies \(0\le \sqcap_M(X,Y)\le \min\{r(X),r(Y)\}\). If \(X\cap Y=\varnothing\), then \(\sqcap_M(X,Y)\) measures the rank lost when the two restrictions are combined; in particular, it is zero exactly when \(r(X\cup Y)=r(X)+r(Y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local connectivity is the rank overlap between two subsets, computed as the sum of their ranks minus the rank of their union.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sqcap_M(X,Y)=r(X)+r(Y)-r(X\cup Y).\)

notation.meaning: local connectivity of X and Y in M

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Connectivity and Skew Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank definition of local connectivity, its basic identities, its representable interpretation, and the induced notion of skewness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $X,Y\subseteq E(M)$, define $\sqcap_M(X,Y)=r_M(X)+r_M(Y)-r_M(X\cup Y)$. Then $\sqcap_M(X,Y)=\sqcap_M(Y,X)$ and $\sqcap_M(X,E(M)\setminus X)=\lambda_M(X)$. If $X\cap Y=\varnothing$, then $\sqcap_M(X,Y)=r_M(X)-r_{M/Y}(X)$. If $M$ is represented by vectors in a vector space $V$, then $\sqcap_M(X,Y)$ is the dimension of the intersection of the subspaces spanned by $X$ and $Y$. Sets $X$ and $Y$ are skew if and only if $r_M(X\cup Y)=r_M(X)+r_M(Y)$, equivalently $\sqcap_M(X,Y)=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local connectivity is the sum of the ranks of two sets minus the rank of their union. It is symmetric, equals the connectivity function across a set and its complement, has a contraction identity for disjoint sets, and in a vector representation measures the dimension of the intersection of their spans. Two sets are skew exactly when their local connectivity is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sqcap_M(X,Y):=r_M(X)+r_M(Y)-r_M(X\cup Y)

children.title: Connectivity-Variant Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Implications, separations, plus dual correspondences among the named variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity-Variant Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duality comparison among ordinary, vertical, and cyclic connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite matroid \(M\) and every \(X\subseteq E(M)\), duality preserves the connectivity function: \(\lambda_{M^*}(X)=\lambda_M(X)\). Consequently ordinary \(k\)-connectivity is self-dual. Because vertical separations impose rank constraints while cyclic separations impose the corresponding dual-rank constraints, a partition is a cyclic \(j\)-separation of \(M\) exactly when it is a vertical \(j\)-separation of \(M^*\). Therefore \(M\) is cyclically \(k\)-connected if and only if \(M^*\) is vertically \(k\)-connected, and conversely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary connectivity is invariant under duality, while vertical and cyclic connectivity are exchanged by matroid duality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{M^*}=\lambda_M,\qquad M\text{ cyclically }k\text{-connected}\iff M^*\text{ vertically }k\text{-connected}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The self-duality of the connectivity function and exchange of vertical and cyclic connectivity are standard-looking, but the exact convention-dependent claims have no cited source.

children.title: Matroid Connectivity Functions

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Connectivity Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard normalized connectivity function of a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,r)\) be a finite matroid. Its connectivity function is the integer-valued set function
\[\lambda_M(X)=r(X)+r(E\setminus X)-r(E),\qquad X\subseteq E.\]
It is normalized, symmetric, and submodular: \(\lambda_M(\varnothing)=0\), \(\lambda_M(X)=\lambda_M(E\setminus X)\), and
\[\lambda_M(X)+\lambda_M(Y)\ge \lambda_M(X\cap Y)+\lambda_M(X\cup Y)\]
for all \(X,Y\subseteq E\). Moreover, \(\lambda_M(X)\ge 0\), and its small values identify low-order separations of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The matroid connectivity function measures rank interaction across a bipartition and is nonnegative, symmetric, normalized, and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_M(X)=r(X)+r(E\setminus X)-r(E)\) is a normalized symmetric submodular function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Connectivity Function Under Deletion and Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds on connectivity after taking a minor, including the exact equality criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X,C,D$ be pairwise disjoint subsets of $E(M)$. Then $\lambda_{M\setminus D/C}(X)\le \lambda_M(X)$, with equality if and only if $r_M(X\cup C)=r_M(X)+r_M(C)$ and $r_M(E(M)\setminus X)+r_M(E(M)\setminus D)=r_M(E(M))+r_M(E(M)\setminus(X\cup D))$. If, in addition, $C$ is independent and $D$ is coindependent, then $\lambda_{M\setminus D/C}(X)\ge \lambda_M(X)-|C|-|D|$, with equality if and only if $C\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_M(X)$ and $D\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_M^*(X)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting D and contracting C cannot increase the connectivity of a disjoint set X, with equality characterized by two rank identities. If C is independent and D is coindependent, the decrease is at most |C|+|D|, with maximum decrease exactly when C lies in the closure of X and D lies in its coclosure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda_{M\setminus D/C}(X)\le\lambda_M(X);\quad C\text{ independent and }D\text{ coindependent}\Rightarrow\lambda_{M\setminus D/C}(X)\ge\lambda_M(X)-|C|-|D|
