children.title: Matroid Branch-Width
children.top_down_role: Branch decompositions, width regimes, plus structural interpretations of bounded width.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Branch-Width
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branch-width with edge width normalized as \(\lambda_M+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\) with \(|E|\ge 2\). A branch-decomposition is a pair \((T,\tau)\), where \(T\) is a tree whose internal vertices have degree three and \(\tau:E\to L(T)\) is a bijection. Each edge \(e\in E(T)\) determines a bipartition \((A_e,E\setminus A_e)\) from the two components of \(T-e\). Its width is \(\lambda_M(A_e)+1\). The width of \((T,\tau)\) is the maximum edge width, and the branch-width \(\operatorname{bw}(M)\) is the minimum such width over all branch-decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid branch-width minimizes the largest connectivity value, plus one, displayed by an edge of a subcubic leaf-labeled tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{bw}(M)=\min_{(T,\tau)}\max_{e\in E(T)}\bigl(\lambda_M(A_e)+1\bigr).\)

notation.meaning: one side of the bipartition displayed by tree edge e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent, but matroid branch-width conventions differ by a plus-one shift. The selected normalization requires an authoritative definition-level citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Duality and Minor Behavior of Matroid Branch-Width
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States dual invariance, minor monotonicity, and the one-step deletion and contraction bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every matroid \(M\), \(\operatorname{bw}(M^*)=\operatorname{bw}(M)\). For every minor \(N\) of \(M\), \(\operatorname{bw}(N)\le \operatorname{bw}(M)\). For every \(e\in E(M)\), both \(\operatorname{bw}(M\setminus e)\) and \(\operatorname{bw}(M/e)\) belong to \(\{\operatorname{bw}(M)-1,\operatorname{bw}(M)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch-width is invariant under duality and cannot increase upon taking a minor. Deleting or contracting one element preserves branch-width or decreases it by one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{bw}(M^*)=\operatorname{bw}(M),\quad \forall N\preceq M:\operatorname{bw}(N)\le\operatorname{bw}(M),\quad \forall e\in E(M):\operatorname{bw}(M\setminus e),\operatorname{bw}(M/e)\in\{\operatorname{bw}(M)-1,\operatorname{bw}(M)\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Branch-Decomposition and Branch-Width of a Matroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines displayed bipartitions, edge width, decomposition width, and branch-width under the convention permitting unlabelled leaves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A branch-decomposition of a matroid \(M\) consists of a cubic tree \(T\), meaning that every nonleaf vertex has degree three, with at least \(|E(M)|\) leaves and an injective labelling of exactly \(|E(M)|\) leaves by \(E(M)\); additional leaves may be unlabelled. Each edge \(e\in E(T)\) displays the bipartition \((X,E(M)\setminus X)\) induced by the components of \(T\setminus e\). Its width is \(w(e)=\lambda_M(X)+1=r(X)+r(E(M)\setminus X)-r(M)+1\). Define \(w(T)=\max_{e\in E(T)}w(e)\) and \(\operatorname{bw}(M)=\min_T w(T)\), where the minimum is over all such branch-decompositions. Under this convention, \(\operatorname{bw}(M)\ge 1\) for every matroid, including matroids with at most one element.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branch-decomposition labels one leaf for each matroid element in a cubic tree and may have additional unlabelled leaves. Each edge displays a ground-set bipartition and has width equal to its connectivity value plus one. The tree width is the maximum edge width, and branch-width is the minimum tree width. Under this convention every matroid has branch-width at least one.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is a tree whose nonleaf vertices all have degree three, with at least }|E(M)|\text{ leaves and an injective labelling of }|E(M)|\text{ leaves by }E(M)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{bw}(M)=\min_T\max_{e\in E(T)}\bigl(\lambda_M(X_e)+1\bigr)\ge 1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linked edge pairs and linked branch-decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines linkedness using local connectivity between the ground-set portions beyond two decomposition edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\neq g\) be edges of a branch-decomposition \(T\) of a matroid \(M\). Let \(F\) be the subset of \(E(M)\) displayed by the component of \(T\setminus f\) not containing \(g\), let \(G\) be the subset displayed by the component of \(T\setminus g\) not containing \(f\), and let \(P\) be the shortest path in \(T\) containing \(f\) and \(g\). Define \[\kappa_M(F,G)=\min\{\lambda_M(S):F\subseteq S\subseteq E(M)\setminus G\}.\] Every edge of \(P\) has width at least \(\kappa_M(F,G)+1\). The pair \(f,g\) is linked if the minimum edge width on \(P\) equals \(\kappa_M(F,G)+1\), and \(T\) is linked if every pair of distinct edges is linked.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two distinct edges of a matroid branch-decomposition, form the ground-set portions lying beyond them and the path joining them. The pair is linked when the smallest width on that path attains the local-connectivity lower bound plus one. The decomposition is linked when every distinct edge pair is linked.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is a branch-decomposition of a matroid }M
F,G\subseteq E(M)\text{ and }P\text{ are defined from }T,f,g\text{ as stated}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ and }g\text{ are linked}\iff\min_{e\in E(P)}\operatorname{width}(e)=\kappa_M(F,G)+1;\qquad T\text{ is linked}\iff\text{every distinct edge pair is linked}

knowledge_statements.title: Branch-Width via Connectivity Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branch-width as the decomposition width induced by a connectivity function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite and let \(f:2^E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) be symmetric. For a branch-decomposition \((T,\tau)\), define
\[w_f(T,\tau)=\max_{e\in E(T)} f(A_e),\qquad \operatorname{bw}(f)=\min_{(T,\tau)}w_f(T,\tau).\]
For a matroid \(M	o E\), use the shifted connectivity function \(f_M(X)=\lambda_M(X)+1\). Then matroid branch-width is exactly the branch-width of this connectivity system:
\[\operatorname{bw}(M)=\operatorname{bw}(f_M)=\min_{(T,\tau)}\max_{e\in E(T)}\bigl(\lambda_M(A_e)+1\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid branch-width is precisely the branch-decomposition width of its connectivity function under the stated plus-one normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{bw}(M)=\operatorname{bw}(\lambda_M+1).\)

branch-width induced by symmetric function f

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Width Structural Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A branch-decomposition as a certificate of bounded matroid branch-width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,r)\) be a finite matroid and let \(b\ge 1\). A branch-decomposition \((T,\tau)\) certifies \(\operatorname{bw}(M)\le b\) if every edge \(e\in E(T)\), displaying \((A_e,E\setminus A_e)\), satisfies
\[r(A_e)+r(E\setminus A_e)-r(E)+1\le b.\]
The certificate is checked by verifying that \(T\) is subcubic, \(\tau\) bijects \(E\) with its leaves, and the displayed inequality holds for every tree edge. Existence of such a certificate is equivalent to membership in the branch-width-at-most-\(b\) regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subcubic leaf-labeled tree certifies branch-width at most b when every displayed matroid separation has width at most b.
assumptions_latex: Rank values for displayed subsets are available for verification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{bw}(M)\le b\iff \exists(T,\tau)\ \forall e\in E(T):\lambda_M(A_e)+1\le b.\)

notation.meaning: side displayed by tree edge e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A displayed branch-decomposition is a suitable certificate for the bounded-width leaf, but the normalization and rank-access verification model depend on the unsourced branch-width convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Excluded minors for binary matroid branch-width at most three
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes binary matroids of branch-width at most three by excluded minors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary matroid \(M\) satisfies \(\operatorname{bw}(M)\leq3\) if and only if it has no minor isomorphic to any of \[M(K_5),M^*(K_5),M(H_8),M^*(H_8),M(K_{2,2,2}),M^*(K_{2,2,2}),R_{10},N_{11},N_{11}^*,N_{23}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary matroid has branch-width at most three exactly when it excludes the listed ten matroids as minors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{bw}(M)\leq3\iff M\text{ has no minor isomorphic to }M(K_5),M^*(K_5),M(H_8),M^*(H_8),M(K_{2,2,2}),M^*(K_{2,2,2}),R_{10},N_{11},N_{11}^*,\text{ or }N_{23}

knowledge_statements.title: Tutte Linking Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-matroid linking theorem for two disjoint terminal sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\), and let \(S,T\subseteq E\) be disjoint. Define
\[\kappa_M(S,T)=\min\{\lambda_M(X):S\subseteq X\subseteq E\setminus T\}.\]
There is a partition \((C,D)\) of \(E\setminus(S\cup T)\) such that the minor \(N=M/C\setminus D\), whose ground set is \(S\cup T\), satisfies \(N|S=M|S\), \(N|T=M|T\), and
\[\kappa_N(S,T)=\kappa_M(S,T).\]
Thus all nonterminal elements can be contracted or deleted while preserving both terminal restrictions and their minimum separation order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tutte's linking theorem produces a minor on two terminal sets that preserves their restrictions and minimum connectivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists C\mathbin{\dot\cup}D=E\setminus(S\cup T):\ N=M/C\setminus D,\ \kappa_N(S,T)=\kappa_M(S,T),\ N|S=M|S,\ N|T=M|T.\)

notation.meaning: minimum connectivity separating S from T
minor formed by contracting C and deleting D

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is an appropriate theorem for Tutte linking theory, but the exact minor conclusion, preservation of both terminal restrictions, and connectivity normalization require an authoritative theorem-level citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linking Minor Preserving Terminal Restrictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a linking minor that preserves local connectivity and the restrictions on both terminal sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be disjoint subsets of \(E(M)\). Then \(M\) has a minor \(N\) such that \[E(N)=X\cup Y,\qquad \kappa_N(X,Y)=\kappa_M(X,Y),\qquad N|X=M|X,\qquad N|Y=M|Y.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For disjoint sets X and Y in a matroid M, there is a minor on exactly X union Y that preserves their local connectivity and agrees with M when restricted separately to X and to Y.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists N\preccurlyeq M:\ E(N)=X\cup Y,\ \kappa_N(X,Y)=\kappa_M(X,Y),\ N|X=M|X,\ N|Y=M|Y

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tutte's Linking Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minor characterization of local connectivity between disjoint subsets of a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be disjoint subsets of the ground set of a matroid \(M\). Then \[\kappa_M(X,Y)=\max\{\kappa_N(X,Y):N\text{ is a minor of }M\text{ and }E(N)=X\cup Y\}.\]

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \kappa_M(X,Y)=\max_{\substack{N\text{ minor of }M\\E(N)=X\cup Y}}\kappa_N(X,Y)

children.top_down_role: Wheel structure within highly connected matroids plus its splitter-theoretic role.

knowledge_statements.title: Wheel Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the finite rank-wheel matroid as the cycle matroid of a wheel graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(r\ge 3\), let \(W_r\) be the graph obtained from a cycle \(v_1v_2\cdots v_rv_1\) by adjoining a hub \(h\) and the spokes \(hv_i\) for \(1\le i\le r\). The rank-\(r\) wheel matroid is the cycle matroid \(M(W_r)\). Its ground set comprises the \(r\) rim edges and \(r\) spokes, and its bases are precisely the edge sets of spanning trees of \(W_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A wheel matroid is the cycle matroid of a cycle joined to a central hub; its bases are the wheel graph's spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(W_r)\) is a rank-\(r\) graphic matroid on \(2r\) elements.

notation.meaning: wheel graph with r rim vertices and one hub
cycle matroid of a graph G

review_flags: Exact supporting definition locator is absent from the supplied source inventory.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition, content kind, notation, and rank/ground-set claims are mathematically standard and fit the Wheel Matroids leaf, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the record. A source specifically defining wheel matroids is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structural properties of M(K_4)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Class, obstruction, minor-universality, series-parallel, and fragility properties of the rank-three wheel matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cycle matroid $M(K_4)$ is isomorphic to $M(\mathcal W_3)$, the rank-three wheel, and to the tipless binary 3-spike. It is regular, graphic, cographic, self-dual but not identically self-dual, algebraic over every field, and has a transitive automorphism group. It is minor-minimal among non-transversal matroids, among matroids that are not strict gammoids, and among non-gammoids. It is neither base-orderable nor strongly base-orderable. Every three-connected binary matroid with at least four elements has an $M(K_4)$ minor. A connected nonempty binary matroid is a series-parallel network if and only if it has no $M(K_4)$ minor. For every $e\in E(M(K_4))$, neither $M(K_4)\setminus e$ nor $M(K_4)/e$ is three-connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: M(K4) is the rank-three wheel and the tipless binary 3-spike. It has the stated class, obstruction, minor-universality, series-parallel, base-orderability, and connectivity-fragility properties.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is three-connected and binary with }|E(M)|\ge4\text{ for the unavoidable-minor assertion.}
N\text{ is connected, nonempty, and binary for the series-parallel characterization.}
e\in E(M(K_4))\text{ for the deletion-contraction assertion.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M(K_4)\cong M(\mathcal W_3)\text{ and has the stated class, obstruction, minor, and fragility properties.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded catalogue of class membership, duality, symmetry, algebraicity, minor universality, minor avoidance, and 2-roundedness for the rank-4 wheel matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The rank-4 wheel matroid $M(\mathcal W_4)$ is regular, graphic, cographic, self-dual but not identically self-dual, and has a non-transitive automorphism group. knowledge_statements.title: Whirl Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard relaxation definition of a finite whirl.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M(W_r)\) be the rank-\(r\) wheel matroid for \(r\ge 3\), and let \(R\) be its set of rim edges. The set \(R\) is a circuit-hyperplane of \(M(W_r)\). The rank-\(r\) whirl \(\mathcal W^r\) is the relaxation of \(R\): its collection of bases is \[\mathcal B(\mathcal W^r)=\mathcal B(M(W_r))\cup\{R\}.\] Thus the relaxation makes the rim a basis while leaving every former wheel basis unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-r whirl is obtained from the rank-r wheel matroid by relaxing its rim circuit-hyperplane, thereby declaring the rim to be a basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal W^r\) is the rank-\(r\) relaxation of \(M(W_r)\) at its rim.
review_flags: Exact supporting definition locator is absent from the supplied source inventory.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relaxation definition is standard and fits the Whirl Matroids leaf, but the record supplies no source for the rim circuit-hyperplane claim or the stated basis description of the relaxation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Properties of the rank-three whirl
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representability, class, duality, fragility, and relaxation properties of $\mathcal W^3$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The matroid $\mathcal W^3$ is the rank-three whirl. It is $\mathbb F$-representable if and only if $|\mathbb F|\ge 3$, and it is near-regular. It is neither graphic, cographic, nor regular, but it is transversal, a strict gammoid, a gammoid, self-dual but not identically self-dual, and algebraic over every field. Its automorphism group is non-transitive. For every $e\in E(\mathcal W^3)$, neither $\mathcal W^3\setminus e$ nor $\mathcal W^3/e$ is three-connected. It is the unique relaxation of $M(K_4)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rank-three whirl has the stated representability, class-membership, duality, automorphism, connectivity-fragility, algebraicity, and unique-relaxation properties.
assumptions_latex: e\in E(\mathcal W^3)\text{ for the deletion-contraction assertion.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal W^3\text{ has the stated representability, class, duality, fragility, and unique-relaxation properties.}

children.title: Deletion–Contraction Fragility
children.top_down_role: Elements whose deletion or contraction disrupts the required connectivity regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Deletion–Contraction Fragility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines fragility relative to a fixed minor in finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) and \(N\) be finite matroids. The matroid \(M\) is \(N\)-fragile if \(N\) is a minor of \(M\) and, for every \(e\in E(M)\), at most one of \(M\backslash e\) and \(M/e\) has an \(N\)-minor. Equivalently, no element is simultaneously deletable and contractible while preserving an \(N\)-minor. An element may nevertheless be essential, meaning that neither operation preserves such a minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is N-fragile when it has an N-minor but no element can be both deleted and contracted while retaining an N-minor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is }N\text{-fragile}\iff N\preccurlyeq M\text{ and }\forall e\in E(M),\;\neg(N\preccurlyeq M\backslash e\text{ and }N\preccurlyeq M/e)\).

notation.meaning: N is isomorphic to a minor of M

review_flags: Terminology varies between fragile and strictly fragile; an exact source is required to certify this convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement coherently defines fragility as absence of N-flexible elements and correctly distinguishes essential elements, but published conventions differ between N-fragile and strictly N-fragile. An exact definition locator is required before selecting this convention.

children.title: Wheel–Whirl Exceptional Regimes
children.top_down_role: Exceptional cases where ordinary splitter extensions require separate treatment.

knowledge_statements.title: Wheel–Whirl Exceptional Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records why wheels and whirls require exceptions in literal splitter statements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r\ge 3\), let \(M\) be the wheel \(M(W_r)\) or the whirl \(\mathcal W^r\). For every \(e\in E(M)\), neither \(M\backslash e\) nor \(M/e\) is 3-connected: one operation exposes a series class and the dual operation exposes a parallel class. Consequently, a splitter assertion demanding a proper 3-connected single-element deletion or contraction cannot be applied literally within a wheel or whirl chain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every single deletion or contraction of a wheel or whirl destroys 3-connectivity, so literal one-element splitter conclusions need an exceptional clause.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall e\in E(M),\;M\backslash e\text{ and }M/e\text{ are not 3-connected}\).
review_flags: A precise wheel–whirl splitter-exception locator is not supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind fits the leaf and the claim is consistent with the standard wheel-whirl obstruction, but no source verifies the universal deletion/contraction statement, including its asserted series/parallel behavior for all ranks covered.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tutte's Wheels-and-Whirls Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the 3-connected matroids for which neither deletion nor contraction of any element preserves 3-connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a 3-connected matroid with \(|E(M)|\ge 1\). The following are equivalent: (i) for every \(e\in E(M)\), neither \(M\setminus e\) nor \(M/e\) is 3-connected; (ii) \(r(M)\ge 3\) and \(M\) is isomorphic to a wheel or a whirl.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty 3-connected matroid loses 3-connectivity under both deletion and contraction of every element exactly when it has rank at least three and is a wheel or whirl.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall e\in E(M),\ M\setminus e\text{ is not 3-connected and }M/e\text{ is not 3-connected}\right]\iff\left[r(M)\ge 3\text{ and }M\text{ is isomorphic to a wheel or a whirl}\right].

children.title: Classical Splitter Regime
children.top_down_role: Scope, hypotheses, plus structural reach of the classical splitter result.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Splitter Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-matroid form of the classical Splitter Theorem with the wheel–whirl proviso.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) and \(N\) be 3-connected finite matroids such that \(N\) is a proper minor of \(M\) and \(|E(N)|\ge 4\). If \(N\) is a wheel or whirl, additionally suppose that \(M\) has no wheel or whirl minor, respectively, with more elements than \(N\). Then some \(e\in E(M)\) satisfies one of the following: \(M\backslash e\) is 3-connected and has an \(N\)-minor, or \(M/e\) is 3-connected and has an \(N\)-minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside the stated wheel–whirl obstruction, a proper 3-connected minor can be retained after a deletion or contraction that preserves 3-connectivity.
assumptions_latex: \(N\) is a proper minor of \(M\) and \(|E(N)|\ge 4\)
The wheel–whirl maximality proviso holds when applicable
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists e\in E(M)\) such that \((N\preccurlyeq M\backslash e\text{ and }M\backslash e\text{ is 3-connected})\) or \((N\preccurlyeq M/e\text{ and }M/e\text{ is 3-connected})\).

notation.meaning: N is isomorphic to a minor of M

review_flags: The supplied inventory contains no exact Splitter Theorem locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is appropriately classified as a theorem and resembles the classical Splitter Theorem, but the precise wheel-whirl maximality proviso and the size hypotheses vary among formulations. No exact theorem locator is supplied, so the hypotheses and conclusion cannot be certified.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Splitter-Based Decomposition of a Minor-Closed Matroid Class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition under a one-element 3-connected extension gap and wheel–whirl maximality assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal N\) be closed under isomorphism and minors, and let \(N\in\mathcal N\) be 3-connected with \(|E(N)|\ge 4\). Assume that no 3-connected member of \(\mathcal N\) with an \(N\)-minor has exactly \(|E(N)|+1\) elements. If \(N\) is a wheel, assume that \(\mathcal N\) contains no larger wheel; if \(N\) is a whirl, assume that \(\mathcal N\) contains no larger whirl. Then every matroid in \(\mathcal N\) can be obtained by a sequence of direct sums and 2-sums from copies of \(N\) and members of \(\mathcal N\) having no \(N\)-minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated extension-gap and wheel–whirl maximality assumptions, every member of the minor-closed class decomposes through direct sums and 2-sums into copies of N and class members without an N-minor.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal N\text{ is closed under isomorphism and minors}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-element test for a matroid splitter
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient splitter criterion for a 3-connected matroid in a minor-closed class, including wheel–whirl maximality conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal N be a class of matroids closed under minors and isomorphism. Let N\in\mathcal N be 3-connected with |E(N)|\ge 4. Suppose that, if N is a wheel, it is the largest wheel in \mathcal N, and, if N is a whirl, it is the largest whirl in \mathcal N. If no 3-connected member of \mathcal N has N as a minor and exactly one more element than N, then N is a splitter for \mathcal N; that is, no 3-connected member of \mathcal N has N as a proper minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a minor- and isomorphism-closed matroid class, let N be 3-connected with at least four elements and maximal among the class's wheels or whirls when applicable. If no 3-connected class member with exactly one more element has N as a minor, then N is a splitter, so no 3-connected class member has N as a proper minor.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal N\text{ is closed under minors and isomorphism}
N\text{ is a wheel}\Rightarrow N\text{ is the largest wheel in }\mathcal N
N\text{ is a whirl}\Rightarrow N\text{ is the largest whirl in }\mathcal N
\nexists M\in\mathcal N:\ M\text{ is 3-connected},\ |E(M)|=|E(N)|+1,\ N\preccurlyeq M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N\text{ is a splitter for }\mathcal N

knowledge_statements.title: Constructive Splitter Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterated sequence form of the classical splitter conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the classical Splitter Theorem hypotheses, there is a sequence \(N=M_0,M_1,\ldots,M_k=M\) of 3-connected matroids such that each \(M_i\) is a minor of \(M\) and \(|E(M_i)|=|E(N)|+i\). For every \(i<k\), the matroid \(M_{i+1}\) is a single-element extension or single-element coextension of \(M_i\). Equivalently, deleting or contracting the newly added element of \(M_{i+1}\) recovers \(M_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The splitter theorem can be iterated into a chain from N to M whose 3-connected members differ by one extension or coextension.
assumptions_latex: The hypotheses of the classical Splitter Theorem hold for \(M\) and \(N\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N=M_0\prec M_1\prec\cdots\prec M_k=M\), with every \(M_i\) 3-connected and \(|E(M_{i+1})\setminus E(M_i)|=1\).

notation.meaning: the ground-set size difference between M and N

review_flags: The sequence formulation requires an exact splitter-theorem source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A sequence representation fits the leaf, but an exact source is needed to justify iteration of the splitter conclusion through every intermediate matroid. The conclusion also uses the undefined relation symbol \(\prec\) and literal ground-set differences despite the statement formulating the objects only as minors up to isomorphism.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constructive splitter sequence between 3-connected minors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A splitter-theorem corollary giving a chain of 3-connected single-element reductions from a matroid to a specified minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) and \(N\) be 3-connected matroids such that \(N\) is a minor of \(M\) and \(|E(N)|\ge 4\). Assume that if \(N\) is a wheel, then \(M\) has no larger wheel as a minor, and if \(N\) is a whirl, then \(M\) has no larger whirl as a minor. Then there are 3-connected matroids \(M_0,M_1,\ldots,M_n\) with \(M_0\cong N\) and \(M_n=M\) such that, for every \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), \(M_i\) is a single-element deletion or a single-element contraction of \(M_{i+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If N is a 3-connected minor of a 3-connected matroid M, has at least four elements, and satisfies the stated wheel or whirl maximality condition, then N and M are joined by a sequence of 3-connected matroids whose successive backward steps are single-element deletions or contractions.
assumptions_latex: N\text{ is a wheel}\implies M\text{ has no larger wheel as a minor}
N\text{ is a whirl}\implies M\text{ has no larger whirl as a minor}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists M_0,\ldots,M_n:\ M_0\cong N,\ M_n=M,\ \text{each }M_i\text{ is 3-connected, and each }M_i\text{ is a single-element deletion or contraction of }M_{i+1}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-step splitter minor theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a connected, simple, cosimple intermediate minor differing from N by one deletion or contraction, subject to wheel–whirl boundary hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let N be a nonempty, connected, simple, cosimple minor of a 3-connected matroid M. Suppose that, if N is a wheel, M has no larger wheel as a minor, and, if N is a whirl, M has no larger whirl as a minor. Then either M=N, or M has a connected, simple, cosimple minor M_1 such that M_1\setminus e\cong N or M_1/e\cong N for some e\in E(M_1). Moreover, if N is 3-connected, then M_1 is 3-connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let N be a nonempty connected, simple, and cosimple minor of a 3-connected matroid M, with no larger wheel or whirl minor when N is respectively a wheel or whirl. Either M equals N, or M has a connected, simple, and cosimple minor M1 from which one deletion or contraction produces N. If N is 3-connected, M1 is also 3-connected.
assumptions_latex: N\text{ is a nonempty, connected, simple, cosimple minor of }M
N\text{ is a wheel}\Rightarrow M\text{ has no larger wheel minor}
N\text{ is a whirl}\Rightarrow M\text{ has no larger whirl minor}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M=N\ \lor\ \exists M_1\preccurlyeq M\ \exists e\in E(M_1):\ M_1\text{ is connected, simple, and cosimple},\ (M_1\setminus e\cong N\ \lor\ M_1/e\cong N),\text{ and }(N\text{ 3-connected}\Rightarrow M_1\text{ 3-connected})

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simple 3-Connected Single-Edge Coextensions by Vertex Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphical characterization of single-edge coextensions preserving simplicity and 3-connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a simple 3-connected graph, and suppose that \(G\) is a single-edge coextension of \(H\). Then \(G\) is simple and 3-connected if and only if \(G\) can be obtained from \(H\) by splitting a vertex of degree at least four into two vertices of degree at least three.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-edge coextension of a simple 3-connected graph is simple and 3-connected exactly when it comes from splitting a vertex of degree at least four into two vertices, each of degree at least three.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a single-edge coextension of }H
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is simple and 3-connected}\iff G\text{ is obtainable from }H\text{ by splitting a vertex of degree at least four into two vertices of degree at least three}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Step Contraction-or-Deletion Splitter Alternative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual two-element reductions preserving a specified 3-connected minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) be a 3-connected minor of a 3-connected matroid \(M\), with \(|E(N)|\ge 4\). If \(|E(M)-E(N)|\ge 5\), then there are distinct \(x,y\in E(M)\) such that either each of \(\operatorname{si}(M/x)\), \(\operatorname{si}(M/y)\), and \(\operatorname{si}(M/x,y)\) is 3-connected and has an \(N\)-minor, or each of \(\operatorname{co}(M\setminus x)\), \(\operatorname{co}(M\setminus y)\), and \(\operatorname{co}(M\setminus x,y)\) is 3-connected and has an \(N\)-minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If at least five elements separate a 3-connected matroid from its 3-connected minor, two elements admit either an individual-and-joint contraction reduction or an individual-and-joint deletion reduction preserving 3-connectivity and the minor after simplification or cosimplification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constructive 3-Connected Splitter Sequence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A stepwise splitter sequence under circuit and cocircuit size restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) be a 3-connected minor of a 3-connected matroid \(M\), and suppose that \(N\) has no circuits or cocircuits with fewer than four elements. Then there is a sequence \(M_0,M_1,\ldots,M_n\) of 3-connected matroids with \(M_0=N\) and \(M_n=M\) such that, for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), there is an element \(e_i\in E(M_i)\) for which \(M_{i-1}\) is a cosimple matroid associated with \(M_i\setminus e_i\), or a simple matroid associated with \(M_i/e_i\), and \(|E(M_i)-E(M_{i-1})|\le 2\).

N\text{ has no circuit or cocircuit with fewer than four elements}

children.top_down_role: Variants imposing stronger connectivity, representation, or sequence-control requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Strengthened Splitter Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong sequence form controlling consecutive extensions and coextensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the classical splitter hypotheses, the 3-connected sequence from \(N\) to \(M\) can, after dualizing if necessary, be chosen in blocks containing at most two consecutive single-element extensions followed by at most one single-element coextension. Whenever a block adds two extension elements and then one coextension element, its three new elements form a triad in the matroid at the end of that block. Thus both intermediate size and the local configuration of added elements are controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong splitter sequence can bound consecutive extensions and coextensions; a maximal three-element block creates a triad.
assumptions_latex: The classical splitter hypotheses hold for \(M\) and \(N\)
Dualization of the sequence is allowed
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence may be ordered into extension–coextension blocks of size at most \(3\), with every size-\(3\) block's new elements forming a triad.
review_flags: Strong Splitter Theorem formulations have technical size and ordering conventions that require source verification.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem content kind fits the strengthened-variant leaf, but strong splitter theorems have formulation-sensitive ordering, fan/triad, size, and exception hypotheses. The informal block formulation cannot be certified without a specific theorem citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Splitter Minor Retaining a Prescribed External Element
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A marked-element splitter variant with a ground-set gap of at most four.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) be a 3-connected minor of a 3-connected matroid \(M\). Suppose that \(|E(N)|\ge 4\) and \(e\in E(M)-E(N)\). Then \(M\) has a 3-connected minor \(M_1\) having \(N\) as a minor such that \(e\in E(M_1)\) and \(|E(M_1)-E(N)|\le 4\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a prescribed element e of M outside a 3-connected minor N of size at least four, there is a 3-connected minor M1 that retains e, still has N as a minor, and contains at most four ground-set elements outside N.
assumptions_latex: N\text{ is a 3-connected minor of the 3-connected matroid }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,M_1\preceq M\text{ 3-connected}:\ N\preceq M_1,\ e\in E(M_1),\ |E(M_1)-E(N)|\le 4

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A designated-element splitter variant preserving the root up to e-isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) be a 3-connected proper minor of a 3-connected matroid \(M\). Suppose that \(|E(N)|\ge 4\) and \(e\in E(N)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded-Gap Splitter Variant via Simplification or Cosimplification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A splitter variant allowing simplification or cosimplification and a ground-set gap of at most three.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) be a 3-connected proper minor of a 3-connected matroid \(M\). Then \(M\) has a 3-connected minor \(M_1\) and an element \(e\in E(M_1)\) such that \(N\) is a cosimple matroid associated with \(M_1\setminus e\), or a simple matroid associated with \(M_1/e\), and \(|E(M_1)-E(N)|\le 3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every 3-connected proper minor N of a 3-connected matroid M is associated, through cosimplification after deletion or simplification after contraction, with a one-element reduction of a 3-connected minor M1 whose ground set has at most three elements outside N.

knowledge_statements.title: Splitter Exceptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested wheels and whirls refute the splitter conclusion without its exceptional proviso.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(r\ge 3\), the rank-\(r\) wheel \(M(W_r)\) is a proper minor of \(M(W_{r+1})\), and the rank-\(r\) whirl \(\mathcal W^r\) is a proper minor of \(\mathcal W^{r+1}\). Nevertheless, for every element \(e\) of the larger matroid, both its deletion and contraction fail to be 3-connected. Hence omitting the wheel–whirl maximality proviso makes the literal single-element conclusion of the classical Splitter Theorem false.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pairs \((M(W_{r+1}),M(W_r))\) and \((\mathcal W^{r+1},\mathcal W^r)\) violate the unqualified splitter conclusion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minor-Closed Classes and Excluded Minors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines minor-closed matroid classes and their minor-minimal obstructions and states the resulting obstruction characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A class \(\mathcal C\) of matroids is minor-closed if every minor of every \(M\in\mathcal C\) also belongs to \(\mathcal C\). A matroid \(N\) is an excluded minor for \(\mathcal C\) if \(N\notin\mathcal C\) but every proper minor of \(N\) lies in \(\mathcal C\). Every minor-closed class of finite matroids is characterized by its excluded minors: \(M\in\mathcal C\) if and only if no excluded minor for \(\mathcal C\) is a minor of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid class is minor-closed when it contains every minor of each member. An excluded minor is a matroid outside the class whose every proper minor belongs to the class. For finite matroids, a minor-closed class consists exactly of the matroids having none of its excluded minors as a minor.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\in\mathcal C\iff\text{ no excluded minor for }\mathcal C\text{ is a minor of }M\).

knowledge_statements.title: Duality across Obstruction Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes how excluded-minor families transform under matroid duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be a minor-closed class of finite matroids, and define \(\mathcal C^*=\{M^*:M\in\mathcal C\}\). If \(\operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C)\) denotes the excluded minors for \(\mathcal C\), then \[\operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C^*)=\{X^*:X\in\operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C)\}.\] Hence graphic and cographic obstruction families are dual, while the regular obstruction family is closed under duality because \(U_{2,4}\) is self-dual and \(F_7^*=F_7^*\) pairs with \(F_7\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing a minor-closed class dualizes every excluded minor; graphic and cographic obstructions correspond, while regular obstructions are duality-invariant.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a minor-closed class of finite matroids
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C^*)=\operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C)^*\).

notation.meaning: class consisting of duals of members of C

The family may be chosen as the excluded minors: every \(N\in\mathcal{X}_q\) is not representable over \(\operatorname{GF}(q)\), while every proper minor of \(N\) is representable over \(\operatorname{GF}(q)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes ternary representability by four forbidden minors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matroid \(M\) is ternary if and only if \(M\) has no minor isomorphic to \(U_{2,5}\), \(U_{3,5}\), \(F_7\), or \(F_7^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is ternary exactly when it has no minor isomorphic to U(2,5), U(3,5), F7, or the dual of F7.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is ternary}\iff M\text{ has no minor isomorphic to }U_{2,5},U_{3,5},F_7,\text{ or }F_7^*.

children.title: Graphic Decomposition Pieces
children.top_down_role: Graphic building blocks appearing in regular-matroid decompositions.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite graph, with loops and parallel edges permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A regular-matroid decomposition leaf is graphic when it is isomorphic to \(M(G)\) for some finite graph \(G\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphic leaves in a regular-matroid decomposition.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graphic matroid of a finite graph \(G\) is the matroid \(M(G)\) on \(E(G)\) whose independent sets are precisely the edge sets containing no graph cycle. Equivalently, its circuits are the edge sets of graph cycles, including a loop as a one-edge cycle and a parallel pair as a two-edge cycle. A graphic decomposition piece is a matroid isomorphic to \(M(G)\) for some \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graphic piece is a cycle matroid: its independent sets are forests and its circuits are graph cycles.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphic Decomposition Pieces

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Cographic Decomposition Pieces
children.top_down_role: Cographic building blocks appearing through dual graphic structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A regular-matroid decomposition leaf is cographic when it is isomorphic to \(M(G)^*\) for some finite graph \(G\).

notation.meaning: the bond matroid, dual to the cycle matroid of G

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cographic leaves in a regular-matroid decomposition.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cographic matroid associated with a finite graph \(G\) is the dual \(M(G)^*\) of its cycle matroid. Its circuits are exactly the bonds of \(G\), namely the inclusion-minimal nonempty edge cuts. A cographic decomposition piece is a matroid isomorphic to \(M(G)^*\) for some \(G\); equivalently, it is the dual of a graphic matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cographic piece is dual to a cycle matroid, and its circuits are the graph's minimal nonempty cuts.
knowledge_statements.title: Cographic Decomposition Pieces

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Sporadic Decomposition Pieces
children.top_down_role: Exceptional finite building blocks outside the graphic or cographic families.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sporadic leaf type in Seymour's regular-matroid decomposition is the matroid \(R_{10}\).

notation.meaning: the ten-element rank-five sporadic regular matroid

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The exceptional leaf type in the regular-matroid decomposition theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(R_{10}\) as the binary vector matroid represented by the \(5\times 10\) matrix \([I_5\mid J_5-I_5]\) over \(\operatorname{GF}(2)\). It is a ten-element rank-five regular matroid that is neither graphic nor cographic. In the piece taxonomy for regular-matroid decomposition, the sporadic pieces are precisely leaves isomorphic to \(R_{10}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sole sporadic leaf type is the ten-element rank-five regular matroid R10, which is neither graphic nor cographic.
knowledge_statements.title: Sporadic Decomposition Pieces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The R10 representation and its role as Seymour's exceptional piece require an inspectable authoritative source; none is cited.

children.title: Piece-Type Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Compatibility boundaries governing how distinct piece types participate in a decomposition.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are binary matroids with identified overlap \(T=E(M_1)\cap E(M_2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface is deleted after gluing, so the recomposed ground set is \((E(M_1)\cup E(M_2))\setminus T\).

notation.meaning: a k-sum of the two pieces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface sizes and deletion convention for binary 1-, 2-, and 3-sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the binary-sum representation of a decomposition edge, a \(1\)-sum has \(T=\varnothing\), a \(2\)-sum uses an identified one-element set \(T\), and a \(3\)-sum uses an identified three-element set \(T\). For a proper \(2\)-sum the interface element is neither a loop nor a coloop in either piece. For a proper binary \(3\)-sum, \(T\) is a circuit in each piece and contains no cocircuit of either piece. The interface elements are auxiliary and are deleted from the recomposed matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decomposition edges carry empty, one-element, or three-element interfaces, with nondegeneracy conditions and deletion after gluing.
knowledge_statements.title: Piece-Type Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Interface sizes, nondegeneracy predicates, and deletion conventions vary among formulations and require a cited primary convention.

children.title: Binary Three-Sums
children.top_down_role: Binary three-sum structure plus its role in regular-matroid decomposition.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are binary matroids with \(E(M_1)\cap E(M_2)=T\).
\(T\) has three elements, is a circuit of each matroid, and contains no cocircuit of either.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The specified cycle family determines the binary three-sum \(M_1\oplus_3 M_2\) on \((E(M_1)\cup E(M_2))\setminus T\).

notation.meaning: the family of cycles of M

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle-space definition of a proper binary three-sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The binary three-sum \(M=M_1\oplus_3 M_2\) has ground set \((E(M_1)\cup E(M_2))\setminus T\). Its cycles are the sets
\[
\mathcal{Z}(M)=\{Z_1\triangle Z_2: Z_i\in\mathcal{Z}(M_i),\ Z_1\cap T=Z_2\cap T\}.
\]
Because the traces on \(T\) agree, every displayed symmetric difference avoids \(T\). The resulting family is a binary cycle space and therefore determines a binary matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary three-sum matches the two cycle spaces along a common triangle and then removes that triangle.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Three-Sums

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cycle-space formula is plausible and well formed, but its hypotheses and exact binary three-sum convention are unsupported by a citation.

children.title: Three-Sum Recomposition
children.top_down_role: Recovery of a global matroid from compatible decomposition pieces.

assumptions_latex: A rooted binary tree has leaf matroids and internal nodes labeled by valid binary \(1\)-, \(2\)-, or \(3\)-sum interfaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The matroid stored at the root is the recomposition represented by the entire decomposition tree.

notation.meaning: the matroid recomposed at tree node v
the sum type labeling an internal node

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bottom-up recomposition of a binary decomposition tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize each leaf \(v\) with its supplied matroid \(M_v\). Process internal nodes in postorder. If \(v\) has children \(a,b\), validate their identified interface and set \(M_v=M_a\oplus_{k_v}M_b\), deleting the interface elements according to the chosen sum convention. Stop after processing the root \(r\), and output \(M_r\). If any interface fails its size, circuit, cocircuit, or element-identification conditions, output an invalid-decomposition report instead of a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recompose a decomposition tree bottom-up, validating each interface and applying its indicated one-, two-, or three-sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Three-Sum Recomposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits recomposition, but correctness depends on exact sum conventions and interface-validation rules for which no source is supplied.

children.title: Three-Sum Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Boundary data controlling which decomposition pieces can be recomposed.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are binary matroids and \(T=E(M_1)\cap E(M_2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under these predicates, the cycle-space gluing along \(T\) defines a proper binary three-sum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility predicate for a proper binary three-sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pieces are three-sum compatible when \(|T|=3\); the restrictions of their labels to \(T\) identify the same three elements; \(T\) is a circuit of both \(M_1\) and \(M_2\); and no cocircuit of either matroid is contained in \(T\). Equivalently, \(T\) contains no circuit of \(M_1^*\) or \(M_2^*\). A proper-sum convention may additionally require each piece to retain sufficiently many elements outside \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three-sum compatibility requires a consistently identified common triangle that contains no cocircuit of either piece.
knowledge_statements.title: Three-Sum Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compatibility conditions are convention-sensitive, and the phrase 'sufficiently many elements' leaves a possible properness hypothesis unspecified.

children.title: Recomposition Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Noncanonical decomposition trees, equivalent recompositions, plus exceptional overlaps.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) have a compatible three-element interface \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Interface maps differing by \(\phi|_T\) can encode isomorphic recomposed matroids, so decomposition data are not uniquely recoverable from the result.

notation.meaning: an automorphism of the second piece

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness caused by interface symmetries and alternative separation choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an interface identification \(f:T\to T\) glues \(M_1\) to \(M_2\). Replacing it by \(\phi|_T\circ f\) changes the labeled gluing data whenever \(\phi|_T\) is nontrivial, but applying \(\phi\) on the second piece induces an isomorphism between the two recomposed matroids. Thus a recomposed matroid need not determine its interface identification. More generally, choosing different valid three-separations can yield nonisomorphic decomposition trees with isomorphic roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interface symmetries or different three-separations can produce distinct decomposition descriptions of the same matroid.
knowledge_statements.title: Recomposition Ambiguity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The automorphism argument is plausible, but the labeled-versus-unlabeled convention and broader claim about nonunique decomposition trees need a source or explicit example.

children.title: Recognition from Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Recognition organized through basic pieces plus decomposition certificates.

assumptions_latex: A supplied tree has graphic, cographic, or \(R_{10}\) leaves and valid \(1\)-, \(2\)-, or \(3\)-sum nodes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The validated tree certifies that \(M\) is regular; conversely, every regular matroid admits such a tree.

notation.meaning: the recomposed matroid at node v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural recognition certificate based on Seymour decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Verify each leaf as graphic, cographic, or isomorphic to \(R_{10}\). At every internal node, verify the stated interface conditions and that its stored matroid equals the indicated \(1\)-, \(2\)-, or \(3\)-sum of its children. Finally verify that the root is isomorphic to \(M\). Since the three leaf classes are regular and regularity is preserved by these sums, the tree certifies regularity. Seymour's decomposition theorem supplies the converse existence statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid tree of graphic, cographic, and R10 pieces certifies regularity, and every regular matroid has such a tree.
knowledge_statements.title: Recognition from Decomposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits recognition from decomposition, but both preservation under the stated sums and the converse decomposition theorem require authoritative support.

children.title: Optimization over Decomposition Trees
children.top_down_role: Optimization interfaces that combine solutions across a decomposition tree.

assumptions_latex: A rooted decomposition tree represents a binary matroid, and every parent-child interface has at most three elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The root table yields the maximum weight of an independent set and backtracking yields an optimizer.

notation.meaning: the rank-marginal signature of I on interface T
the best weight at node v with signature sigma

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-interface dynamic programming for maximum-weight independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each node \(v\), each independent set \(I\) in its submatroid induces the interface signature \(\sigma_I(X)=r(I\cup X)-r(I)\) for every \(X\subseteq T_v\). At a leaf, compute \(F_v(\sigma)=\max\{w(I):I\text{ is independent and has signature }\sigma\}\). At an internal node, enumerate pairs of child signatures compatible with its sum, combine their values while subtracting any counted interface contribution, and retain the maximum for each parent signature. Output the unrestricted optimum at the root and recover a maximizing set by stored back-pointers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic programming records each partial independent set's rank behavior on the small interface and combines compatible child states.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization over Decomposition Trees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source establishes that the proposed rank-marginal signature is sufficient to combine independent-set solutions across every permitted interface.

children.title: Piecewise Certificate Transfer
children.top_down_role: Transfer of local recognition or optimization certificates to the recomposed matroid.

assumptions_latex: Every leaf supplies a locally checkable certificate and every internal sum supplies its interface map.
The certified property is preserved by each permitted sum when the interface predicates hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The collection of leaf certificates, interface checks, and bottom-up transfer records is a certificate for the root property.

notation.meaning: a certificate attached to tree node v
the matroid represented at tree node v
the interface at an internal node v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compositional certificate schema for properties preserved by matroid sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Attach to each leaf \(v\) a certificate \(C_v\) verifiable directly for \(M_v\). For an internal node \(v\) with children \(a,b\), verify the interface \(T_v\), verify that \(M_v=M_a\oplus_{k_v}M_b\), and apply the property's stated transfer rule to \(C_a,C_b\) to construct \(C_v\). A verifier processes the tree in postorder and accepts only if every local certificate, interface predicate, and transfer step succeeds. The resulting root object \(C_r\) certifies the property for \(M_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Leaf certificates transfer to the root when every interface is valid and the certified property is preserved by each sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise Certificate Transfer

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is only an abstract conditional schema; a specific certified property, local verifier, and sum-preservation theorem are needed to make the certificate claim substantive.

children.title: Decomposition Overheads
children.top_down_role: Costs caused by finding, representing, traversing, or recomposing decomposition pieces.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Overheads
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ground-set duplication overhead in a bounded-adhesion regular-matroid decomposition tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) have \(n\) elements and be represented by a tree \(T\) of \(t\) pieces combined by 1-, 2-, or 3-sums. Suppose every tree edge has an adhesion set of size at most \(3\), stored in both incident pieces, and reconstruction deletes the copied adhesion elements. Then the aggregate number of stored ground-set incidences is at most \(n+6(t-1)\). Consequently, tree navigation and interface storage require \(O(t)\) additional space, while scanning all explicitly stored pieces requires \(O(n+t)\) time, excluding decomposition construction and piece-local optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-adhesion decomposition duplicates only constantly many elements per tree edge, so explicit piece storage and traversal add linear overhead.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite tree of 1-, 2-, or 3-sum pieces.
Each adhesion set has cardinality at most \(3\).
Each adhesion element is stored at most once at each endpoint of its tree edge.

notation.meaning: stored ground set of the piece at node v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bound depends on the precise conventions for 1-, 2-, and 3-sum interfaces, copied adhesion elements, and deletion during reconstruction. No source is supplied, so the exact coefficient and accounting model cannot be validated reliably.

children.title: Matroid Computational Model Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Computational interfaces precede algorithm branches so complexity claims are interpreted in the appropriate oracle or explicit-representation model.

children.title: Independence Oracles
children.top_down_role: Information access, query costs, plus certifying limits for independence queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Independence Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean independence-query model for a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), an independence oracle is a procedure \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{ind}}\) that accepts any subset \(X\subseteq E\) and returns \(1\) exactly when \(X\in\mathcal I\), and returns \(0\) otherwise. Oracle complexity counts calls to \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{ind}}\) separately from ordinary computation and from the cost of encoding or reading subsets of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independence oracle answers whether a queried subset of the ground set is independent in the matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{ind}}(X)=1\iff X\in\mathcal I\).

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Independence and rank p. 173
1.2 Oracles p. 26

source_witnesses.locator: 5.1 Independence and rank p. 173
1.2 Oracles p. 26

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Independence Oracle and Probes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the unit-cost independence-query model and the hereditary deductions supplied by each answer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matroid M=(E,\mathcal I), an independence oracle is a function \Omega:2^E\to\{\mathrm{YES},\mathrm{NO}\} such that \Omega(X)=\mathrm{YES} if X\in\mathcal I and \Omega(X)=\mathrm{NO} if X\notin\mathcal I. Each unit-time application of \Omega to a subset X\subseteq E is a probe. If \Omega(X)=\mathrm{YES}, then \Omega(Y)=\mathrm{YES} for every Y\subseteq X; if \Omega(X)=\mathrm{NO}, then \Omega(Z)=\mathrm{NO} for every Z\supseteq X.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independence oracle reports in unit time whether a queried subset is independent, and each query is called a probe. A YES answer also certifies every subset as independent, while a NO answer certifies every superset as dependent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Omega(X)=\mathrm{YES}\iff X\in\mathcal I;\quad \Omega(X)=\mathrm{YES}\Rightarrow\forall Y\subseteq X,\ \Omega(Y)=\mathrm{YES};\quad \Omega(X)=\mathrm{NO}\Rightarrow\forall Z\supseteq X,\ \Omega(Z)=\mathrm{NO}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Polynomial Independence-Oracle Bound for Recognizing Binary Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An oracle-query lower-bound statement for deciding whether an arbitrary matroid is binary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is no f\in\mathbb Z[x] such that, for every positive integer n and every n-element matroid M, at most f(n) probes to an independence oracle suffice to determine whether M is binary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: No integer-coefficient polynomial in the ground-set size uniformly bounds the number of independence-oracle probes required to decide whether an arbitrary matroid is binary.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is accessed through an independence oracle}

children.title: Rank Oracles
children.top_down_role: Information access through subset ranks plus comparisons with weaker oracle models.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-valued rank-query model for a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), a rank oracle is a procedure \(\mathcal O_r\) that accepts any subset \(X\subseteq E\) and returns its matroid rank \[\mathcal O_r(X)=r_M(X)=\max\{ |I|:I\subseteq X,\ I\in\mathcal I\}.\] Thus every response is an integer between \(0\) and \(|X|\), inclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank oracle returns the maximum cardinality of an independent subset of the queried set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_r(X)=r_M(X)\in\{0,\ldots,|X|\}\).

children.title: Closure Oracles
children.top_down_role: Information access through closure queries plus representation-sensitive uses.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued closure-query model for a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M\) with rank function \(r_M\), a closure oracle is a procedure \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{cl}}\) that accepts \(X\subseteq E\) and returns \[\mathcal O_{\mathrm{cl}}(X)=\operatorname{cl}_M(X)=\{e\in E:r_M(X\cup\{e\})=r_M(X)\}.\] The response is the entire closure subset, so one oracle call may have output length proportional to \(|E|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closure oracle returns all elements whose addition does not increase the queried set's rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e\in\mathcal O_{\mathrm{cl}}(X)\iff r_M(X\cup\{e\})=r_M(X)\).

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Oracle Simulation Relationships
children.top_down_role: Relative simulation power plus query overheads among the three interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Simulation Relationships
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial query equivalence of independence, rank, and full-set closure oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matroid on \(E\), with \(n=|E|\). A rank query decides independence by testing \(r_M(X)=|X|\). Scanning \(X\) and greedily retaining an element when independence is preserved computes \(r_M(X)\) with at most \(|X|\) independence queries. Rank computes \(\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\) with at most \(n+1\) rank queries. Conversely, scanning \(X\) and adding \(e\) precisely when \(e\notin\operatorname{cl}_M(I)\) computes rank with at most \(|X|\) closure queries. Hence the three models polynomially simulate one another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independence, rank, and full-set closure oracles simulate one another using only linearly many queries per derived query.
assumptions_latex: A closure response explicitly returns all of \(\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\).
Complexity is measured by oracle-query count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{ind}}\equiv_{\mathrm{poly}}\mathcal O_r\equiv_{\mathrm{poly}}\mathcal O_{\mathrm{cl}}\), with \(O(n)\) queries per simulation.

children.title: Basis Oracles
children.top_down_role: Access models exposing bases, basis membership, or basis-completion information.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean basis-membership query model for a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), a basis oracle is a procedure \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{bas}}\) accepting any subset \(B\subseteq E\) and returning \(1\) exactly when \(B\) is a basis of \(M\); equivalently, \(B\in\mathcal I\) and no proper superset of \(B\) belongs to \(\mathcal I\). It returns \(0\) for every other subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis oracle decides whether a queried subset is a maximal independent set of the matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{bas}}(B)=1\iff B\text{ is a basis of }M\).

knowledge_statements.title: Circuit Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean circuit-membership query model for a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), a circuit oracle is a procedure \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{circ}}\) accepting any subset \(C\subseteq E\) and returning \(1\) exactly when \(C\) is a circuit: \(C\notin\mathcal I\), \(C\ne\varnothing\), and every proper subset of \(C\) belongs to \(\mathcal I\). It returns \(0\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A circuit oracle decides whether a queried nonempty set is minimally dependent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{circ}}(C)=1\iff C\text{ is a circuit of }M\).

children.title: Fundamental-Circuit Oracles
children.top_down_role: Access to circuits relative to a chosen basis plus exchange-sensitive information.

knowledge_statements.title: Fundamental-Circuit Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued fundamental-circuit query model relative to a supplied basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid, let \(B\) be a basis, and let \(e\in E\setminus B\). A fundamental-circuit oracle returns the unique circuit \(C_M(e,B)\) contained in \(B\cup\{e\}\). Its output satisfies \(e\in C_M(e,B)\) and, for every \(x\in B\), \[x\in C_M(e,B)\setminus\{e\}\iff (B\setminus\{x\})\cup\{e\}\text{ is a basis of }M.\] Queries whose supplied set is not a basis lie outside this oracle's promised input domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a basis and an outside element, the oracle returns the unique circuit created by adjoining that element.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_M(e,B)\) is the unique circuit contained in \(B\cup\{e\}\).

notation.meaning: fundamental circuit of e relative to B

children.title: Structural-Oracle Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Simulation power, query overheads, plus information gaps among the structural oracles.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural-Oracle Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank predicates characterizing bases, circuits, and fundamental-circuit membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M\) on \(E\), rank queries characterize the structural predicates by \[B\text{ is a basis}\iff r_M(B)=|B|=r_M(E),\] and, for nonempty \(C\), \[C\text{ is a circuit}\iff r_M(C)=|C|-1\text{ and }r_M(C\setminus\{e\})=|C|-1\text{ for every }e\in C.\] If \(B\) is a basis and \(f\notin B\), then \(e\in C_M(f,B)\setminus\{f\}\) exactly when \((B\setminus\{e\})\cup\{f\}\) is a basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank determines basis and circuit membership, while basis-exchange tests determine every element of a fundamental circuit.
assumptions_latex: For the exchange formula, \(B\) is a basis and \(f\notin B\).

children.title: Explicit Graphic Representations
children.top_down_role: Graph-based encodings of graphic matroids plus their direct computational access.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Graphic Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph presentation of a finite graphic matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite undirected multigraph \(G=(V,E)\), allowing loops and parallel edges, its cycle matroid \(M(G)\) has ground set \(E\) and independent sets \[\mathcal I(G)=\{F\subseteq E:(V,F)\text{ contains no graph cycle}\}.\] Thus bases restrict on each connected component to spanning trees, nonloop circuits are edge sets of simple cycles, loops form singleton circuits, and parallel nonloop edges form two-element circuits. The explicit input consists of the vertex and edge lists with each edge's endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph explicitly represents its cycle matroid: independent edge sets are exactly forests.
assumptions_latex: Loops and parallel edges are permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\in\mathcal I(M(G))\iff (V,F)\text{ is a forest}\).

children.title: Explicit Linear Representations
children.top_down_role: Matrix-based encodings over specified fields plus their direct computational access.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Linear Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix presentation of a finite field-representable matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}\) be a matrix over a field \(\mathbb F\), with columns indexed by a finite set \(E\). The column matroid \(M[A]\) has ground set \(E\), and \(X\subseteq E\) is independent exactly when the columns \(A_X\) are linearly independent over \(\mathbb F\). Consequently, \[r_{M[A]}(X)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A_X).\] An explicit linear representation specifies \(\mathbb F\), the matrix entries, and the column-to-element indexing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix represents a matroid whose independent sets are the linearly independent subsets of its indexed columns.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}\) has columns indexed by \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\in\mathcal I(M[A])\iff \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A_X)=|X|\).

notation.meaning: submatrix formed by columns indexed by X

children.title: Representation Conversion
children.top_down_role: Conversion or recovery between explicit encodings when structural conditions permit.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Conversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of an explicit graph into a linear representation of its cycle matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected multigraph, choose an orientation of every nonloop edge, and let \(D\) be its signed vertex-edge incidence matrix over a field \(\mathbb F\): a nonloop column has entries \(1\) and \(-1\) at its head and tail, and a loop column is zero. Then \[M[D]=M(G).\] Hence an explicit graphic representation converts to an explicit linear representation over every field in time \(O(|V|+|E|)\) when columns are stored sparsely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The signed incidence matrix converts any explicit graph into a linear representation of the same cycle matroid over every field.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is stored by its nonzero column entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M[D]=M(G)\), and sparse construction takes \(O(|V|+|E|)\) time.

children.title: Representation-Sensitive Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity changes caused by encoding size, field choice, or representation availability.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid with a valid encoding in \(\mathcal R\).

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21; Encoding p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\) be an explicit representation class for finite matroids, and let \(\operatorname{enc}_{\mathcal R}(M)\) be the binary encoding of \(M\) in \(\mathcal R\). An algorithm has representation-sensitive running time \(T_{\mathcal R}\) if, on every valid encoding \(x=\operatorname{enc}_{\mathcal R}(M)\), it terminates within \(T_{\mathcal R}(|x|)\) elementary bit operations. It is polynomial-time for \(\mathcal R\) when some constant \(c\) satisfies \(T_{\mathcal R}(L)=O(L^c)\). This classification is attached to the representation: changing \(\mathcal R\) can change the input length, available primitive operations, and resulting complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complexity is measured against the length and primitive operations of a chosen matroid encoding; changing the representation can change whether an algorithm is polynomial-time.

children.top_down_role: Groups of oracle models mutually simulable within the stated resource regime.

assumptions_latex: All interfaces describe the same matroid from a fixed class \(\mathfrak M\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-query equivalence for matroid oracle interfaces on a common input class.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a class \(\mathfrak M\) of finite matroids and oracle interfaces \(O_1,O_2\). Write \(O_1\preceq_{\mathrm p}O_2\) when every query to \(O_1\) on an \(n\)-element matroid in \(\mathfrak M\) can be answered correctly by an adaptive algorithm using at most \(p(n)\) queries to \(O_2\) and polynomially many additional bit operations, for some polynomial \(p\). Define \(O_1\equiv_{\mathrm p}O_2\) exactly when both \(O_1\preceq_{\mathrm p}O_2\) and \(O_2\preceq_{\mathrm p}O_1\). The equivalence classes of \(\equiv_{\mathrm p}\) partition the oracle interfaces under consideration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two matroid oracles are equivalent when each can answer the other's queries with polynomially many oracle calls and polynomial auxiliary work.

children.title: One-Way Oracle Simulations
children.top_down_role: Directional reductions where one interface can emulate another without a matching reverse reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Way Oracle Simulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed simulation between two matroid oracle interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For oracle interfaces \(O_A\) and \(O_B\) on the same class of finite matroids, a one-way simulation \(O_A\preceq O_B\) is an algorithm that receives a query \(q\) admissible for \(O_A\), accesses the unknown matroid only through adaptive queries to \(O_B\), and returns exactly \(O_A(M,q)\). If at most \(f(n,|q|)\) calls to \(O_B\) and \(g(n,|q|)\) auxiliary bit operations are used, then \((f,g)\) is the simulation cost. No reverse simulation is implied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-way simulation answers every query of one interface by querying another interface, with separately stated oracle-call and auxiliary-work costs.
assumptions_latex: \(O_A\) and \(O_B\) refer to the same finite matroid \(M\).
Every simulated query \(q\) is valid for \(O_A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The simulator returns \(O_A(M,q)\) using only access to \(O_B\).

children.title: Simulation Overheads
children.top_down_role: Query, arithmetic, encoding, plus adaptivity costs incurred by oracle simulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Simulation Overheads
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition law for directed oracle simulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(O_A\) is simulated by \(O_B\) using at most \(f(n)\) calls per query, and \(O_B\) is simulated by \(O_C\) using at most \(h(n)\) calls per query. Replacing every \(O_B\)-call in the first simulator by the second simulator yields an \(O_C\)-simulation of \(O_A\) using at most \(f(n)h(n)\) oracle calls. If their auxiliary costs are \(g(n)\) and \(k(n)\) per simulated query, respectively, the composed auxiliary cost is at most \(g(n)+f(n)k(n)\), excluding query-copying costs already included in those bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulation overheads compose multiplicatively for oracle calls and by substitution for auxiliary work.
assumptions_latex: Both simulations apply to the same \(n\)-element input class.
The inner cost bounds hold uniformly for every adaptive query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{A\leftarrow C}(n)\le f(n)h(n)\) and \(W_{A\leftarrow C}(n)\le g(n)+f(n)k(n)\).

notation.meaning: number of calls to the underlying oracle

children.title: Oracle Separation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Information gaps preventing efficient simulation between oracle models.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Separation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of unrestricted conversion from abstract oracle access to linear representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V_8\) denote the Vámos matroid and let \(V_8^{\oplus k}\) be the direct sum of \(k\) copies. An independence oracle is well defined for every \(V_8^{\oplus k}\), but no algorithm, regardless of its number of independence queries, can output a matrix over any field representing that matroid: \(V_8\) is not representable over any field, and a restriction of a representable matroid is representable. Thus independence-oracle access cannot simulate a total linear-representation interface on the class of all matroids; a representability promise is indispensable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independence access cannot produce linear representations for arbitrary matroids: direct sums of the Vámos matroid have valid oracles but no field representation.
assumptions_latex: The input class contains arbitrary finite matroids.
A successful representation query must output a matrix over some field representing the input matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No total simulation from independence oracles to linear-representation output exists on this class.

children.title: Dual-Matroid Oracle Construction
children.top_down_role: Derived oracle access for a dual matroid from an oracle for the primal matroid.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Matroid Oracle Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructing a dual independence oracle from a primal independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input an independence oracle for \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) and a query \(X\subseteq E\). Compute \(r_M(E)\) and \(r_M(E\setminus X)\) by scanning each relevant set in any order, retaining an element exactly when its addition preserves independence. Return YES precisely when
\[r_M(E\setminus X)=r_M(E)-|X|.\]
The equality is equivalent to \(r_{M^*}(X)=|X|\), so the answer is YES exactly when \(X\) is independent in the dual matroid \(M^*\). The value \(r_M(E)\) may be cached for later queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute two primal ranks greedily; a set is dual-independent exactly when deleting it lowers the primal rank by its cardinality.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid on known ground set \(E\).
The oracle decides primal independence for every subset of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\in\mathcal I(M^*)\iff r_M(E\setminus X)=r_M(E)-|X|\).

notation.meaning: rank function of the primal matroid
