children.title: Minor Oracle Construction
children.top_down_role: Derived oracle access for deletion or contraction minors.

knowledge_statements.title: Minor Oracle Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independence-oracle construction for a deletion-contraction minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C,D\subseteq E\) be disjoint and set \(N=M/C\setminus D\), whose ground set is \(E\setminus(C\cup D)\). Given a query \(X\) in this ground set, compute \(r_M(C)\) and \(r_M(C\cup X)\) using the independence oracle and greedy rank computation. Return YES precisely when
\[r_M(C\cup X)-r_M(C)=|X|.\]
Because \(r_{M/C}(X)=r_M(C\cup X)-r_M(C)\), this answers independence in \(N\); deletion requires no further oracle calls. Cache \(r_M(C)\) across queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is independent in a deletion-contraction minor exactly when adjoining it to the contracted set increases primal rank by its size.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is finite and supplied by an independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\in\mathcal I(M/C\setminus D)\iff r_M(C\cup X)-r_M(C)=|X|\).

notation.meaning: contraction of C followed by deletion of D
rank function obtained from the primal independence oracle

children.title: Sum Oracle Construction
children.top_down_role: Derived oracle access for matroids assembled through direct sums or higher sums.

knowledge_statements.title: Sum Oracle Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independence oracle for a direct sum of matroids on disjoint ground sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input independence oracles for matroids \(M_i=(E_i,\mathcal I_i)\), where the sets \(E_1,\ldots,E_k\) are pairwise disjoint. For a query \(X\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^k E_i\), form \(X_i=X\cap E_i\) and submit \(X_i\) to the oracle for \(M_i\). Return YES if and only if every component oracle returns YES. The resulting interface is an independence oracle for the direct sum \(M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^k M_i\), since
\[X\in\mathcal I(M)\iff (\forall i)\;X_i\in\mathcal I_i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: To test independence in a direct sum, intersect the query with each component ground set and accept exactly when every component accepts.
assumptions_latex: The component ground sets \(E_i\) are pairwise disjoint.
Each component independence oracle is correct.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\in\mathcal I(\bigoplus_i M_i)\iff (\forall i)\;X\cap E_i\in\mathcal I_i\).

notation.meaning: direct sum of the component matroids
component query X intersected with the i-th ground set

children.title: Derived-Oracle Overheads
children.top_down_role: Query plus representation costs introduced by the derived constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Derived-Oracle Overheads
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independence-query bounds for standard derived-matroid oracle constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an \(n\)-element matroid, greedy computation of \(r_M(S)\) uses at most \(|S|\) independence calls. Consequently, after caching \(r_M(E)\), a dual-independence query on \(X\) uses at most \(n-|X|\) calls. After caching \(r_M(C)\), an independence query to \(M/C\setminus D\) uses at most \(|C|+|X|\le n\) calls by computing \(r_M(C\cup X)\). For a direct sum of \(k\) oracle-presented components, one independence query uses exactly one component-oracle call per component, hence \(k\) calls, plus set-partitioning work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cached rank values make dual and minor queries linear in ground-set size; a direct-sum query uses one call to each component oracle.
assumptions_latex: Rank is computed greedily from an independence oracle.
Cached preprocessing costs are excluded from each subsequent query.
Direct-sum components have disjoint ground sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{M^*}(X)\le n-|X|\), \(Q_{M/C\setminus D}(X)\le |C|+|X|\), and \(Q_{\oplus_iM_i}=k\).

notation.meaning: underlying oracle calls needed for a query to derived matroid N

children.title: Oracle-Call Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity measured by the number or structure of oracle queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Call Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query complexity for algorithms accessing a matroid through a fixed oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a matroid oracle interface \(O\). For an algorithm \(A\) and an \(n\)-element input matroid \(M\), the oracle-call complexity is the maximum number \(Q_A^O(n)\) of calls to \(O\) made before termination, maximized over all admissible \(M\), ordinary inputs of the prescribed size, and, for randomized algorithms, internal random outcomes unless an expected bound is explicitly declared. Computation between calls is not charged to \(Q_A^O\). A polynomial-query algorithm satisfies \(Q_A^O(n)\le p(n)\) for some polynomial \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle-call complexity counts worst-case queries to the chosen matroid interface, separately from computation performed between queries.
assumptions_latex: The oracle interface \(O\) and admissible input class are fixed.
Each oracle invocation counts as one call regardless of its implementation cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_A^O(n)\le p(n)\) characterizes polynomial oracle-call complexity.

notation.meaning: worst-case number of calls made by algorithm A to oracle O

children.title: Arithmetic Complexity
children.top_down_role: Field-operation or numerical-operation costs beyond oracle access.

knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operation-count complexity for explicitly represented numerical matroid data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a field \(\mathbb F\) and an arithmetic model in which addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero element, and equality tests in \(\mathbb F\) have specified unit or separately stated costs. For an algorithm \(A\) operating on an explicit representation of size parameter \(N\), its arithmetic complexity \(C_A^{\mathrm{arith}}(N)\) is the maximum number of such field operations performed on any admissible input of size \(N\). This measure excludes coefficient bit lengths and bit-level operation costs unless they are incorporated explicitly; therefore an arithmetic polynomial bound alone need not imply polynomial bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arithmetic complexity counts field operations on an explicit representation and does not by itself control coefficient growth or bit complexity.
assumptions_latex: Inputs are explicitly represented over a specified field \(\mathbb F\).
The charged arithmetic operations are fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_A^{\mathrm{arith}}(N)\) counts charged field operations, independently of uncharged operand bit lengths.

children.title: Encoding Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-length accounting for explicit matroid inputs, queries, and numerical data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed binary encoding map \(\operatorname{enc}\), the encoding complexity of an instance \(I\) is its bit length \(L(I)=|\operatorname{enc}(I)|\). For a matrix-represented matroid, the encoding must specify the dimensions, field or coefficient domain, entries, and any auxiliary weights; rational entries are encoded by signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators under a stated convention. An algorithm is polynomial in the encoding when its bit-operation count is bounded by a polynomial in \(L(I)\), including the cost of reading, writing, and manipulating all queries, answers, and intermediate numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding complexity is total binary input length; polynomial bit complexity must also account for queries, answers, and growth of intermediate numbers.
assumptions_latex: A uniquely decodable binary encoding convention is fixed.
All explicit numerical and combinatorial input data are included.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial encoding complexity means a bit-operation bound \(O(L(I)^c)\) for some constant \(c\).

children.title: Cost-Measure Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Regimes where improvements under one cost measure increase another resource.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Measure Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates oracle calls, auxiliary computation, and representation-dependent oracle-evaluation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an algorithm issuing queries \(q_1,\ldots,q_Q\), let \(A\) be its auxiliary bit-operation cost and let \(C_\rho(q_i)\) be the cost of answering \(q_i\) from representation \(\rho\). Its implemented running time satisfies \[T_\rho=A+\sum_{i=1}^{Q}C_\rho(q_i).\] Thus a bound on \(Q\) alone is a unit-cost oracle bound. It yields a polynomial bit-time bound only when \(A\), \(Q\), and every relevant \(C_\rho(q_i)\) are polynomially bounded in the encoded input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle-call complexity becomes a bit-time guarantee only after accounting for auxiliary work and the representation-dependent cost of answering each query.
assumptions_latex: \(Q<\infty\) and each oracle response is computed from an encoding \(\rho\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\rho=A+\sum_{i=1}^{Q}C_\rho(q_i)\), so query and bit complexities need not coincide.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider instances with combinatorial dimension \(n\) and finitely encoded rational numerical data. Relative to a specified arithmetic and oracle model, an algorithm is strongly polynomial if the number \(N_{\mathrm{op}}\) of arithmetic operations, comparisons, and specified unit-cost oracle calls is bounded by a polynomial in \(n\), independently of the numerical values and their encoding lengths, and every intermediate rational number has encoding length polynomial in the input length. Thus the operation-count bound, though not necessarily the actual operation count, is unaffected when numerical magnitudes grow while \(n\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polynomiality requires a combinatorial operation bound independent of numerical magnitudes and polynomially bounded intermediate encodings; the bound need not make the actual operation count identical on all inputs of the same combinatorial size.

children.title: Weakly Polynomial Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Polynomial Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes ordinary bit-polynomial algorithms from strongly polynomial and pseudopolynomial algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\) be combinatorial size, \(L\) the total binary encoding length, and \(U\) the largest encoded magnitude. A running-time bound polynomial in \(n\) and \(L\), but whose arithmetic or iteration count depends on \(L\), is polynomial-time yet not thereby strongly polynomial. A bound polynomial in \(n\) and \(U\) is only pseudopolynomial: because \(L\) may be \(\Theta(\log U)\), such a bound can be exponential in the binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dependence polynomial in encoding length may prevent strong polynomiality; dependence polynomial in numeric magnitude may even be exponential in binary input size.
assumptions_latex: \(U\ge 2\) is binary encoded, so its contribution to \(L\) is \(\Theta(\log U)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{poly}(n,L)\) need not be strongly polynomial, while \(\operatorname{poly}(n,U)\) need not be polynomial in \(L\).

Computation between queries is unrestricted unless the model explicitly imposes another cost bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptivity Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Round-adaptivity lower bounds in a batched matroid-oracle decision model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An \(r\)-round oracle algorithm partitions its queries into batches \(B_1,\ldots,B_r\), where \(B_i\) may depend on all answers to earlier batches but queries within \(B_i\) are fixed before any answer from that batch is received. An adaptivity lower bound \(r(n)\) for a task means that every algorithm correct on all size-\(n\) instances requires at least \(r(n)\) such rounds on some instance, subject to the stated query budget and success criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptivity lower bound forces many sequential batches even though every query within a batch may be issued in parallel.
assumptions_latex: The oracle, correctness requirement, and any total-query budget are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall A\,\exists x\in\mathcal X_n:\ \operatorname{rounds}_A(x)\ge r(n)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Query Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-error randomized query complexity with explicit worst-case success and cost conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Query–Adaptivity Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto representation of total-query cost versus sequential oracle rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed task and oracle model, define \(Q_r(n)\) as the minimum worst-case number of queries among algorithms using at most \(r\) adaptive rounds, with value \(+\infty\) if no such algorithm exists. Then \[Q_{r+1}(n)\le Q_r(n).\] Dually, if \(R_Q(n)\) is the minimum number of rounds among algorithms using at most \(Q\) queries, then \(R_{Q+1}(n)\le R_Q(n)\). The attainable pairs \((r,Q)\) form an upward-closed set whose minimal elements describe the query–adaptivity frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing more rounds cannot increase minimum query complexity, and allowing more queries cannot increase minimum round complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Sensitive Tractability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfers oracle tractability to bit tractability only through an efficient representation-specific simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\rho\) encode a matroid on a ground set of size \(n\). Suppose an oracle algorithm makes at most \(Q(n)\) queries, performs \(A(n,|\rho|)\) auxiliary bit operations, and every query can be answered from \(\rho\) in at most \(C(n,|\rho|)\) bit operations. Then its implementation runs in at most \[A(n,|\rho|)+Q(n)C(n,|\rho|)\] bit operations. Hence polynomial oracle complexity implies polynomial-time tractability for \(\rho\) only when the representation and required oracle simulation are polynomially manageable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-query matroid algorithm is polynomial in an explicit representation only when its required oracle can also be simulated polynomially.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho\) is a finite representation from which every required oracle answer is computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\rho\le A(n,|\rho|)+Q(n)C(n,|\rho|)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Exchange Sufficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficiency direction of the finite matroid greedy characterization for nonnegative weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and let \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\) be nonempty, hereditary, and satisfy augmentation: whenever \(I,J\in\mathcal I\) and \(|I|<|J|\), some \(e\in J\setminus I\) has \(I\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). For any weight function \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), inspect elements in nonincreasing weight order and add an inspected element exactly when independence is preserved. The resulting set \(G\) satisfies \[w(G)=\max\{w(I):I\in\mathcal I\}.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Universal-Weight Converse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse greedy characterization for finite hereditary independence systems and nonnegative weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and let \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\) be nonempty and hereditary. Suppose that, for every \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) and every ordering nonincreasing in \(w\), the algorithm that accepts an element exactly when its addition preserves membership in \(\mathcal I\) returns a maximum-weight member of \(\mathcal I\). Then augmentation holds: for all \(I,J\in\mathcal I\) with \(|I|<|J|\), there exists \(e\in J\setminus I\) such that \(I\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). Thus \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid.

Greedy is optimal for every nonnegative weight function and every compatible tie ordering.

knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Regime Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weight domains sufficient for the finite greedy characterization of matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite nonempty hereditary independence system. The descending-weight greedy algorithm is optimal over \(\mathcal I\) for every nonnegative weight vector \(w\in\mathbb R_+^E\) if and only if \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid. It is enough to quantify over strictly positive, pairwise distinct weights, since sufficiently small perturbations can preserve any prescribed ordering and strict objective gap. For maximum-weight bases, arbitrary real weights \(w\in\mathbb R^E\) are permitted because all bases have the same cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Universal greedy optimality for nonnegative independent-set weights, equivalently for distinct positive weights, characterizes matroids; basis optimization permits arbitrary real weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid}\iff\text{greedy is optimal for every }w\in\mathbb R_+^E.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmatroid Greedy Witnesses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An augmentation failure yields an explicit weight vector defeating greedy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a finite hereditary system \((E,\mathcal I)\) is not a matroid. Then there exist \(I,J\in\mathcal I\) with \(|I|<|J|\) and \(I\cup\{e\}\notin\mathcal I\) for every \(e\in J\setminus I\). Give elements of \(I\) weight \(1+\varepsilon\), elements of \(J\setminus I\) weight \(1\), and all other elements weight \(0\). If \(|I\setminus J|>0\), choose \(0<\varepsilon<( |J\setminus I|-|I\setminus J|)/|I\setminus J|\); if \(|I\setminus J|=0\), choose any \(\varepsilon>0\). A weight-compatible order scans \(I\) before \(J\setminus I\), so the positive-weight part accepted by greedy is \(I\) and its total weight is \(w(I)\), while \(w(J)>w(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonmatroid augmentation failure can be weighted so that greedy accepts the smaller blocking set as its positive-weight part while a larger independent set has greater weight.
assumptions_latex: The augmentation axiom fails for \(I,J\in\mathcal I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists w\in\mathbb R_+^E\text{ and a compatible greedy order such that greedy is not optimal.}\)

knowledge_statements.title: Equicardinality of Maximal Independent Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equicardinality in every restriction characterizes finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite hereditary independence system. It is a matroid if and only if, for every subset \(X\subseteq E\), all inclusion-maximal members of \(\{I\in\mathcal I:I\subseteq X\}\) have the same cardinality. When these conditions hold, that common cardinality is the rank \(r(X)\) of \(X\); in particular, all maximal independent subsets of \(E\) are bases and have cardinality \(r(E)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite hereditary system is a matroid exactly when every restriction has equicardinal maximal independent sets; their common size is its rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid}\iff\forall X\subseteq E,\ \text{all maximal independent subsets of }X\text{ are equicardinal}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equicardinality characterization by maximal independent subsets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward and converse characterization using maximal independent subsets of every ground-set subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) be the independent-set family of a matroid on \(E\). For every \(A\subseteq E\), if \(I,I'\in\mathcal I\) are inclusion-maximal among the members of \(\mathcal I\) contained in \(A\), then \(|I|=|I'|\). Conversely, if a finite structure \((E,\mathcal I)\) satisfies axiom \((3.1)\) and this equicardinality condition, then \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within every subset of a matroid ground set, all maximal independent subsets have equal cardinality. Conversely, on a finite ground set, this condition together with the referenced axiom (3.1) characterizes matroids.
assumptions_latex: For the forward implication, \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid.
For the converse, \(E\) is finite and \((E,\mathcal I)\) satisfies axiom \((3.1)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted matroid greedy algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States descending-weight, independence-preserving selection and distinguishes the nonnegative-weight base regime from the negative-weight maximum-independent-set boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M=(E,\mathcal I)$ be a matroid and order $E$ so that $w(e_1)\ge\cdots\ge w(e_{|E|})$. Starting with $S=\varnothing$, scan the elements in this order and add $e_i$ exactly when $S\cup\{e_i\}\in\mathcal I$. If $w\ge0$, scanning all elements yields a lexicographically maximum base, hence a maximum-weight and Gale-optimal base. For arbitrary real weights when the objective is a maximum-weight independent set, stop before the negative-weight elements, equivalently delete them before running greedy. Execution requires an independence test for each proposed addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process elements from greatest to least weight and accept one exactly when it preserves independence. With nonnegative weights, the output is a lexicographically maximum, maximum-weight, Gale-optimal base. For a maximum-weight independent set with negative weights, reject all negative-weight elements, equivalently delete them first. The implementation relies on independence testing.
assumptions_latex: \text{independence of each trial set can be decided}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w\ge0\Rightarrow S\text{ is a lexicographically maximum, maximum-weight, Gale-optimal base};\qquad w:E\to\mathbb R\Rightarrow S\in\arg\max_{I\in\mathcal I}\sum_{e\in I}w(e)\text{ when all negative-weight elements are rejected}.

children.title: Weighted Independent-Set Optimization
children.top_down_role: Maximum-weight independent sets under unrestricted or sign-sensitive weight regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Independent-Set Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy maximization over all independent sets with arbitrary real weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) and weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), order the elements so that \(w(e_1)\ge\cdots\ge w(e_m)\). Initialize \(S=\varnothing\). Scan the positive-weight elements in this order; replace \(S\) by \(S\cup\{e_i\}\) exactly when that set lies in \(\mathcal I\). The resulting set satisfies \(w(S)=\max\{w(I):I\in\mathcal I\}\). Zero-weight feasible elements may optionally be appended without changing optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort by weight, greedily accept feasible positive-weight elements, and stop before nonpositive weights; the output is a maximum-weight independent set, with feasible zero-weight elements optionally appendable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{I\in\mathcal I}\sum_{e\in I}w(e).\)

notation.meaning: sum of weights of elements in I

children.title: Weighted Basis Optimization
children.top_down_role: Maximum-weight or minimum-weight bases under fixed-rank feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Basis Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy maximization over bases allows weights of either sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) and arbitrary weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), order \(E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_m\}\) so that \(w(e_1)\ge\cdots\ge w(e_m)\). Starting with \(B=\varnothing\), scan every element and add \(e_i\) whenever \(B\cup\{e_i\}\in\mathcal I\). After the scan, \(B\) is a basis and \(w(B)=\max\{w(B'):B'\text{ is a basis of }M\}\). Negative-weight elements are not skipped because basis cardinality is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scan every element in nonincreasing weight order and accept feasible additions; the resulting basis has maximum total weight, even with negative weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{B'\text{ basis of }M}\sum_{e\in B'}w(e).\)

notation.meaning: current greedy set and final basis

children.title: Independent-Set versus Basis Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Set versus Basis Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The two optimization regimes coincide under nonnegative weights but may differ for arbitrary real weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), every independent set extends to a basis. Hence, if \(w\ge0\), the maximum weight over \(\mathcal I\) equals the maximum weight over the bases. With arbitrary real weights the values can differ: independent-set optimization may omit negative-weight elements, whereas every basis contains exactly \(r(E)\) elements. Thus basis greedy scans all elements, while independent-set greedy may stop before the negative-weight portion; feasible zero-weight elements are optional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative weights make independent-set and basis optima coincide; negative weights can separate them because independent sets may omit elements while bases have fixed size.
assumptions_latex: Weights are additive over selected elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w\ge0\implies\max_{I\in\mathcal I}w(I)=\max_{B\text{ basis}}w(B),\) with equality not guaranteed for arbitrary real weights.

notation.meaning: total weight of a set S

knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Sensitive Optimality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negative weights invalidate unmodified independent-set greedy but not basis greedy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The rule that scans all elements and accepts every independence-preserving addition need not solve maximum-weight independent-set optimization when negative weights are allowed. In the one-element free matroid on \(E=\{e\}\) with \(w(e)=-1\), that rule returns \(\{e\}\), although \(\varnothing\) has larger weight. Correctness is restored by discarding negative-weight elements or by requiring \(w\ge0\). For basis optimization, scanning all elements remains correct for arbitrary real weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accepting every feasible element fails for independent-set optimization with negative weights; skip negatives or assume nonnegative weights. Basis greedy remains valid.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility is given by a finite matroid.
Weights are additive and may be negative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w(e)<0\) can make unmodified independent-set greedy suboptimal, while maximum-weight basis greedy remains valid.

children.title: Greedy Tie Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Tie Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality is invariant under arbitrary ordering within equal-weight classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid, and let the scan order be any linear order satisfying \(w(e_i)>w(e_j)\Rightarrow i<j\). Greedy basis selection under this order produces a maximum-weight basis. Greedy independent-set selection restricted to positive weights produces a maximum-weight independent set. Different tie-breakings may produce different sets, but all resulting sets in the same regime have the same optimal total weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any ordering within equal-weight classes preserves matroid greedy optimality, though different tie-breakings may return different optimal sets.
assumptions_latex: The scan order is nonincreasing in weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Every weight-compatible tie-breaking yields an optimal greedy output.}\)

notation.meaning: elements in a weight-compatible scan order

children.title: Matroid Truncation
children.top_down_role: Truncated matroid structure as an interface for bounded-size independent sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Truncation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-capping a matroid by a cardinality bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) and an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le r_M(E)\), the rank-\(k\) truncation is \(T_k(M)=(E,\mathcal I_k)\), where \(\mathcal I_k=\{I\in\mathcal I:|I|\le k\}\). This is a matroid with rank function \(r_{T_k}(X)=\min\{r_M(X),k\}\) for every \(X\subseteq E\). Its bases are exactly the independent sets of \(M\) having cardinality \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rank-k truncation retains exactly the original independent sets of size at most k and has rank function equal to the original rank capped at k.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_k(M)=(E,\{I\in\mathcal I:|I|\le k\}),\qquad r_{T_k}(X)=\min\{r_M(X),k\}.\)

children.title: Cardinality-Constrained Greedy Optimization
children.top_down_role: Greedy optimization under exact or upper-bounded cardinality requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality-Constrained Greedy Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy optimization under upper or exact cardinality constraints via truncation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), and \(0\le k\le r_M(E)\), sort elements by nonincreasing weight. For the constraint \(|I|\le k\), greedily accept independence-preserving positive-weight elements until \(k\) are chosen or no positive-weight element remains; feasible zero-weight elements may optionally be added up to the bound. For the constraint \(|I|=k\), accept every independence-preserving element until \(k\) are chosen. These are respectively independent-set and basis greedy on the truncation \(T_k(M)\) and are optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply greedy to the rank-k truncation: skip negative weights and optionally accept zero weights for size at most k, or continue to k elements for exact size k.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the upper-bound regime, \(S\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}\{w(I):I\in\mathcal I,\ |I|\le k\}\); for the exact-cardinality regime, \(S\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}\{w(I):I\in\mathcal I,\ |I|=k\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Greedy Optimality at Every Matroid Cardinality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous optimality of weighted-greedy prefixes for every attainable cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid with element weights \(c:E\to\mathbb R\). For every integer \(k\) with \(1\le k\le r_M(E)\), the weighted greedy algorithm produces an independent set \(S_k\) of cardinality \(k\) such that \(c(S_k)=\max\{c(S):S\in\mathcal I,\ |S|=k\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Interaction Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additional constraints preserve greedy validity only when the combined family retains matroid structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Intersecting matroid independence with an arbitrary side constraint need not preserve greedy optimality. Let \(E=\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}\) be the edges of a three-edge path, start from the free matroid, and require the selected edges to form a matching. With \(w(e_2)=2\) and \(w(e_1)=w(e_3)=3/2\), descending greedy selects only \(e_2\), with weight \(2\), whereas \(\{e_1,e_3\}\) is feasible with weight \(3\). Thus truncation is safe, but general constraint intersection is not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrary side constraints can destroy matroid structure: weighted matching on a three-edge path already defeats descending greedy.
assumptions_latex: The original feasibility family is the free matroid on three edges.
A matching side constraint is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w(\{e_2\})=2<3=w(\{e_1,e_3\}),\) so descending greedy is suboptimal after adding the constraint.

notation.meaning: consecutive edges of a three-edge path

children.title: Oracle-Based Greedy Implementation
children.top_down_role: Greedy execution using independence, rank, or related oracle access.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Based Greedy Implementation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy matroid optimization using only an independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite ground set \(E\) of size \(n\), weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), and an oracle returning whether \(S\in\mathcal I\). Sort \(E\) by nonincreasing weight and initialize \(S=\varnothing\). For each element eligible in the selected regime, query whether \(S\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\) and add \(e\) exactly on a positive answer. Scan all elements for basis optimization. For unrestricted independent-set optimization, scan all positive-weight elements; zero-weight elements may optionally be queried and added. The implementation uses at most \(n\) oracle calls and \(O(n\log n)\) comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort elements and issue at most one independence query per eligible element; basis greedy scans all elements, while independent-set greedy need only scan positive weights and may optionally include zero weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Oracle calls}\le n,\qquad\text{comparison cost}=O(n\log n),\) and the returned set is optimal for the selected regime.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cardinality Greedy Algorithm for a Matroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independence-oracle construction of a base in arbitrary element order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(S:=\varnothing\) and \(U:=E(M)\). While \(U\neq\varnothing\), choose any \(e\in U\), remove it from \(U\), and set \(S:=S\cup\{e\}\) exactly when \(S\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I(M)\). Throughout, \(S\in\mathcal I(M)\), and upon termination \(|S|=r_M(E(M))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(F=\varnothing\) and one disjoint-set component for each vertex. Process the edges in nonincreasing order of \(w(e)\), breaking ties arbitrarily. When processing \(e=uv\), add \(e\) to \(F\) and unite the components of \(u\) and \(v\) exactly when those components are distinct; otherwise discard \(e\). Stop after every edge has been processed. The output \(F\) is a maximum-weight spanning forest, hence a maximum-weight basis of the graphic matroid. Sorting costs \(O(|E|\log |E|)\), and the disjoint-set operations cost \(O(|E|\alpha(|V|))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort edges by decreasing weight and accept exactly those joining distinct components. The resulting spanning forest is a maximum-weight graphic-matroid basis.

children.title: Exchange Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates based on feasible exchanges that justify greedy choices or optimality.

assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite matroid and \(w:E\to\mathbb R\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exchange certificate for \(B\) consists of the verifiable inequalities \(w(e)\le w(f)\) for every \(e\in E\setminus B\) and every \(f\in B\) such that \(B-f+e\) is a basis. Equivalently, no feasible single-element exchange strictly increases total weight. Under the matroid basis-exchange axiom, these local inequalities imply \(w(B')\le w(B)\) for every basis \(B'\). Thus the certificate proves global maximum-weight optimality of \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis is certified optimal when every feasible replacement of one chosen element by one unchosen element is nonimproving.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A certificate failure witness is a pair \((e,f)\) with \(e\in E\setminus B\), \(f\in C_B(e)\setminus\{e\}\), and \(w(e)>w(f)\). Because \(f\) lies on the fundamental circuit, \(B'=B-f+e\) is a basis. Its weight satisfies \(w(B')=w(B)+w(e)-w(f)>w(B)\). The pair is therefore directly checkable and refutes both the proposed exchange certificate and the claim that \(B\) is a maximum-weight basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unchosen element heavier than a chosen element on its fundamental circuit gives an improving exchange and disproves optimality.

assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite matroid, \(B\) is a basis, and \(w:E\to\mathbb R\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(b\in B\), let \(D_B(b)\) be the unique cocircuit contained in \((E\setminus B)\cup\{b\}\). Then \(B-b+e\) is a basis exactly when \(e\in D_B(b)\setminus\{b\}\). Consequently, \(B\) is a maximum-weight basis if and only if \(w(b)\ge w(e)\) for every \(b\in B\) and \(e\in D_B(b)\setminus\{b\}\). These inequalities are the dual cocircuit form of the fundamental-circuit certificate, obtained through \(M^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each chosen element must be at least as heavy as every replacement in its fundamental cocircuit; these dual inequalities exactly certify optimality.

children.title: Spanning-Tree Applications
children.top_down_role: Greedy optimization for graphic bases through spanning-tree instances.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with edge costs \(c:E\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The greedy output is a minimum-cost spanning forest, and a minimum-cost spanning tree when \(G\) is connected.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum spanning forest as minimization over graphic-matroid bases.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Regard the forests of \(G\) as the independent sets of its graphic matroid. Initialize \(T=\varnothing\), process edges in nondecreasing order of \(c(e)\), and add an edge exactly when it does not create a cycle. After all edges are processed, \(T\) is a basis of the graphic matroid minimizing \(c(T)\). Thus \(T\) is a minimum-cost spanning forest; if \(G\) is connected, it has \(|V|-1\) edges and is a minimum-cost spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kruskal's increasing-cost greedy rule is matroid greedy on forests, yielding a minimum spanning forest and, for connected graphs, a minimum spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Tree Applications

children.title: Transversal Applications

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\) is a maximum-weight basis of the transversal matroid presented by \(H\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The independent sets are the subsets of \(L\) that can be saturated by a matching into \(R\). Initialize \(I=\varnothing\) and \(N=\varnothing\). Process \(x\in L\) in nonincreasing order of \(w(x)\). Search for an augmenting path that extends \(N\) to saturate \(I\cup\{x\}\); if one exists, augment \(N\) and add \(x\) to \(I\), and otherwise reject \(x\). After all vertices are processed, \(I\) is a maximum-weight basis of the transversal matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Greedy accepts a left vertex exactly when the current matching can be augmented to cover it, producing a maximum-weight transversal-matroid basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-time, single-machine deadline scheduling with nonnegative job weights, viewed as a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(S\subseteq J\) is schedulable by its deadlines exactly when \(|S_{\le t}|\le t\) for every positive integer \(t\). These schedulable sets form a matroid on \(J\). Initialize \(S=\varnothing\), process the jobs in nonincreasing order of \(w_j\), and accept job \(j\) exactly when \(S\cup\{j\}\) continues to satisfy all deadline inequalities. The resulting set \(S\) is a maximum-weight basis of the scheduling matroid and, because all weights are nonnegative, a maximum-weight schedulable subset of \(J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For unit-time jobs with deadlines and nonnegative weights, schedulable subsets form a matroid, so decreasing-weight greedy with deadline-feasibility tests returns a maximum-weight schedulable set.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is a finite set of unit-processing-time jobs, each with an integer deadline \(d_j\ge 1\) and a weight \(w_j\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\).
At most one job is processed in each integer time slot.

knowledge_statements.title: Application-Class Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for universal correctness of decreasing-weight feasibility greedy on finite hereditary systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a weight function \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{>0}\), let \(G_w\) be obtained by processing \(E\) in nonincreasing weight order and accepting each element whose addition preserves membership in \(\mathcal I\). The system \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid if and only if, for every such \(w\) and every ordering consistent with its weight ties, \(G_w\) is a maximum-weight member of \(\mathcal I\). If \((E,\mathcal I)\) is not a matroid, there exists a strictly positive weight function, which may be chosen with distinct weights, for which this greedy rule returns a suboptimal maximal feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decreasing-weight feasibility greedy is universally correct exactly for matroids; every finite hereditary nonmatroid admits positive weights for which greedy returns a suboptimal maximal feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite, \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\subseteq 2^E\), and \(\mathcal I\) is hereditary: if \(X\in\mathcal I\) and \(Y\subseteq X\), then \(Y\in\mathcal I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Universal correctness of weight-ordered greedy holds exactly when \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid.

children.title: Rank-Inequality Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral descriptions organized by rank constraints plus ground-set bounds.

assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite matroid with rank function \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P_I(M)=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}^E:x(S)\le r(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E\},\qquad B(M)=P_I(M)\cap\{x:x(E)=r(E)\}.\]

notation.meaning: Incidence vector of a subset of the ground set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-matroid descriptions of both the independence and base polytopes.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.3. Polyhedral Descriptions p. 144
1.7 The Matroid Polytope p. 66
source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(P_I(M):=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I\}\) and \(B(M):=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^B:B\text{ is a base of }M\}\). Then
\[P_I(M)=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x_e\ge 0\ (e\in E),\ x(S)\le r(S)\ (S\subseteq E)\}.\]
Moreover, every base has cardinality \(r(E)\), and the base polytope is the maximum-cardinality face
\[B(M)=\{x\in P_I(M):x(E)=r(E)\}=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x_e\ge0,\ x(S)\le r(S)\ (S\subseteq E),\ x(E)=r(E)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The independence polytope is described by nonnegativity and all rank inequalities; imposing total coordinate sum equal to the matroid rank gives the base polytope.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Inequality Descriptions

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.3. Polyhedral Descriptions p. 144
1.7 The Matroid Polytope p. 66

children.title: Polyhedral Integrality
children.top_down_role: Integral vertices plus the combinatorial objects represented by those vertices.

assumptions_latex: \(P_I(M)\) and \(B(M)\) have the rank-inequality descriptions in the preceding record.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{vert}P_I(M)=\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I\},\qquad \operatorname{vert}B(M)=\{\chi^B:B\text{ is a base of }M\}.\]

notation.meaning: Set of vertices of a polytope.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality of finite matroid independence and base polytopes.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.3. Polyhedral Descriptions p. 144
1.7 The Matroid Polytope p. 66
source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every vertex of \(P_I(M)\) is integral and is the incidence vector of an independent set; conversely, every independent-set incidence vector is a vertex. Hence
\[P_I(M)\cap\mathbb Z^E=\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I\},\qquad \operatorname{vert}P_I(M)=\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I\}.\]
The face \(B(M)=\{x\in P_I(M):x(E)=r(E)\}\) is likewise integral, with
\[B(M)\cap\mathbb Z^E=\operatorname{vert}B(M)=\{\chi^B:B\text{ is a base of }M\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both matroid polytopes are integral: their vertices are exactly the incidence vectors of independent sets and bases, respectively.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Integrality

children.title: Total Dual Integrality
children.top_down_role: The total-dual-integrality regime associated with rank-based systems.

assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite matroid with integer-valued rank function \(r\).
The rank system includes \(x(S)\le r(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq E\) and \(x_e\ge0\) for every \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[\min\left\{\sum_{S\subseteq E}r(S)y_S:\sum_{S\ni e}y_S\ge c_e\ (e\in E),\ y\ge0\right\}\]
\text{has an integral optimum whenever its value is finite and \(c\in\mathbb Z^E\).}

notation.meaning: Integral objective vector for the primal system.
Dual multiplier of the rank inequality indexed by S.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: TDI form of the nonnegative matroid rank system.

source_refs.locator: Section 5.3. Total Dual Integrality p. 111
5.17 Total dual integrality p. 76

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The system
\[x(S)\le r(S)\quad(S\subseteq E),\qquad -x_e\le0\quad(e\in E)\]
is totally dual integral. Equivalently, for every \(c\in\mathbb Z^E\) for which the primal maximum is finite, the dual of
\[\max\{c^\top x:x(S)\le r(S)\ (S\subseteq E),\ x\ge0\}\]
has an integral optimum. In the reduced dual formulation, this means that there is \(y\in\mathbb Z_{ge0}^{2^E}\) satisfying \(\sum_{S\ni e}y_S\ge c_e\) for all \(e\in E\) and minimizing \(\sum_{S\subseteq E}r(S)y_S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The matroid rank system is TDI: every finite linear program with an integral objective admits an integral optimal dual solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Total Dual Integrality

source_witnesses.locator: Section 5.3. Total Dual Integrality p. 111
5.17 Total dual integrality p. 76

children.title: Integrality Consequences
children.top_down_role: Optimization plus certification consequences flowing from integral polyhedral structure.

assumptions_latex: \(c\in\mathbb R^E\), and \(P_I(M)\) and \(B(M)\) are its independence and base polytopes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max_{x\in P_I(M)}c^\top x=\max_{I\in\mathcal I}\sum_{e\in I}c_e,\qquad \max_{x\in B(M)}c^\top x=\max_{B\text{ base of }M}\sum_{e\in B}c_e.\]

notation.meaning: Incidence vector of a set S.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization consequences of rank-system integrality and TDI.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.3. Polyhedral Descriptions p. 144
1.7 The Matroid Polytope p. 66
source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(c\in\mathbb R^E\), linear optimization over \(P_I(M)\) attains an optimum at \(\chi^I\) for some \(I\in\mathcal I\), and linear optimization over \(B(M)\) attains an optimum at \(\chi^B\) for some base \(B\) of \(M\). Consequently,
\[\max_{x\in P_I(M)}c^\top x=\max_{I\in\mathcal I}\sum_{e\in I}c_e,\qquad \max_{x\in B(M)}c^\top x=\max_{B\text{ base of }M}\sum_{e\in B}c_e.\]
For integral \(c\), total dual integrality additionally supplies an integral optimal dual solution for the rank system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear optimization over either matroid polytope attains an incidence-vector optimum, so the rank descriptions exactly model weighted independent-set and weighted-base optimization.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrality Consequences

children.title: Face Structure
children.top_down_role: Faces arising from tight rank constraints, restrictions, contractions, or decomposition structure.

assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite matroid with base polytope \(B(M)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in B(M)}w^\top x=B\!\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^k(M|F_i)/F_{i-1}\right),\quad F_i:=\{e:w_e\ge\alpha_i\}.\]

notation.meaning: Prefix of weight levels through level i.
Restriction to F followed by contraction of A.
Direct sum of matroids on disjoint weight blocks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposed faces of a finite matroid base polytope.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.3. Polyhedral Descriptions p. 144

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Put \(F_0:=\varnothing\) and \(F_i:=\{e\in E:w_e\ge\alpha_i\}\). The face maximizing \(w\) is
\[Q_w:=\{x\in B(M):w^\top x=\max_{z\in B(M)}w^\top z\}=\{x\in B(M):x(F_i)=r(F_i)\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,k\}.\]
Its vertices are precisely the maximum-weight bases. Moreover, after identifying each block \(F_i\setminus F_{i-1}\) with its coordinates, \(Q_w\) is the base polytope of the direct sum
\[\bigoplus_{i=1}^k (M|F_i)/F_{i-1}.\]
Every nonempty face of \(B(M)\) arises in this way for some \(w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A base-polytope face consists of maximum-weight bases and is itself the base polytope of a direct sum of successive restriction-contraction minors.
knowledge_statements.title: Face Structure

children.title: Facet Structure
children.top_down_role: Facet-defining constraint families plus redundancy boundaries.

assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a loopless finite matroid with rank function \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x(F)\le r(F)\text{ defines a facet of }P_I(M)\iff F\text{ is closed and }M|F\text{ is inseparable}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank facets of the full-dimensional independence polytope of a loopless matroid.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.3. Polyhedral Descriptions p. 144

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The rank inequality \(x(F)\le r(F)\) defines a facet of the full-dimensional independence polytope \(P_I(M)\) if and only if \(F\) is closed and inseparable: 
\[\operatorname{cl}_M(F)=F,\qquad r(F_1)+r(F_2)>r(F)\]
for every partition \(F=F_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}F_2\) into two nonempty sets. Equivalently, the restriction \(M|F\) is connected. Under these conditions, the equality set \(\{x\in P_I(M):x(F)=r(F)\}\) has dimension \(|E|-1\). Rank inequalities failing closure or inseparability are implied by stronger rank inequalities or decompose into lower-support inequalities and therefore are not facets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper rank inequality is facet-defining for a loopless matroid independence polytope exactly when its set is closed and its restriction is connected.
knowledge_statements.title: Facet Structure

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.3. Polyhedral Descriptions p. 144

children.title: Exchange Adjacency
children.top_down_role: Edge adjacency interpreted through elementary exchanges between feasible combinatorial objects.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\chi^{B_1}\text{ and }\chi^{B_2}\text{ are adjacent in }B(M)\iff B_2=B_1-e+f\text{ for some }e\in B_1\setminus B_2\text{ and }f\in B_2\setminus B_1.\]

notation.meaning: Incidence vector of a base B.
Set obtained by deleting e and adding f.
Coordinate unit vector indexed by e.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edges of the finite matroid base polytope.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The vertices \(\chi^{B_1}\) and \(\chi^{B_2}\) are joined by an edge of \(B(M)\) if and only if their bases differ by one valid exchange: there exist \(e\in B_1\setminus B_2\) and \(f\in B_2\setminus B_1\) such that
\[B_2=B_1-e+f.\]
Equivalently, \(|B_1\mathbin\triangle B_2|=2\). In that case the edge direction is
\[\chi^{B_2}-\chi^{B_1}=\mathbf e_f-\mathbf e_e,\]
so every edge of a matroid base polytope is parallel to a difference of two coordinate unit vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two base-polytope vertices are adjacent exactly when their bases differ by one feasible element exchange; every edge direction is a coordinate difference.

children.title: Face–Exchange Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between facial incidence, edge directions, plus matroid exchange structure.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is a nonempty face of \(B(M)\), exposed by some \(w\in\mathbb R^E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[Q=B(N_w),\qquad N_w=\bigoplus_{i=1}^k(M|F_i)/F_{i-1},\]
\text{and the graph of \(Q\) is the single-exchange graph of the bases of \(N_w\).}

notation.meaning: Face matroid associated with weight w.
Base polytope of a matroid N.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between base-polytope faces and exchange systems of face matroids.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.3. Polyhedral Descriptions p. 144

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\alpha_1>\cdots>\alpha_k\) be the values of \(w\), set \(F_0:=\varnothing\), and set \(F_i:=\{e:w_e\ge\alpha_i\}\). Define the face matroid
\[N_w:=\bigoplus_{i=1}^k(M|F_i)/F_{i-1}.\]
Then \(Q=B(N_w)\) under the natural coordinate identification. Thus the vertices of \(Q\) correspond exactly to the \(w\)-maximum bases of \(M\), and two such vertices form an edge of \(Q\) exactly when the corresponding bases differ by a single exchange that remains within the maximum-weight family. Hence the one-skeleton of every face is the basis-exchange graph of its face matroid.

children.title: Base-Polytope Duality
children.top_down_role: Geometric correspondence between primal-base structure plus dual-matroid base structure.

assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite matroid with rank function \(r_M\).
\(M^*\) denotes the dual matroid and \(\mathbf1\in\mathbb R^E\) is the all-ones vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[B(M^*)=\mathbf1-B(M),\qquad r_{M^*}(S)=|S|-r_M(E)+r_M(E\setminus S).\]

notation.meaning: Affine reflection of a set P.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine complement duality for finite matroid base polytopes.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172
1.7 The Matroid Polytope p. 66

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(B\subseteq E\) is a base of \(M\) if and only if \(E\setminus B\) is a base of \(M^*\). Therefore complementation of incidence vectors gives the affine identity
\[B(M^*)=\{\mathbf1-x:x\in B(M)\}=\mathbf1-B(M).\]
The compatible rank transformation is
\[r_{M^*}(S)=|S|-r_M(E)+r_M(E\setminus S)\qquad(S\subseteq E).\]
Consequently, maximizing \(w^\top x\) over \(B(M^*)\) is equivalent, up to the constant \(w^\top\mathbf1\), to minimizing \(w^\top x\) over \(B(M)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementing every base reflects the base polytope through the all-ones vector and converts optimization on a matroid into opposite optimization on its dual.
knowledge_statements.title: Base-Polytope Duality

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The base polytope \(B(M)\) has the integer decomposition property. Explicitly, for every positive integer \(k\) and every lattice point \(z\in kB(M)\cap\mathbb Z^E\), there exist bases \(B_1,\ldots,B_k\) of \(M\), with repetitions permitted, such that
\[z=\sum_{i=1}^k\chi^{B_i}.\]
Each coordinate \(z_e\) counts how many members of the resulting multiset of bases contain \(e\).

\[k\mathbf1-z=\sum_{i=1}^k\chi^{E\setminus B_i}\in kB(M^*)\cap\mathbb Z^E,\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the affine bijection \(z\mapsto k\mathbf1-z\) from \(kB(M)\) to \(kB(M^*)\), integer decompositions correspond term by term. If
\[z=\sum_{i=1}^k\chi^{B_i},\]
then every \(E\setminus B_i\) is a base of \(M^*\) and
\[k\mathbf1-z=\sum_{i=1}^k(\mathbf1-\chi^{B_i})=\sum_{i=1}^k\chi^{E\setminus B_i}.\]
Conversely, complementing the bases in any decomposition of \(k\mathbf1-z\) recovers a decomposition of \(z\). Thus the integer decomposition property and its decomposition fibers are preserved by matroid duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementing every base converts any integer decomposition for a matroid base polytope bijectively into a decomposition for the dual base polytope.
knowledge_statements.title: Duality-Compatible Decompositions

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Integrality of a polytope alone does not imply integer decomposition. For \(m\ge2\), the Reeve tetrahedron
\[R_m:=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(1,1,m)\}\]
is an integral polytope whose only lattice points are its four vertices. Nevertheless, \((1,1,1)\in2R_m\cap\mathbb Z^3\): using barycentric coefficients in the dilation, it is represented by coefficients \(1-1/m\), \(1-1/m\), and \(1/m\) on the three nonzero vertices, whose sum is at most \(2\). No sum of two vertices equals \((1,1,1)\). Thus removing the matroidal rank-submodular structure permits failure of integer decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral polytopes need not have integer decomposition: a Reeve tetrahedron has a lattice point in its double that is not a sum of two lattice points.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Order the elements with positive weight as \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\) so that \(w_{e_1}\geq\cdots\geq w_{e_m}>0\). Initialize \(I_0=\varnothing\). For \(j=1,\ldots,m\), set \(I_j=I_{j-1}\cup\{e_j\}\) when this set belongs to \(\mathcal I\), and otherwise set \(I_j=I_{j-1}\). Output \(I_g=I_m\). Then \(I_g\) maximizes \(w(I)\) over all \(I\in\mathcal I\), and its incidence vector maximizes \(w^\top x\) over \(P(M)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Greedy optimality for polymatroid linear optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successive rank increments solve the nonnegative polymatroid linear program, with a stated boundary where coordinate nonnegativity and R2 may be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $E=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $T_e=\{1,\ldots,e\}$, and $T_0=\varnothing$. Suppose $r$ satisfies R2 and R3, $r(\varnothing)=0$, and $c(1)\ge\cdots\ge c(n)$. If $k$ is the greatest index with $c(k)\ge0$, define $x_e=r(T_e)-r(T_{e-1})$ for $e\le k$ and $x_e=0$ for $e>k$. Then $x$ solves $\max\{c^\top y:y(T)\le r(T)\ \forall T\subseteq E,\ y\ge0\}$. Furthermore, if $k=n$ and the constraints $y\ge0$ are dropped, the same greedy construction is optimal without assuming R2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After ordering the weights, successive rank increments through the last nonnegative weight solve the polymatroid linear program. If every weight is nonnegative and coordinate nonnegativity is removed, the theorem does not require R2.
assumptions_latex: r\text{ satisfies R2 and R3 in the nonnegative formulation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname*{argmax}\{c^\top y:y(T)\le r(T)\ \forall T\subseteq E,\ y\ge0\},\qquad x_e=\begin{cases}r(T_e)-r(T_{e-1}),&e\le k,\\0,&e>k.\end{cases}

children.title: Rank-Inequality Separation
children.top_down_role: Separation interfaces for detecting violated rank constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite matroid with rank function \(r\).
\(x\in\mathbb Q^E\) is the point to be separated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns \(S\subseteq E\) with \(x(S)>r(S)\), or certifies \(x(S)\leq r(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq E\).

notation.meaning: sum of coordinates indexed by a set

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Minimize the submodular function \(g_x(S)=r(S)-x(S)\) over \(S\subseteq E\). If a minimizer \(S^*\) satisfies \(g_x(S^*)<0\), return the violated valid inequality \(x(S^*)\leq r(S^*)\). If \(g_x(S^*)\geq0\), certify that every rank inequality \(x(S)\leq r(S)\) holds. Coordinate constraints such as \(x_e\geq0\) must be checked separately when separating over the full independence polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize rank minus coordinate sum. A negative minimum identifies a violated rank inequality; a nonnegative minimum certifies that all rank inequalities hold.

children.title: Most-Violated Rank Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Identification of rank constraints having maximum violation.

assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite matroid with rank function \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every minimizer of \(r(S)-x(S)\) indexes a rank inequality of maximum additive violation.

notation.meaning: additive violation of the rank inequality indexed by a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive, rather than normalized, violation of matroid rank inequalities.

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Independence and rank p. 173

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(S\subseteq E\), define \(v_x(S)=x(S)-r(S)\). Then
\[\max_{S\subseteq E}v_x(S)=-\min_{S\subseteq E}\bigl(r(S)-x(S)\bigr).\]
Consequently, if \(S^*\in\arg\min_{S\subseteq E}(r(S)-x(S))\), then \(x(S^*)\leq r(S^*)\) is a most-additively-violated rank inequality. A rank inequality is violated exactly when the displayed maximum is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A most-violated rank inequality is obtained by minimizing rank minus coordinate sum; the negative minimum equals the maximum additive violation.

children.title: Separation-to-Violation Reductions

assumptions_latex: A value oracle supplies \(r(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq E\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form the value oracle \(g_x(S)=r(S)-x(S)\), which is submodular because \(r\) is submodular and \(x(S)\) is modular. Invoke a submodular-minimization algorithm to obtain \(S^*\in\arg\min_{S\subseteq E}g_x(S)\). If \(g_x(S^*)<0\), output \(x(S^*)\leq r(S^*)\); otherwise certify every rank inequality. Thus any polynomial-time submodular-minimization implementation yields polynomial-time rank-inequality separation under the rank-value oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract the modular coordinate sum from the submodular rank function, minimize the result, and use the minimum's sign to separate or certify feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization–Separation Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong oracle equivalence for bounded well-described rational polyhedra in the Turing model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty bounded well-described rational polyhedron with a supplied facet-complexity bound \(\varphi\). There is an oracle-polynomial algorithm that, given a strong separation oracle for \(P\) and \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\), computes a maximizer of \(c^\top x\) over \(P\). Conversely, there is an oracle-polynomial algorithm that, given a strong optimization oracle for \(P\) and \(y\in\mathbb Q^n\), either certifies \(y\in P\) or returns \(a\in\mathbb Q^n\) satisfying \(a^\top y>\max_{x\in P}a^\top x\). The running times are polynomial in \(n\), \(\varphi\), and the binary encoding lengths of the rational query data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded well-described rational polyhedron with a known facet-complexity bound, exact linear optimization and exact separation can each be implemented in oracle-polynomial time using an oracle for the other.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty bounded well-described rational polyhedron.
A valid facet-complexity bound \(\varphi\) for \(P\) is supplied.
Queries and objective vectors are rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong linear optimization over \(P\) and strong separation for \(P\) are oracle-polynomially equivalent, with complexity polynomial in \(n\), \(\varphi\), and the query encoding lengths.

assumptions_latex: Feasibility is the uniform matroid of rank \(2\) on \(E=\{a,b,c\}\).
Greedy repeatedly chooses a feasible element of largest current marginal gain.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit finite counterexample directly checkable

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the monotone function \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R_+\) by \(f(S)=100\) when \(\{b,c\}\subseteq S\), by \(f(S)=2\) when \(a\in S\) but \(\{b,c\}\nsubseteq S\), and by \(f(S)=|S\cap\{b,c\}|\) otherwise. children.title: Online Objective Regimes
children.top_down_role: Greedy limitations under sequential information or irrevocable choices.

assumptions_latex: Elements with arbitrary nonnegative weights arrive sequentially in adversarial order.
At most one element may be accepted, and acceptance is immediate and irrevocable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No deterministic online algorithm has a finite competitive ratio against the offline maximum without additional value or arrival assumptions.

notation.meaning: value obtained by an online algorithm on a sequence

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: adversarial rank-one construction directly checkable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic adversarial-order online selection for a rank-one uniform matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Present a first element of weight \(1\). If the algorithm rejects it, terminate; then \(\operatorname{ALG}=0\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}=1\). If the algorithm accepts it, present a second element of weight \(K\), where \(K>1\); rank-one feasibility forces rejection of the second element, so \(\operatorname{ALG}=1\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}=K\). Since \(K\) is arbitrary, no constant \(C<\infty\) guarantees \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)\leq C\operatorname{ALG}(\sigma)\) for every arrival sequence \(\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under adversarial arrivals and irrevocable rank-one selection, accepting or rejecting the first item can both be exploited, precluding any finite deterministic competitive ratio.

children.title: Cross-Regime Greedy Failure
children.top_down_role: Failure mechanisms shared across nonlinear and online settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Regime Greedy Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the classical offline-linear matroid greedy theorem across objective and information regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact weight-ordered greedy for \(\max\{\sum_{e\in I}w_e:I\in\mathcal I\}\) relies jointly on linear additivity and complete offline knowledge. Removing additivity permits complementarity examples in which a locally best marginal choice blocks the optimum, even for a uniform matroid. Removing offline knowledge permits adversarial rank-one sequences for which every deterministic irrevocable rule has unbounded competitive ratio. Hence the exchange axiom alone supplies neither exact nonlinear marginal greedy nor bounded deterministic online greedy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid exchange guarantees classical greedy only in the offline linear regime; nonlinear complementarities and adversarial arrivals each independently destroy that guarantee.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility is a matroid independence family.
Greedy decisions use only currently visible weights or marginal gains and are irrevocable within the applicable regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The matroid exchange axiom does not extend exact greedy optimization from offline linear objectives to arbitrary nonlinear or adversarial online objectives.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conclusion follows from the two explicit regime counterexamples

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unweighted Matroid Intersection Augmentation Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Augmenting-path procedure for common independent sets of two matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(J=\varnothing\). Repeatedly construct \(G=G(M_1,M_2,J)\). If \(G\) contains an \((r,s)\)-dipath, choose a chordless one with node sequence
\[
r,e_1,f_1,\ldots,e_m,f_m,e_{m+1},s
\]
and replace
\[
J\leftarrow J\mathbin{\triangle}\{e_1,f_1,\ldots,e_m,f_m,e_{m+1}\}.
\]
If no \((r,s)\)-dipath exists, set
\[
A=\{e\in S:\text{an }(r,e)\text{-dipath exists in }G\}
\]
and stop.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with the empty set. While the auxiliary digraph has a directed source-to-sink path, choose a chordless such path and update J by symmetric difference with its ground-set vertices. If no such path exists, form the set of ground-set vertices reachable from the source and stop.
assumptions_latex: M_1=(S,\mathcal I_1)\text{ and }M_2=(S,\mathcal I_2)\text{ are matroids on }S.
G(M_1,M_2,J)\text{ is the matroid-intersection auxiliary digraph.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J\leftarrow J\triangle\{e_1,f_1,\ldots,e_m,f_m,e_{m+1}\}\text{ when an augmenting path exists; otherwise form }A=\{e\in S:r\leadsto e\}\text{ and stop.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a split-weight certificate and its fixed-cardinality optimality consequence.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the common independent-set family \(\mathcal F=\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\),
\[\max_{I\in\mathcal F}|I|=\max_{I\in\mathcal F}\sum_{e\in I}1.\]
Thus maximum-cardinality matroid intersection is exactly the unit-weight instance of
\[\max_{I\in\mathcal F}w(I),\qquad w(I)=\sum_{e\in I}w(e).\]
General weights may distinguish common independent sets having equal cardinality. If negative weights are allowed and neither cardinality nor a base constraint is imposed, an optimum need not have maximum cardinality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\[\max\left\{w(B):B\in\mathcal B(M_1)\cap\mathcal B(M_2)\right\},\qquad w(B)=\sum_{e\in B}w(e).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(B\subseteq E\),
\[B\in\mathcal B(M_2)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad E\setminus B\in\mathcal B(M_2^*).\]
Consequently,
\[B\in\mathcal B(M_1)\cap\mathcal B(M_2)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B\in\mathcal B(M_1)\ \text{ and }\ E\setminus B\in\mathcal B(M_2^*).\]
Thus common-base feasibility is equivalent to partitioning \(E\) into a base of \(M_1\) and a base of \(M_2^*\). Under equal ranks, this complementary-base formulation is equivalent to the rank-partition inequalities for common-base feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is a common base precisely when it is a base of the first matroid and its complement is a base of the second matroid's dual.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A subset of \(F\) is independent in both \(M_U\) and \(M_V\) exactly when it is a matching of \(G\). Under this specialization, the matroid-intersection rank-partition formula yields the bipartite matching min-max relation
\[\nu(G)=\tau(G),\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The directed exchange graph \(D_I\) has vertex set \(E\). For \(x\in I\) and \(y\in E\setminus I\), include the arc \(y\to x\) when \(I-x+y\in\mathcal I_1\), and include the arc \(x\to y\) when \(I-x+y\in\mathcal I_2\). Define

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Border graph of a common independent set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the directed exchange representation used for the intersection of two matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)$ and $M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)$, and let $I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2$. The border graph $BG(I)$ is the directed bipartite graph with parts $I$ and $E\setminus I$. For each $e\in E\setminus I$ with $e\in\operatorname{sp}_1(I)$, let $C_e^{(1)}$ be the unique $M_1$-circuit in $I+e$ and include every arc $(f,e)$ with $f\in C_e^{(1)}\setminus\{e\}$; if $e\notin\operatorname{sp}_1(I)$, then $e$ has indegree zero and is a source. For each $e\in E\setminus I$ with $e\in\operatorname{sp}_2(I)$, let $C_e^{(2)}$ be the unique $M_2$-circuit in $I+e$ and include every arc $(e,f)$ with $f\in C_e^{(2)}\setminus\{e\}$; if $e\notin\operatorname{sp}_2(I)$, then $e$ has outdegree zero and is a sink. The simple border graphs $BG_1(I)$ and $BG_2(I)$ contain, respectively, the arcs directed from $I$ to $E\setminus I$ and from $E\setminus I$ to $I$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The border graph is a directed bipartite graph on a common independent set and its complement. Fundamental circuits of the first matroid give arcs from the independent set to outside elements, while those of the second matroid give arcs in the reverse direction. Unspanned outside elements are respectively sources or sinks. The two directional subgraphs are called simple border graphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: BG(I),\ BG_1(I),\text{ and }BG_2(I)\text{ are defined by the stated fundamental-circuit arcs and source--sink conditions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize with any \(I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\), for example \(I=\varnothing\). Construct \(D_I\), \(S_I\), and \(T_I\). If \(S_I\cap T_I\ne\varnothing\), add one element from the intersection. Otherwise, find a shortest directed path \(P\) from \(S_I\) to \(T_I\). If such a path exists, update
\[I\leftarrow I\triangle V(P).\]
Rebuild the exchange graph and repeat. If no directed \(S_I\)-to-
\(T_I\) path exists, stop and output \(I\); then \(I\) has maximum cardinality among all common independent sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly augment a common independent set along a shortest source-to-sink path in its exchange graph. Absence of such a path certifies maximum cardinality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cardinality Matroid-Intersection Augmentation Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterative augmenting-sequence procedure for cardinality matroid intersection; its optimality guarantee is stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize S\in\mathcal I(M_1)\cap\mathcal I(M_2), for example S:=\varnothing. While \mathcal G(S) has a source--sink dipath, choose an augmenting sequence e_0,e_1,f_1,e_2,f_2,\ldots,f_n,e_n and set S:=\bigl(S\cup\{e_j:0\le j\le n\}\bigr)\setminus\{f_j:1\le j\le n\}. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Breadth-first search partitions the exchange digraph into layers \(L_0,\ldots,L_d\). Retain only admissible arcs from \(L_j\) to \(L_{j+1}\). Within this layered graph, repeatedly select augmenting structures whose combined symmetric-difference update remains independent in both matroids. A phase is blocking when, after applying its feasible updates and deleting invalidated arcs, no directed path from \(L_0\) to \(L_d\) remains. Rebuild the exchange digraph after the phase; terminate when its source and sink sets are disconnected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A blocking phase performs a feasible batch of shortest augmentations until every path at the current shortest distance is destroyed, forcing the distance to increase.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(d(I)\) as the minimum number of arcs in an augmenting path of \(D_I\), with \(d(I)=\infty\) if none exists. A layered augmentation phase computes the breadth-first-search layers \(L_j\) containing vertices at distance \(j\) from the source set and permits only exchanges compatible with consecutive layers. A shortest-path phase performs one feasible augmentation of length \(d(I)\); a blocking phase continues with compatible feasible augmentations until no path of that length remains. The regime terminates exactly when \(d(I)=\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Least-cost augmenting-path algorithm for weighted matroid intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality-by-cardinality weighted matroid-intersection augmentation procedure, including its stated zero-iteration boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize k=0 and J_0=\varnothing. Repeatedly construct G(M_1,M_2,c,J_k). If an (r,s)-dipath exists, choose a least-cost such dipath P having as few arcs as possible, augment J_k along P to obtain J_{k+1}, and replace k by k+1. Otherwise, choose p\in\{1,\ldots,k\} such that c(J_p)\ge c(J_i) for every 1\le i\le k, output J=J_p, and stop. As written, this output step is undefined if termination occurs with k=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from the empty set, the procedure repeatedly augments along a least-cost source-to-sink exchange path, breaking ties by arc count. When no path exists, it returns the heaviest positive-index iterate; the stated selection is undefined if no augmentation has occurred.
assumptions_latex: M_1,M_2\text{ are matroids on a common ground set }S
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\ge 1\Rightarrow J=J_p\text{ for some }p\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\text{ with }c(J_p)\ge c(J_i)\text{ for all }1\le i\le k;\quad k=0\Rightarrow\text{the stated output rule is undefined}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a common independent set \(I\) together with dual labels \(\pi\) such that every exchange arc \(a\) has reduced cost \(\bar c_\pi(a)\ge 0\). Form the admissible exchange graph from arcs satisfying \(\bar c_\pi(a)=0\). If it contains a feasible augmenting sequence, update \(I\) by its symmetric difference while preserving complementary slackness on used exchanges. If no such sequence exists, change \(\pi\) by the largest step that retains nonnegative reduced costs; this makes at least one additional exchange arc admissible. Stop when the maintained primal and dual values coincide.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an initial scale \(\delta\) at least as large as the largest relevant weight magnitude and define \(w_\delta(e)=\delta\lfloor w(e)/\delta\rfloor\). At each phase, optimize the common independent set for \(w_\delta\), using the preceding phase's set and labels as a warm start when available. Replace \(\delta\) by \(\delta/2\), refine the rounded weights, and repeat. Since \(0\le w(X)-w_\delta(X)<|X|\delta\le n\delta\), a phase with \(n\delta<1\) resolves all nonzero differences between integral objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weight scaling repeatedly halves a rounding unit, reoptimizes the rounded instance, and becomes exact once total rounding error is below one integral objective unit.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong polynomiality in the independence-oracle model for exact weighted matroid intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the independence-oracle model, a regime is strongly polynomial when there exist polynomials \(Q\) and \(A\) such that every instance on \(n\) elements is solved using at most \(Q(n)\) oracle calls and \(A(n)\) other arithmetic operations, irrespective of the numerical values and binary encoding lengths of the weights. Additionally, every number produced during the computation must have encoding length bounded polynomially in the total input encoding length. A bound polynomial in \(\log\max_{e\in E}|w(e)|\) alone establishes ordinary polynomiality, not strong polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polynomiality requires operation and oracle-call bounds depending only on ground-set size, not on weight magnitudes, together with intermediate encodings bounded polynomially in the total input encoding length.
assumptions_latex: Inputs are two finite matroids on \(E\), accessed through a specified independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A weighted-intersection algorithm is strongly polynomial only if its oracle-call count and its remaining arithmetic-operation count are bounded by a polynomial in \(|E|\), independently of the numerical weight magnitudes, and every intermediate number has encoding length bounded polynomially in the total input encoding length.

The common-base polytope is the rank-\(r\) face of the common independent-set polytope:
