knowledge_statements.title: Total-Dual-Integrality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chain-supported integral dual certificate for nonnegative integral objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal program \(\max\{c^Tx:x(S)\le f(S)\ (S\subseteq E),\ x\ge 0\}\), assign dual multipliers \(y_{S_i}=c_{e_i}-c_{e_{i+1}}\) to the prefix inequalities and zero to all other subset inequalities. These multipliers are nonnegative integers and satisfy \(\sum_{S\ni e}y_S\ge c_e\) for every \(e\in E\). Their objective value is \[\sum_{i=1}^n(c_{e_i}-c_{e_{i+1}})f(S_i),\] which equals the value of the greedy primal vector. Feasibility, integrality, and equality of the two displayed values certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral differences between consecutive sorted weights give a chain-supported dual certificate whose value equals the greedy solution's value.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp singleton obstruction to primal integrality when rank integrality is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{e\}\), \(f(\varnothing)=0\), and \(f(\{e\})=\tfrac12\). This function is normalized, nondecreasing, and submodular, but not integer-valued. Its polymatroid is \[P(f)=\{x_e\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}:x_e\le\tfrac12\}=[0,\tfrac12],\] whose nonzero vertex is fractional. For the integral objective \(c_e=1\), the greedy optimum is \(x_e^*=\tfrac12\) with value \(\tfrac12\), so no integral primal point attains the linear-programming optimum. Hence submodularity alone does not imply polyhedral integrality; integer-valued rank data is essential for the integral-vertex and integral-greedy conclusions. This example does not by itself refute total dual integrality, which is a property of the constraint system's dual certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singleton rank of one half yields a fractional optimal vertex, showing that submodularity without integer-valued rank data does not ensure primal polyhedral integrality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality form of the integral polymatroid-intersection theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite and let \(f_1,f_2:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) be normalized, nondecreasing, submodular functions. For \(i\in\{1,2\}\), define \(P(f_i)=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^E:x(S)\le f_i(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E\}\). Then \(P(f_1)\cap P(f_2)\) is an integral polytope and
\[\max\{x(E):x\in P(f_1)\cap P(f_2)\}=\min_{S\subseteq E}\bigl(f_1(S)+f_2(E\setminus S)\bigr).\]
Consequently, the maximum is attained by an integral vector whenever the intersection is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum total size of a common polymatroid vector equals a submodular cut minimum, and integer rank functions guarantee an integer optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are normalized, integer-valued, nondecreasing, and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(f_1)\cap P(f_2)\) is integral and satisfies the displayed min–max equality.

notation.meaning: The sum of coordinates of x indexed by S.
The polymatroid determined by rank function f_i.

children.title: Integer Decomposition Property
children.top_down_role: Decomposition behavior of integral points in scaled polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Decomposition Property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer decomposition for an integral polymatroid polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite, let \(f:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) be normalized, nondecreasing, and submodular, and let \(P(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^E:x(S)\le f(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E\}\). For every integer \(k\ge1\) and every \(z\in kP(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E\), there exist \(z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(k)}\in P(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E\) such that
\[z=z^{(1)}+\cdots+z^{(k)}.\]
Thus every lattice point in an integral dilation decomposes into lattice points of the original polymatroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every lattice point in a positive integer dilation of an integral polymatroid is a sum of lattice points from that polymatroid.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is normalized, integer-valued, nondecreasing, and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(kP(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E=(P(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E)+\cdots+(P(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E)\), with \(k\) summands.

notation.meaning: The scalar dilation of P(f) by k.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection–Decomposition Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer decomposition within the intersection of two integral polymatroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_1,f_2:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) be normalized, nondecreasing, submodular functions on a finite set \(E\), and put \(Q=P(f_1)\cap P(f_2)\). For every integer \(k\ge1\) and every \(z\in kQ\cap\mathbb Z^E\), there are integral common polymatroid vectors \(z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(k)}\in Q\cap\mathbb Z^E\) satisfying
\[z=z^{(1)}+\cdots+z^{(k)}.\]
Hence the polymatroid-intersection integrality mechanism is stable under integer dilation and yields the integer decomposition property for \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer point in a dilation of two intersecting integral polymatroids decomposes into integer points feasible for both polymatroids.
assumptions_latex: \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are normalized, integer-valued, nondecreasing, and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(kQ\cap\mathbb Z^E=(Q\cap\mathbb Z^E)+\cdots+(Q\cap\mathbb Z^E)\), with \(k\) summands.

notation.meaning: The intersection of the two polymatroid polytopes.
The scalar dilation of Q by k.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three polymatroids already destroy the two-polymatroid integrality mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{000,011,101,110\}\). For each coordinate \(j\in\{1,2,3\}\), let \(M_j\) be the partition matroid imposing capacity one on each class of triples having a fixed value in coordinate \(j\). The vector \(x\in\mathbb R^E\) with \(x_e=\tfrac12\) for every \(e\in E\) belongs to \(P(M_1)\cap P(M_2)\cap P(M_3)\) and has \(x(E)=2\). Any two distinct triples in \(E\) agree in some coordinate, so every common independent set has size at most one. Thus the three-polymatroid intersection is nonintegral, and the two-polymatroid decomposition conclusion cannot be extended without additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A four-triple three-dimensional matching instance has fractional value two but integral value one, showing failure for intersections of three matroids.
assumptions_latex: Each \(P(M_j)\) is the independent-set polytope of the stated partition matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(M_1)\cap P(M_2)\cap P(M_3)\) is not integral.

notation.meaning: The independent-set polytope of partition matroid M_j.
The coordinate associated with triple e.

children.title: Generalized Polymatroid Structure

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Polymatroid Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized polymatroid defined by an integral paramodular pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite. A pair \((p,b)\) with \(p,b:2^E\to\mathbb R\), \(p(\varnothing)=b(\varnothing)=0\), is paramodular when \(p\) is supermodular, \(b\) is submodular, and
\[b(X)-p(Y)\ge b(X\setminus Y)-p(Y\setminus X)\qquad(X,Y\subseteq E).\]
Its generalized polymatroid is
\[Q(p,b)=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:p(S)\le x(S)\le b(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E\}.\]
It is integral when \(p\) and \(b\) are integer-valued; in that case every nonempty face contains an integral point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized polymatroid is the set of vectors bounded below and above on every subset by a paramodular supermodular–submodular pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(p,b)=\{x:p(S)\le x(S)\le b(S)\text{ for all }S\subseteq E\}\).

notation.meaning: The sum of coordinates of x over S.
The generalized polymatroid defined by p and b.

review_flags: No generalized-polymatroid definition locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The paramodular-pair definition is plausible, but neither it nor the appended integrality assertion has an inspectable source. The latter is a property rather than part of the definition and particularly requires support.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized Polymatroids as Projections of Base Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bidirectional projection representation connecting generalized polymatroids and base polyhedra of submodular systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (\mathcal D,f) be a submodular system on E, let e\in E, and set E'=E\setminus\{e\}, \mathcal D_1=\{X\in\mathcal D:e\notin X\}, and \mathcal D_2=\{E\setminus X:X\in\mathcal D,\ e\in X\}. With f'=f|_{\mathcal D_1} and g'=f^{\#}|_{\mathcal D_2}, the projection of B(f) along the e-axis onto x(e)=0 is P(f',g')\subseteq\mathbb R^{E'}. Conversely, every generalized polymatroid in \mathbb R^{E'} is obtained this way. Its representing base polyhedron in \mathbb R^{E'\cup\{e\}} is unique up to translation along the e-axis, and projection of the hyperplane x(E)=f(E) onto x(e)=0 induces an isomorphism of the two polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting a submodular-system base polyhedron along one coordinate produces a generalized polymatroid determined by the stated restrictions. Conversely, every generalized polymatroid has such a lift, unique up to translation in the added coordinate, and the projection induces a polyhedral isomorphism.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal D,f)\text{ is a submodular system on }E
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_{e}B(f)=P(f',g'),\quad\text{and every generalized polymatroid has such a lift uniquely up to translation along }e.

knowledge_statements.title: Submodular-Flow Feasible Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible submodular flows with box-constrained arcs and base-polyhedron boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph, let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be submodular with \(f(\varnothing)=f(V)=0\), and let \(\ell,u\in(\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\})^A\) satisfy \(\ell\le u\). For \(x\in\mathbb R^A\), define \(\partial x(v)=x(\delta^-(v))-x(\delta^+(v))\). The submodular-flow feasible region is
\[F(D,f,\ell,u)=\{x\in\mathbb R^A:\ell\le x\le u,\ \partial x\in B(f)\},\]
where \(B(f)=\{y\in\mathbb R^V:y(S)\le f(S)\text{ for all }S\subseteq V,\ y(V)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A submodular flow obeys arc bounds and has its net boundary vector in a submodular base polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(D,f,\ell,u)=\{x:\ell\le x\le u,\ \partial x\in B(f)\}\).
review_flags: Supplied network-flow locators do not cover the submodular base constraint.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent and fits the leaf, but the inventory locators cover ordinary flows rather than the base-polyhedron constraint defining submodular flows.

children.title: Generalized-Polymatroid Flow Reductions

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Polymatroid Flow Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-extra-vertex representation of a generalized polymatroid by submodular-flow boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a paramodular pair \((p,b)\) on \(E\), introduce \(s\notin E\) and define \(f:2^{E\cup\{s\}}\to\mathbb R\) by
\[f(X)=b(X),\qquad f(X\cup\{s\})=-p(E\setminus X)\qquad(X\subseteq E).\]
Then \(f\) is submodular and
\[Q(p,b)=\{x|_E:x\in B(f)\}.\]
Equivalently, on the star with arcs \(s\to e\) for \(e\in E\), an arc vector \(z\) satisfies \(\partial z|_E=z\) and \(\partial z(s)=-z(E)\); hence \(z\in Q(p,b)\) exactly when \(\partial z\in B(f)\). Linear objectives are preserved coordinatewise by this reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding one root converts generalized-polymatroid lower and upper bounds into a base-polyhedron boundary constraint on a directed star.
assumptions_latex: \((p,b)\) is a paramodular pair on finite \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(p,b)=\{x|_E:x\in B(f)\}=\{z\in\mathbb R^E:\partial z\in B(f)\}\) under the star identification.

notation.meaning: The additional root element or star vertex.
The lifted submodular function on the extended ground set.

review_flags: The exact lifted-base representation requires a generalized-polymatroid source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lifted-base and directed-star representation is nontrivial and needs a specific generalized-polymatroid or submodular-flow source locator.

children.title: Flow-Interface Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Interface Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The crossing inequality is necessary for the lifted function to be submodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E=\{1,2\}\), define \(b(\varnothing)=0\), \(b(\{1\})=0\), \(b(\{2\})=1\), \(b(E)=1\), and define \(p(\varnothing)=p(\{1\})=p(\{2\})=0\), \(p(E)=1\). Although \(b\) is submodular and \(p\) is supermodular, the crossing inequality fails for \(X=\{1\}\) and \(Y=E\), since
\[b(X)-p(Y)=-1<0=b(X\setminus Y)-p(Y\setminus X).\]
For the one-root lift, \(f(\{1\})=0\), \(f(\{s\})=-1\), \(f(\{1,s\})=0\), and \(f(\varnothing)=0\). Consequently,
\[f(\{1\})+f(\{s\})=-1<0=f(\{1,s\})+f(\varnothing),\]
so \(f\) is not submodular. Thus the star construction is not a submodular-flow reduction without paramodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate submodularity and supermodularity do not suffice: violating the crossing inequality makes the lifted boundary function non-submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifted \(f\) is not submodular, so the generalized-polymatroid flow interface fails.

notation.meaning: The added root element in the lifted construction.
The function obtained from p and b by the one-root lift.

children.title: Accessibility Axiom
children.top_down_role: The accessibility component of greedoid feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Accessibility Axiom
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion accessibility for a finite greedoid feasible-set system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite and let \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\) with \(\varnothing\in\mathcal F\). The accessibility axiom is
\[X\in\mathcal F,\ X\ne\varnothing\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{there exists }e\in X\text{ such that }X\setminus\{e\}\in\mathcal F.\]
Thus every nonempty feasible set admits at least one feasible one-element deletion. Together with the greedoid augmentation axiom, accessibility makes \((E,\mathcal F)\) a greedoid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty feasible set must contain an element whose deletion leaves another feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall X\in\mathcal F\setminus\{\varnothing\}\ \exists e\in X:\ X\setminus\{e\}\in\mathcal F\).
review_flags: No greedoid source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The accessibility condition is standard, explicit, and correctly classified, but no greedoid source locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Accessible Set System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accessibility through feasible single-element deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set system $(E,\mathcal F)$ is accessible if $\varnothing\in\mathcal F$ and, for every $X\in\mathcal F\setminus\{\varnothing\}$, there exists $x\in X$ such that $X\setminus\{x\}\in\mathcal F$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set system is accessible if the empty set is feasible and every nonempty feasible set admits deletion of some element while remaining feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (E,\mathcal F)\text{ is accessible}\iff \varnothing\in\mathcal F\ \land\ \forall X\in\mathcal F\setminus\{\varnothing\}\ \exists x\in X:\ X\setminus\{x\}\in\mathcal F

children.title: Feasible Continuation Sets

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Continuation Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elements that extend a feasible greedoid set by one step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((E,\mathcal F)\) be a greedoid and let \(X\in\mathcal F\). The feasible continuation set of \(X\) is
\[\Gamma(X)=\{e\in E\setminus X:X\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal F\}.\]
The greedoid augmentation axiom is equivalently expressed as follows: whenever \(X,Y\in\mathcal F\) and \(|X|<|Y|\), one has
\[\Gamma(X)\cap(Y\setminus X)\ne\varnothing.\]
Hence a larger feasible set always supplies at least one feasible next element for the smaller set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The continuation set contains precisely the unused elements that can be appended while preserving feasibility; augmentation guarantees a continuation from any larger feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma(X)=\{e\in E\setminus X:X\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal F\}\).

notation.meaning: The feasible continuation set at X.

review_flags: No greedoid continuation-set source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The continuation-set definition and augmentation reformulation are precise, but both lack a specific greedoid source locator.

children.title: Prefix Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Feasibility organization along prefixes of admissible constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Prefix Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accessibility is equivalent to existence of a feasible ordering for every feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite and let \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\) contain \(\varnothing\). The system satisfies accessibility if and only if every \(X\in\mathcal F\) has an ordering \(X=\{e_1,\ldots,e_k\}\) such that
\[\{e_1,\ldots,e_i\}\in\mathcal F\qquad(0\le i\le k),\]
where the prefix for \(i=0\) is \(\varnothing\). Such an ordering is called a feasible ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite feasible system is accessible exactly when every feasible set can be ordered so that all initial prefixes remain feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accessibility holds if and only if every \(X\in\mathcal F\) admits a feasible ordering.

notation.meaning: An ordering of the elements of a feasible set X.

review_flags: No source locator for the accessibility–prefix equivalence was supplied.

children.title: Continuation Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Obstructions to extending feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuation Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accessibility alone does not imply greedoid augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E=\{a,b,c\}\) and
\[\mathcal F=\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{b\},\{a,c\}\}.\]
This feasible system is accessible: each singleton deletes to \(\varnothing\), and \(\{a,c\}\) deletes \(c\) to obtain \(\{a\}\). However, for \(X=\{b\}\) and \(Y=\{a,c\}\), one has \(|X|<|Y|\) but
\[\Gamma(X)\cap(Y\setminus X)=\varnothing,\]
because neither \(\{a,b\}\) nor \(\{b,c\}\) is feasible. Thus accessibility and prefix feasibility do not by themselves guarantee the continuation property or define a greedoid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An accessible four-set system has a smaller feasible set that cannot be extended by either element of a larger feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system is accessible but violates greedoid augmentation.

notation.meaning: The feasible continuation set of X.
The smaller and larger feasible sets in the counterexample.

children.title: Antimatroid Structures
children.top_down_role: Feasible-set organization specific to antimatroids.

assumptions_latex: The family \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^E\) has ground support \(E=\bigcup_{F\in\mathcal F}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((E,\mathcal F)\) is an antimatroid exactly when it satisfies accessibility and union closure.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite feasible-set definition of an antimatroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite, loopless feasible-set formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((E,\mathcal F)\) is an antimatroid if \(\varnothing\in\mathcal F\) and the following hold. Accessibility: for every nonempty \(F\in\mathcal F\), there exists \(x\in F\) such that \(F\setminus\{x\}\in\mathcal F\). Union closure: for all \(F_1,F_2\in\mathcal F\), one has \(F_1\cup F_2\in\mathcal F\). Because \(E\) is finite and equals the union of all feasible sets, union closure also gives \(E\in\mathcal F\).

children.title: Convex Geometry Structures
children.top_down_role: Closure-system organization specific to convex geometries.

assumptions_latex: The map \(\operatorname{cl}:2^E\to2^E\) is a closure operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((E,\operatorname{cl})\) is a convex geometry exactly when empty-set closure and anti-exchange hold.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite closure-operator definition of a convex geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite anti-exchange closure formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closure operator \(\operatorname{cl}\) is extensive, isotone, and idempotent. The pair \((E,\operatorname{cl})\) is a convex geometry if \(\operatorname{cl}(\varnothing)=\varnothing\) and it satisfies anti-exchange: for every closed set \(C=\operatorname{cl}(C)\) and distinct \(x,y\in E\setminus C\),
\[y\in\operatorname{cl}(C\cup\{x\})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\notin\operatorname{cl}(C\cup\{y\}).\]
Equivalently, its closed sets form an intersection-closed family containing \(\varnothing\) and \(E\), with closure obtained by intersecting all closed supersets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex geometry is a closure system with empty-set closure and the anti-exchange property for two distinct points outside a closed set.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Geometry Structures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The anti-exchange definition fits the Convex Geometry Structures container, but it has no citation. The final equivalence sentence should also be checked against a source because intersection closure with empty and full sets alone does not characterize convex geometries without the anti-exchange condition.

children.title: Closure–Feasibility Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual viewpoints relating closure structure to feasible-set structure.

assumptions_latex: The pair \((E,\mathcal F)\) is a finite antimatroid.
The family of complementary sets is \(\mathcal C=\{E\setminus F:F\in\mathcal F\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility and closedness are complementary: \(F\in\mathcal F\iff E\setminus F\in\mathcal C\).

notation.meaning: closure induced by the closed sets

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard complement duality between finite antimatroids and convex geometries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complement duality on a fixed finite ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(\mathcal C=\{E\setminus F:F\in\mathcal F\}\). Union closure of \(\mathcal F\) makes \(\mathcal C\) intersection closed, and its closure operator is
\[\operatorname{cl}(X)=\bigcap\{C\in\mathcal C:X\subseteq C\}.\]
The resulting \((E,\operatorname{cl})\) is a convex geometry, and
\[F\in\mathcal F\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad E\setminus F\text{ is closed}.\]
Conversely, complements of the closed sets of any finite convex geometry form the feasible sets of an antimatroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementation converts feasible antimatroid sets into closed convex-geometry sets, with closure given by intersection of closed supersets; the construction also works in reverse.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure–Feasibility Duality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complement construction has the correct duality role and is standard for finite antimatroids and convex geometries, but no source or inspectable locator supports the asserted converse and induced closure structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Operator Induced by Union-Closed Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a closure operator from complements of a union-closed feasible family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(E,\mathcal F)$ be a set system such that $\varnothing\in\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal F$ is closed under union. For $A\subseteq E$, define $\tau(A):=\bigcap\{X\subseteq E:A\subseteq X,\ E\setminus X\in\mathcal F\}$. Then $\tau$ is a closure operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a union-closed feasible family containing the empty set, intersecting all supersets of a set whose complements are feasible defines a closure operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \tau\text{ is a closure operator}

children.title: Antimatroid–Convex-Geometry Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Translation between antimatroid and convex-geometry presentations.

assumptions_latex: All structures use the same finite ground set \(E\).
Antimatroids are loopless, and convex geometries satisfy \(\operatorname{cl}(\varnothing)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complementation induces mutually inverse correspondences between antimatroids and convex geometries on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bijection between finite structures, not merely an analogy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The assignments
\[\mathcal F\longmapsto\mathcal C_{\mathcal F}:=\{E\setminus F:F\in\mathcal F\}\]
and
\[\mathcal C\longmapsto\mathcal F_{\mathcal C}:=\{E\setminus C:C\in\mathcal C\}\]
are mutually inverse. Under these assignments, accessibility and union closure of \(\mathcal F\) correspond to anti-exchange and intersection closure of \(\mathcal C\), respectively. Hence antimatroid feasible-set systems on \(E\) are in bijection with convex geometries on \(E\), and applying the correspondence twice returns the original family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking complements gives a reversible, one-to-one correspondence between finite antimatroids and finite convex geometries on the same ground set.
knowledge_statements.title: Antimatroid–Convex-Geometry Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A theorem-level bijective correspondence fits this terminal container, but it lacks evidence. The componentwise claim that accessibility and union closure correspond respectively to anti-exchange and intersection closure requires source confirmation and careful formulation.

children.title: Branching Greedoids
children.top_down_role: Greedoid structures arising from rooted branching systems.

assumptions_latex: The directed graph \(D=(V,A)\\) is finite and has a distinguished root \(r\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible arborescence edge sets form the branching greedoid \((A,\mathcal F_r)\).

notation.meaning: directed graph with arc set as ground set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed, arc-ground-set version rooted at one vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_r\) consist of those \(X\subseteq A\) for which the subgraph formed by \(X\), its incident vertices, and \(r\) is an out-arborescence rooted at \(r\): every represented vertex is reachable from \(r\), every represented vertex other than \(r\) has indegree one in \(X\), and the underlying undirected graph is acyclic. Then \((A,\mathcal F_r)\) is called the branching greedoid of \((D,r)\). Its feasible sets are precisely the arc sets of partial rooted out-arborescences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed branching greedoid has as feasible sets the arc sets of partial out-arborescences rooted at a fixed vertex.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching Greedoids

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Branching Greedoids and clearly selects the directed arc-ground-set convention, but branching-greedoid conventions vary and no authoritative definition with a section or page locator is cited.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The greedoid formed by rooted arborescences is called a directed branching greedoid, and the corresponding greedoid formed by root-containing undirected trees is called an undirected branching greedoid.

children.title: Path Greedoids
children.top_down_role: Greedoid structures arising from feasible path systems.

assumptions_latex: A designated family \(\mathcal P\subseteq2^E\) represents rooted paths and satisfies greedoid accessibility and augmentation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set system \((E,\mathcal P)\) is a path greedoid under the stated rooted-path convention.

notation.meaning: family of sets represented by rooted paths

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract rooted-path system; graph conventions vary across sources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A path greedoid is a greedoid \((E,\mathcal P)\) whose feasible sets are the ground-element sets represented by admissible rooted paths in a specified path system. Thus \(\varnothing\in\mathcal P\); every nonempty \(P\in\mathcal P\) has an endpoint element \(x\) with \(P\setminus\{x\}\in\mathcal P\); and whenever \(P,Q\in\mathcal P\) with \(|P|>|Q|\), some \(x\in P\setminus Q\) satisfies \(Q\cup\{x\}\in\mathcal P\). The admissible-path model is part of the structure and cannot be replaced by arbitrary rooted paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path greedoid is a rooted-path set system satisfying accessibility and augmentation; arbitrary path families need not satisfy these axioms.
knowledge_statements.title: Path Greedoids

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected definition role fits the leaf, but the admissible rooted-path model is not defined independently of the greedoid axioms. A source is necessary to fix the intended path-greedoid convention and determine a precise noncircular statement.

children.title: Language Greedoids
children.top_down_role: Greedoid structures presented through admissible word systems.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A prefix-closed language satisfying word augmentation is a greedoid language.

notation.meaning: set of letters occurring in a word

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard feasible-word formulation of a language greedoid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simple words over a finite alphabet.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A language greedoid on \(E\) is a nonempty language \(\mathcal L\) of words with distinct letters such that every prefix of a word in \(\mathcal L\) also belongs to \(\mathcal L\), and the following augmentation property holds: whenever \(u,v\in\mathcal L\) and \(|u|>|v|\), there exists \(x\in\operatorname{supp}(u)\setminus\operatorname{supp}(v)\) for which the concatenation \(vx\in\mathcal L\). The supports of feasible words form a greedoid when membership depends only on support, while the language retains admissible ordering information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A language greedoid is a prefix-closed collection of repetition-free words satisfying an augmentation rule that appends a letter from a longer feasible word.
knowledge_statements.title: Language Greedoids

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasible-word definition has the correct role for Language Greedoids, but it has no authoritative citation. The additional qualification concerning when word supports form a greedoid should be checked against the selected language-greedoid convention.

children.title: Cross-Family Separations
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions among the branching, path, and language families.

assumptions_latex: Let \(D\) have vertices \(\{r,a,b,c\}\) and arcs \(r\to a\), \(r\to b\), and \(b\to c\).
Represent a rooted path by its set of nonroot vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family of all rooted-path vertex sets in \(D\) fails greedoid augmentation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct finite counterexample to identifying arbitrary rooted paths with greedoids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates arbitrary rooted-path families from branching and language greedoids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The rooted-path vertex sets are \(\mathcal P=\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{b\},\{b,c\}\}\). Take \(X=\{b,c\}\) and \(Y=\{a\}\). Although \(|X|>|Y|\), neither \(Y\cup\{b\}=\{a,b\}\) nor \(Y\cup\{c\}=\{a,c\}\) is the vertex set of a rooted path. Thus augmentation fails. By contrast, the arc sets of partial rooted arborescences form a branching greedoid, and feasible words require an explicit word-augmentation axiom. The three descriptions therefore cannot be identified without additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small branching digraph shows that all rooted paths need not form a greedoid, so path, branching, and language constructions require distinct hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Family Separations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed rooted-path family does fail augmentation, and a counterexample is an appropriate kind for Cross-Family Separations. However, the broader comparison among path, branching, and language families has no cited taxonomy source or inspectable locator.

assumptions_latex: Greedy starts from \(S=\varnothing\), repeatedly adding a maximum-weight feasible continuation.
Feasibility is given by the branching greedoid of the displayed rooted digraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordinary element-weight greedy can be suboptimal on a greedoid, even when every maximal feasible set has the same size.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit branching-greedoid counterexample to unrestricted weight greedy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for unrestricted additive weights and feasible-continuation greedy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the rooted digraph have arcs \(a:r\to u\), \(b:r\to v\), and \(c:v\to u\), with weights \(w(a)=10\), \(w(b)=9\), and \(w(c)=100\). Initially \(c\) is infeasible, so greedy selects \(a\), then \(b\), and returns the maximal feasible set \(\{a,b\}\) of weight \(19\). However, \(\{b,c\}\) is a rooted arborescence of weight \(109\). Hence the greedoid axioms alone do not guarantee optimality of ordinary element-weight greedy; additional objective compatibility is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A three-arc branching greedoid makes greedy choose weight 19 although another feasible basis has weight 109, showing that greedoid axioms alone are insufficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Greedoid Greedy-Optimality Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit branching-greedoid example supports the stated failure boundary and the chosen content kind is appropriate, but no authoritative source or specific locator is supplied for the greedy-optimality boundary being recorded.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Exchange Characterization of Greedy Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes universal optimality of the greedoid greedy algorithm for nonnegative modular weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(E,\mathcal F)$ be a greedoid. The greedy algorithm for greedoids finds a maximum-weight member of $\mathcal F$ for every modular weight function $c:2^E\to\mathbb R_+$ if and only if the following strong exchange property holds: for every $A\in\mathcal F$, every inclusion-maximal $B\in\mathcal F$ with $A\subseteq B$, and every $x\in E\setminus B$ such that $A\cup\{x\}\in\mathcal F$, there exists $y\in B\setminus A$ such that $A\cup\{y\}\in\mathcal F$ and $(B\setminus\{y\})\cup\{x\}\in\mathcal F$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The greedoid greedy algorithm is optimal for every nonnegative modular weight function exactly when the greedoid satisfies the stated strong exchange property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\text{greedy is optimal for every modular }c:2^E\to\mathbb R_+\bigr]\iff\bigl[\forall A,B,x\text{ as specified},\ \exists y\in B\setminus A:\ A\cup\{y\}\in\mathcal F\land(B\setminus\{y\})\cup\{x\}\in\mathcal F\bigr].

children.title: Symmetric Exchange Axiom
children.top_down_role: The symmetric exchange component of delta-matroid structure.

assumptions_latex: The feasible family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The symmetric exchange predicate characterizes delta-matroid feasible families.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: defining symmetric exchange axiom for finite delta-matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite delta-matroid feasible-set axiom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The symmetric exchange axiom is
\[\forall X,Y\in\mathcal F\;\forall e\in X\triangle Y\;\exists f\in X\triangle Y:\quad X\triangle\{e,f\}\in\mathcal F.\]
The witness \(f\) may equal \(e\); in that case \(\{e,f\}=\{e\}\). A nonempty finite set system \((E,\mathcal F)\) is a delta-matroid precisely when it satisfies this axiom. Unlike matroid basis exchange, feasible sets in \(\mathcal F\) need not have equal cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any two feasible sets and any element in their symmetric difference, toggling that element together with a suitable second differing element must preserve feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Exchange Axiom

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The symmetric exchange condition is standard, precise, and correctly placed as a condition in this axiom leaf, including the convention that the witness may equal the selected element. It nevertheless lacks a cited definition, section, theorem, or page locator.

children.title: Twist Operations
children.top_down_role: Twist transformations of feasible-set systems.

assumptions_latex: The pair \(D=(E,\mathcal F)\) is a finite set system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Twisting replaces every feasible set \(F\) by \(F\triangle A\), and twists compose by symmetric difference.

notation.meaning: twist of the set system by a subset

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard twist operation for delta-matroids and set systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Twisting on a fixed finite ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The twist of \(D=(E,\mathcal F)\) by \(A\subseteq E\) is
\[D*A:=\bigl(E,\mathcal F*A\bigr),\qquad \mathcal F*A:=\{F\triangle A:F\in\mathcal F\}.\]
Twisting does not change the ground set. For all \(A,B\subseteq E\), it satisfies
\[(D*A)*B=D*(A\triangle B),\qquad D*\varnothing=D,\qquad (D*A)*A=D.\]
Thus every twist is an involutive relabeling of feasible sets by symmetric difference.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Twisting by a subset toggles that subset in every feasible set; twists compose by symmetric difference and each twist is its own inverse.
knowledge_statements.title: Twist Operations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The twist definition and composition identities fit Twist Operations and are internally consistent, but no inspectable source supports the definition and identities.

children.title: Twist-Invariant Structure
children.top_down_role: Structural features preserved under twisting.

assumptions_latex: The pair \(D=(E,\mathcal F)\) is a finite delta-matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The twist \(D*A\) is again a delta-matroid.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical twist invariance of the symmetric exchange axiom
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural invariance, not invariance of feasible-set cardinalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(A\subseteq E\), define \(D*A=(E,\{F\triangle A:F\in\mathcal F\})\). If \(X'=X\triangle A\) and \(Y'=Y\triangle A\), then
\[X'\triangle Y'=X\triangle Y.\]
Consequently, the symmetric exchange condition for \(X,Y\in\mathcal F\) is equivalent to the symmetric exchange condition for \(X',Y'\in\mathcal F*A\). Therefore the class of delta-matroids is closed under every twist, although twisting may change the sizes and parities of individual feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Twisting preserves the symmetric exchange axiom, so every twist of a delta-matroid is again a delta-matroid, though feasible-set sizes may change.
knowledge_statements.title: Twist-Invariant Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Twist closure is the correct structural property for this leaf, but the record has no citation and includes a proof-style derivation through transformed feasible sets. A sourced statement should retain the invariance claim while removing proof text.

children.title: Parity Changes Under Twisting
children.top_down_role: Parity behavior across twist transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Parity Changes Under Twisting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity law for twisting a delta-matroid by a fixed subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(E,\mathcal F)\) be a delta-matroid and let \(X\subseteq E\). Its twist is \(D*X=(E,\{F\mathbin{\triangle}X:F\in\mathcal F\})\). For every \(F\in\mathcal F\), \[|F\mathbin{\triangle}X|\equiv |F|+|X|\pmod 2.\] Consequently, if all feasible sets of \(D\) have common parity \(\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}\), then every feasible set of \(D*X\) has parity \(\varepsilon+|X|\pmod 2\). Thus twisting preserves evenness while possibly reversing the common feasible-set parity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Twisting preserves equality of feasible-set parities; it reverses their common parity exactly when the twisting set has odd cardinality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|F\triangle X|\equiv |F|+|X|\pmod 2\), so \(D*X\) is even whenever \(D\) is even.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parity identity and property classification are mathematically appropriate, but no cited source with a specific locator supports the twist convention or terminology.

children.title: Even Delta-Matroids
children.top_down_role: Delta-matroids distinguished by uniform feasible-set parity.

knowledge_statements.title: Even Delta-Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard parity-based definition of an even delta-matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A delta-matroid \(D=(E,\mathcal F)\) is even if all its feasible sets have the same cardinality parity: \[|F|\equiv |F'|\pmod 2\qquad\text{for all }F,F'\in\mathcal F.\] Equivalently, for every pair of feasible sets, \(|F\mathbin{\triangle}F'|\) is even. The common parity may be even or odd; the adjective “even” refers to parity agreement, not to every feasible set necessarily having even cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A delta-matroid is even when all feasible sets have the same parity, which may itself be even or odd.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is even exactly when \(|F|\equiv |F'|\pmod 2\) for all \(F,F'\in\mathcal F\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and its symmetric-difference equivalence are precise and appropriate, but the record provides no inspectable citation.

children.title: Binary Delta-Matroids
children.top_down_role: Delta-matroids arising from binary representation frameworks.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Delta-Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representability by a symmetric matrix over the binary field, up to twisting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a symmetric matrix \(A\) indexed by a finite set \(E\) over \(\mathbb F_2\), define \(D(A)=(E,\mathcal F_A)\) by \[\mathcal F_A=\{X\subseteq E:A[X]\text{ is nonsingular}\},\] where the empty principal submatrix is nonsingular by convention. A delta-matroid \(D\) on \(E\) is binary if there exist such an \(A\) and a set \(T\subseteq E\) for which \(D=D(A)*T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary delta-matroid is, up to twisting, represented by the nonsingular principal submatrices of a symmetric binary matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is binary when \(D=D(A)*T\) for some \(A\) and \(T\subseteq E\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated binary-representability convention is plausible and fits the definition container, but its matrix and twist conventions require an authoritative, specifically located source.

children.title: Even Binary Delta-Matroids
children.top_down_role: The structural overlap of the even and binary classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Even Binary Delta-Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersection of the even and binary delta-matroid classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A delta-matroid \(D=(E,\mathcal F)\) is even binary if it is both even and binary: all members of \(\mathcal F\) have one common cardinality parity, and there exist a symmetric matrix \(A\) over \(\mathbb F_2\) and \(T\subseteq E\) such that \[D=D(A)*T.\] Equivalently, the class of even binary delta-matroids is the intersection of the even and binary classes; neither condition is omitted by the compound terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An even binary delta-matroid simultaneously has uniform feasible-set parity and a symmetric binary-matrix representation up to twisting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is even binary exactly when \(D\in\mathcal E\cap\mathcal B\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intersection definition fits the leaf and is internally consistent, but neither constituent convention is supported by a cited locator.

children.title: Binary Representability Separations
children.top_down_role: Boundaries between binary representability and parity restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Representability Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete witnesses separating evenness from binary representability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The even and binary classes are incomparable. The delta-matroid \(D([1])\) on \(\{e\}\), represented over \(\mathbb F_2\) by the matrix \([1]\), has feasible sets \(\varnothing\) and \(\{e\}\); hence it is binary but not even. Conversely, the bases of the uniform matroid \(U_{2,4}\), viewed as feasible sets of a delta-matroid, all have size two, so the resulting delta-matroid is even, but it is not binary-representable. Therefore \(\mathcal E\nsubseteq\mathcal B\) and \(\mathcal B\nsubseteq\mathcal E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-element matrix example is binary but not even, while the basis delta-matroid of the nonbinary matroid U₂,₄ is even but not binary.
assumptions_latex: Binary delta-matroids use symmetric-matrix representation over \(\mathbb F_2\), up to twisting.
Matroids are identified with their basis delta-matroids.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal E\nsubseteq\mathcal B\) and \(\mathcal B\nsubseteq\mathcal E\).

notation.meaning: rank-two uniform matroid on four elements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexamples appear suitable, but the claim that the basis delta-matroid of U_{2,4} is not binary even under the allowed twisting convention requires authoritative support.

children.title: Matching Delta-Matroids
children.top_down_role: Delta-matroid structures induced by matching systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching Delta-Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Delta-matroid generated by vertex sets admitting perfect matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, with loops excluded and parallel edges allowed. Its matching set system is \[D_{\mathrm{mat}}(G)=\bigl(V,\{X\subseteq V:G[X]\text{ has a perfect matching}\}\bigr),\] where \(\varnothing\) is feasible. This set system satisfies the symmetric exchange axiom and is called the matching delta-matroid of \(G\). Every feasible set has even cardinality, so \(D_{\mathrm{mat}}(G)\) is an even delta-matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The feasible sets are vertex subsets whose induced subgraphs possess perfect matchings; they form an even delta-matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{mat}}(G)\) is an even delta-matroid.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The construction is stated precisely and the definition container is appropriate, but the symmetric-exchange assertion and matching-delta-matroid terminology lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Embedded-Graph Delta-Matroids
children.top_down_role: Delta-matroid structures associated with graph embeddings.

knowledge_statements.title: Embedded-Graph Delta-Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ribbon-graphic delta-matroid defined through spanning quasi-trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite ribbon graph with edge set \(E\). A spanning ribbon subgraph \((V(G),F)\) is a spanning quasi-tree if each of its connected components has exactly one boundary component. The embedded-graph delta-matroid is \[D(G)=\bigl(E,\{F\subseteq E:(V(G),F)\text{ is a spanning quasi-tree}\}\bigr).\] Its feasible sets satisfy symmetric exchange. When \(G\) is connected and cellularly embedded in the sphere, its spanning quasi-trees are precisely its spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An embedded graph defines a delta-matroid whose feasible edge sets are spanning ribbon subgraphs having one boundary component per connected component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(G)\) is a delta-matroid, reducing to the cycle matroid in the connected plane case.

notation.meaning: edge set of a spanning ribbon subgraph

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent, but the disconnected quasi-tree convention, symmetric-exchange assertion, and plane specialization require a specifically located source.

children.title: Matching–Topology Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between matching presentations and topological graph presentations.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching–Topology Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Plane specialization via the rooted Temperley correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a connected plane graph, choose an incident root vertex \(v_0\) and root face \(f_0\), and form the bipartite incidence graph whose white vertices are \(E(G)\) and whose black vertices are \((V(G)\setminus\{v_0\})\cup(F(G)\setminus\{f_0\})\), with incidence inherited from the embedding. The rooted Temperley correspondence gives a bijection between spanning trees of \(G\) and perfect matchings of this incidence graph. Since feasible sets of the plane embedded-graph delta-matroid are spanning trees, this realizes its feasible objects through matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a rooted connected plane graph, the Temperley construction bijects its spanning trees—and hence its embedded-delta-matroid feasible sets—with perfect matchings.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite connected plane graph.
The chosen root vertex \(v_0\) is incident with the root face \(f_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\text{feasible sets of }D(G)\}\longleftrightarrow\{\text{perfect matchings of the rooted incidence graph}\}\) bijectively.

notation.meaning: incident root vertex and root face

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation claim is appropriately scoped to the rooted plane case, but the exact incidence-graph construction and bijection depend on a Temperley-correspondence variant that must be cited precisely.

children.title: Representation-Interface Limitations
children.top_down_role: Limits of matching-based and embedding-based representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Interface Limitations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of adjacency nonsingularity to capture matching existence over the binary field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G\) with adjacency matrix \(A_G\) over \(\mathbb F_2\), nonsingularity of \(A_G[X]\) detects whether the number of perfect matchings of \(G[X]\) is odd, not merely nonzero. Hence the matching delta-matroid need not equal \(D(A_G)\). For \(G=C_4\) and \(X=V(G)\), the induced graph has two perfect matchings, so \(X\) is matching-feasible, whereas \(\det A_G[X]=0\) in \(\mathbb F_2\), so \(X\notin\mathcal F_{A_G}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary adjacency determinants record perfect-matching parity, so they can miss feasible sets having a positive even number of perfect matchings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{mat}}(G)\) cannot generally be identified with the principal-nonsingularity system \(D(A_G)\).

notation.meaning: principal adjacency submatrix indexed by X

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Valuated matroids and induced matroid base families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines valuated matroids by valuated simultaneous exchange and records the support, maximizer, modular-perturbation, and polynomial-matrix consequences stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let V be finite and let \omega:2^V\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}, with nonempty support \mathcal B=\{J\subseteq V\mid \omega(J)\neq-\infty\}. The pair (V,\omega) is a valuated matroid if, for every J,J'\in\mathcal B and i\in J\setminus J', there exists j\in J'\setminus J such that J-i+j,J'+i-j\in\mathcal B and \omega(J)+\omega(J')\leq\omega(J-i+j)+\omega(J'+i-j). Then \mathcal B is a matroid base family. Moreover, \operatorname*{argmax}\omega is a matroid base family, and for every p\in\mathbb R^V the function \omega[-p](J)=\omega(J)-\sum_{j\in J}p(j) is a valuated matroid whose maximizers form a matroid base family. For a polynomial matrix A(s), setting \omega(J)=\deg\det A[J] for nonzero square minors and \omega(J)=-\infty otherwise yields this valuated-exchange property when the support is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valuated matroid is a function with nonempty support satisfying valuated simultaneous basis exchange. Its support and its maximizers, including maximizers after any modular perturbation, are matroid base families. Degrees of nonzero square minors of a polynomial matrix provide such a valuation.
assumptions_latex: p\in\mathbb R^V\text{ for the modular-perturbation assertion}.
A(s)\text{ is a polynomial matrix and the degree construction has nonempty support for the realization assertion}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \omega\text{ satisfies valuated simultaneous exchange, and }\mathcal B,\operatorname*{argmax}\omega,\operatorname*{argmax}\omega[-p]\text{ are matroid base families for every }p\in\mathbb R^V.

source_evidence.locator: Convex Functions with Combinatorial Structures / 2.4. Matroids / Definition 2.4-extra-3

knowledge_statements.title: Valuated Basis Exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization convention for finite valuated matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite, let \(r\geq 0\), and let \(p:\binom{E}{r}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) have nonempty finite domain \(\mathcal B=\{B:p(B)<+\infty\}\). The function \(p\) is a valuated matroid if, for every \(B,B'\in\mathcal B\) and \(i\in B\setminus B'\), there exists \(j\in B'\setminus B\) such that \[p(B)+p(B')\geq p(B-i+j)+p(B'-j+i).\] Its finite domain is then the basis family of an ordinary rank-\(r\) matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valuated matroid assigns extended-real costs to equal-size sets and satisfies a two-basis exchange inequality; its finite sets are matroid bases.
assumptions_latex: The finite domain of \(p\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) satisfies valuated basis exchange, and \(\operatorname{dom}p\) is a matroid basis family.

notation.meaning: sets on which p is finite

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally consistent under its minimization convention and fits the topic, but the exchange-sign convention and induced matroid-basis assertion require a specific source locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Exchange Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-to-global optimality for valuated matroid minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p:\binom{E}{r}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a valuated matroid in the minimization convention, and let \(B\in\operatorname{dom}p\). If \[p(B)\leq p(B-i+j)\] for every \(i\in B\) and \(j\in E\setminus B\) with \(B-i+j\in\operatorname{dom}p\), then \(B\) is a global minimizer: \[p(B)=\min\{p(B'):B'\in\operatorname{dom}p\}.\] Thus the absence of a strictly improving feasible single-element exchange is an exact optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a valuated matroid, any feasible basis with no improving one-element exchange is globally cost-minimal.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a finite-ground-set valuated matroid under the minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local exchange optimality of \(B\) implies global optimality of \(B\).

notation.meaning: single-element exchange of i for j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local-to-global theorem is precise and appropriately classified, but no cited theorem or section supports the stated hypotheses and conclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Tropical Linear-Space Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuit-minimum representation of the tropical linear space of a valuated matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p:\binom{E}{r}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a rank-\(r\) valuated matroid satisfying the tropical Plücker relations in the minimum convention. Its tropical linear space is \[L(p)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E:\min_{i\in S}\bigl(p(S\setminus\{i\})+x_i\bigr)\text{ is attained at least twice for every }S\in\binom{E}{r+1}\right\}.\] Terms with value \(+\infty\) are ignored; if all terms are infinite, the condition is vacuous. Adding a constant multiple of the all-ones vector to \(x\) preserves membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tropical linear space consists of vectors for which every valuated circuit expression attains its minimum at least twice.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a rank-\(r\) valuated matroid in the minimum convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in L(p)\) exactly when every displayed tropical circuit minimum is attained at least twice.

notation.meaning: tropical linear space associated with p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the node, but the sign convention, treatment of infinite circuit terms, and vacuous all-infinite case require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Oriented-Matroid Boundary
children.top_down_role: Only the matroid-facing representation and realizability interfaces are retained.

children.title: Signed Circuits
children.top_down_role: Circuit-level signed representations of oriented matroids.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family \(\mathcal C\) is the signed-circuit system of an oriented matroid on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite oriented matroids in signed-circuit form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A signed-circuit system on \(E\) is a nonempty family \(\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,+,-\}^{E}\) such that: \(0\notin\mathcal C\); if \(X\in\mathcal C\), then \(-X\in\mathcal C\); if \(X,Y\in\mathcal C\) and \(\operatorname{supp}(X)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(Y)\), then \(X=Y\) or \(X=-Y\); and if \(X,Y\in\mathcal C\), \(X\ne-Y\), and \(e\in S(X,Y)\), then some \(Z\in\mathcal C\) satisfies \(Z_e=0\) and, for every \(f\in E\), \(Z_f\in\{0,X_f,Y_f\}\). The supports of members of \(\mathcal C\) are the circuits of the underlying matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Signed circuits are nonzero, sign-symmetric, support-minimal sign vectors satisfying circuit elimination; their supports are exactly the circuits of the underlying matroid.
knowledge_statements.title: Signed Circuits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The signed-circuit axiomatization is mathematically standard, locally appropriate, and correctly classified as a definition, but it has no citation or inspectable locator. An authoritative oriented-matroid source is required before the exact elimination formulation can enter candidate review.

children.title: Signed Cocircuits
children.top_down_role: Cocircuit-level signed representations of oriented matroids.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is a finite oriented matroid on ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C^{*}(\mathcal M)=\mathcal C(\mathcal M^{*})\), and their supports are the cocircuits of the underlying matroid.

notation.meaning: signed circuits of the dual, called signed cocircuits

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: signed cocircuits are defined through oriented-matroid duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual definition for finite oriented matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The signed cocircuits of \(\mathcal M\) are, by definition, the signed circuits of \(\mathcal M^{*}\): \[\mathcal C^{*}(\mathcal M):=\mathcal C(\mathcal M^{*}).\] Consequently \(\mathcal C^{*}(\mathcal M)\) is closed under sign reversal and satisfies the signed-circuit incomparability and elimination axioms. Its supports are precisely the cocircuits of the underlying matroid of \(\mathcal M\), equivalently the circuits of the dual underlying matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Signed cocircuits of an oriented matroid are the signed circuits of its dual, and their supports are the ordinary cocircuits of the underlying matroid.
knowledge_statements.title: Signed Cocircuits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual characterization of signed cocircuits is standard, agrees with the node context, and is appropriately classified as duality. No source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Covector Systems
children.top_down_role: Covector presentations and their structural organization.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A family satisfying the displayed axioms is the covector system of an oriented matroid on \(E\).

notation.meaning: composition, taking the first nonzero coordinate

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard covector axioms for finite oriented matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covector axiomatization using composition and strong elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A covector system is a family \(\mathcal V\subseteq\{0,+,-\}^{E}\) satisfying \(0\in\mathcal V\), \(X\in\mathcal V\Rightarrow -X\in\mathcal V\), and \(X,Y\in\mathcal V\Rightarrow X\circ Y\in\mathcal V\). It also satisfies strong elimination: for every \(X,Y\in\mathcal V\) and \(e\in S(X,Y)\), there exists \(Z\in\mathcal V\) with \(Z_e=0\) and \(Z_f=(X\circ Y)_f\) for every \(f\notin S(X,Y)\). These axioms define the covectors of an oriented matroid on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Covectors form a sign-symmetric family containing zero, closed under composition, and satisfying strong elimination on coordinates where two sign vectors conflict.
knowledge_statements.title: Covector Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed covector axioms are standard and the definition fits the exact leaf, but the strong-elimination formulation has no cited authoritative source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Topes
children.top_down_role: Maximal covector structures and their combinatorial role.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal V\) is the covector system of an oriented matroid on finite ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The topes are exactly the maximal elements of \(\mathcal V\) under \(\leq\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard maximal-covector definition of a tope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition valid with loops; loopless simplification stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the specialization order by \(X\leq Y\) when \(X_e\in\{0,Y_e\}\) for every \(e\in E\). A tope is a covector maximal in this order: \[\mathcal T:=\{T\in\mathcal V: T\leq Y\in\mathcal V\Rightarrow Y=T\}.\] If the oriented matroid is loopless, then its topes are precisely its zero-free covectors, so \(\mathcal T=\mathcal V\cap\{+,-\}^{E}\). In the presence of loops, every covector, including every tope, is zero on each loop.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tope is a maximal covector in the specialization order. In a loopless oriented matroid, topes are exactly the covectors having no zero coordinate.
knowledge_statements.title: Topes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximal-covector definition and the loopless qualification are precise and locally appropriate. The record nevertheless lacks the required citation and specific locator.

children.title: Orthogonality Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Compatibility relations across circuit, cocircuit, covector, and tope presentations.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is the signed-circuit system of an oriented matroid on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal V=\mathcal C^{\perp}\), and \(\mathcal C^{*}\subseteq\mathcal C^{\perp}\).

notation.meaning: coordinatewise sign product set after deleting zeros
orthogonal complement of a sign-vector family

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard orthogonality characterization of covectors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-vector orthogonality linking circuits, cocircuits, and covectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sign vectors \(X,Y\in\{0,+,-\}^{E}\), define \(X\perp Y\) when \(P(X,Y)=\varnothing\) or \(P(X,Y)=\{+,-\}\). The covector system associated with \(\mathcal C\) is the orthogonal complement \[\mathcal V=\mathcal C^{\perp}:=\{Y\in\{0,+,-\}^{E}:Y\perp X\text{ for every }X\in\mathcal C\}.\] In particular, every signed circuit is orthogonal to every signed cocircuit: \(X\perp Y\) for all \(X\in\mathcal C\) and \(Y\in\mathcal C^{*}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two sign vectors are orthogonal when their common nonzero coordinates exhibit both product signs, or none. Covectors are precisely the sign vectors orthogonal to every circuit.
knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonality Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orthogonality definition and characterization of covectors are standard, internally consistent, and suitable for this interface leaf. No authoritative source or specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Realizable Oriented Matroids
children.top_down_role: Oriented-matroid structures admitting geometric realization.

assumptions_latex: \(A=(a_e)_{e\in E}\) is a real vector configuration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting signed-circuit and covector systems define a realizable oriented matroid on \(E\).

notation.meaning: row space of the configuration matrix

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard real-vector representation of oriented matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Realizability by a finite real vector configuration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An oriented matroid on \(E\) is realizable over \(\mathbb R\) if some real matrix \(A\), whose columns are indexed by \(E\), represents it. Concretely, its signed circuits are the support-minimal nonzero vectors among \(\{\operatorname{sgn}(z):z\in\ker A\}\), and its covectors are \[\mathcal V=\{\operatorname{sgn}(A^{\mathsf T}y):y\in\mathbb R^{r}\}=\{\operatorname{sgn}(w):w\in\operatorname{row}(A)\}.\] Thus the underlying matroid is the linear-dependence matroid of the columns of \(A\), while the signs retain the orientations of minimal dependencies and linear functionals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A realizable oriented matroid comes from real vectors: minimal signed kernel dependencies are its circuits, and signs of row-space vectors are its covectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Realizable Oriented Matroids

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The kernel-circuit and row-space-covector representation is mathematically appropriate and correctly classified as a representation. It requires a cited oriented-matroid source with a specific section, theorem, definition, or page locator.

children.title: Nonrealizable Oriented Matroids
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial structures outside geometric realizability.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is an oriented matroid on a finite labeled ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is nonrealizable precisely when no real matrix has its signed-circuit system.

notation.meaning: signed-circuit family of the oriented matroid

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nonrealizability is the negation of real representability
removed incorrect comparison with underlying-matroid nonrepresentability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonrealizability over the real field on a fixed labeled ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The oriented matroid \(\mathcal M\) is nonrealizable over \(\mathbb R\) if there is no real matrix \(A\), with columns indexed by \(E\), for which \[\mathcal C(\mathcal M)=\min_{\operatorname{supp}}\{\operatorname{sgn}(z):z\in\ker A,\ z\ne0\},\] where \(\min_{\operatorname{supp}}\) selects the nonzero sign vectors having inclusion-minimal support. Equivalently, no real vector configuration on \(E\) has the same oriented dependence data as \(\mathcal M\). The underlying unoriented matroid may nevertheless be representable over \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oriented matroid is nonrealizable when no real vector configuration reproduces its signed minimal dependencies; its underlying unoriented matroid may still be representable.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonrealizable Oriented Matroids

children.title: Oriented-Matroid Programming
children.top_down_role: Programming structures formulated in the oriented-matroid setting.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is an oriented matroid on \(E\sqcup\{f,g\}\).
The distinguished elements \(f\) and \(g\) are respectively the objective and infinity elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The triple \((\mathcal M,g,f)\), together with its feasible covectors and improving pivots, defines an oriented-matroid program.
review_flags: exact pivot convention requires authoritative oriented-matroid programming source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covector form of finite oriented-matroid programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An oriented-matroid program is a triple \((\mathcal M,g,f)\). Its feasible covectors are \[\mathcal F:=\{X\in\mathcal V(\mathcal M):X_g=+,\ X_e\in\{0,+\}\text{ for every }e\in E\}.\] A combinatorial simplex procedure starts from a feasible cocircuit, moves through adjacent feasible cocircuits by pivots whose orientation is improving with respect to \(f\), and stops when no improving pivot exists or when a prescribed infeasibility or unboundedness sign certificate is encountered. The output is respectively an optimal feasible cocircuit, an infeasibility certificate, or an unboundedness certificate, all expressed solely through oriented-matroid sign data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oriented-matroid programming replaces linear constraints, objectives, and simplex pivots by covector feasibility, objective signs, adjacent cocircuit pivots, and combinatorial certificates.
knowledge_statements.title: Oriented-Matroid Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record blends a definition of an oriented-matroid program with an informal simplex algorithm and three certificate outcomes. The exact feasibility convention, feasible-cocircuit notion, pivot orientation, and terminal certificates depend on authoritative conventions. A specific oriented-matroid programming source is needed before the mathematical statement and whether algorithm is the correct terminal kind can be settled.

children.title: Programming–Realizability Interface
children.top_down_role: Dependence of programming behavior on realizability regimes.

assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal M,g,f)\) is represented by a real vector or hyperplane configuration.
The associated linear program uses the same distinguished infinity and objective elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility, improving pivots, optimality, infeasibility, and unboundedness agree in the oriented-matroid and linear programs.

notation.meaning: covector of a point or face in the realization

review_flags: exact realization and pivot correspondence requires authoritative oriented-matroid programming source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between realizable oriented-matroid programs and linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a realizable oriented-matroid program \((\mathcal M,g,f)\), choose a real representation and form the corresponding linear program. Covector signs encode which constraints are tight or satisfied, the condition \(X_g=+\) selects the affine chart, and the sign at \(f\) orients objective improvement. Under this correspondence, feasible cocircuits represent basic feasible solutions, adjacent-cocircuit pivots represent simplex pivots, and the oriented-matroid terminal sign conditions coincide with linear-program optimality, infeasibility, or unboundedness certificates. Hence oriented-matroid programming extends the combinatorial pivot structure of linear programming beyond realizable instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the oriented matroid is realizable, its feasible cocircuits and pivots match basic feasible solutions and simplex pivots of an associated linear program.
knowledge_statements.title: Programming–Realizability Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed correspondence is plausible but broad: the realization model, nondegeneracy assumptions, pivot convention, and precise optimality, infeasibility, and unboundedness sign conditions are not specified. An authoritative oriented-matroid programming locator is required to determine the exact valid formulation.
